problem: False stress in the stress lesson itself. By the rule three paragraphs up, a word ending in a vowel stresses the second-to-last syllable, so unaccented Bogota reads bo-GO-ta, never BO-go-ta. A learner who is trying to absorb the rule is told the opposite of what it predicts.
reason: The stress rule in this same script makes unaccented Bogota bo-GO-ta, and the new line agrees with yourTurn[0].why. Nothing else in the lesson leans on the old wrong stress.
quote: Without the mark, a Spanish reader says BO-go-ta. The mark is part of the spelling, and the checker reads it like a Bogotano would.
replacement: Without the mark, a Spanish reader says bo-GO-ta, stress on the second-to-last syllable. The mark is part of the spelling, and the checker reads it like a Bogotano would.

problem: First contact with agreement is framed entirely as sex (man or woman). Every example, Read and Pick, Your Turn and pitfall in the script is about people: 0 of the 28 examples and practice items agree with an inanimate noun. An English speaker leaves with "the a is for women", which undoes the gender lesson ("It's a label, not a meaning") and gives no model for la casa es pequena or el pan esta listo, la leche esta lista.
reason: Real, and LA1-005 gives it a model sentence. I keep the first reviewer's fix for el agua but say the noun's label, the course's own word from g:gender-articles ("It's a label, not a meaning"), since gender so far appears only in small print; the whys that say for a woman stay true because they are about people.
quote:
A describing word matches the person or thing it describes: a man or a woman, one or more.

Words ending in *o* switch to *a* for a woman: *cansado*, *cansada*; *colombiano*, *colombiana*.
replacement:
A describing word matches the noun it describes: masculine or feminine, one or more. With people, that usually means man or woman. With things, it goes by the noun's label: *el pan está listo*, *la leche está lista*.

Words ending in *o* switch to *a* for anything feminine: *cansado*, *cansada*; *colombiano*, *colombiana*.

problem: Me gusta plus a named person commonly means attraction, and in Colombia it is read that way by default. The script drills it with no warning (readAndPick[0] Me gusta Tomas, [1] Te gusta Mariana), and the fix for liking someone as a person, me cae bien, arrives at u15 without mentioning the trap either. An English speaker will say Me gusta tu hermana to a friend and mean something innocent.
reason: The trap is real (usage, from memory) and the first reviewer was right to move it out of smallPrint into the rule. But about a person fails on Me gusta Shakira, so I narrowed it to someone you know; readAndPick[0] and [1] can stay, since English like carries the same ambiguity.
quote: And never put *yo* in front: it's *me gusta*, not *yo gusto*.
replacement:
And never put *yo* in front: it's *me gusta*, not *yo gusto*.

One warning: about someone you know, *me gusta* usually means you're attracted to them. For things, places and activities it's always safe.

problem: The rule says -a is usually feminine and lists one exception. The large family in -ma (el problema, el idioma, el tema, el sistema, el programa, el clima) is never explained anywhere in the 916 scripts; a scan finds only the passing "a masculine noun like problema" in g:indefinites. La problema is the signature English-speaker error, and the node es for this very lesson contains la mano, which the script also never mentions.
reason: Real, and the graph note for this node asks for it. The first reviewer's text stands: many leaves room for la cama and la forma, A few counts honestly with agua in the next sentence, and it absorbs LC-033, which should not also go into smallPrint.
quote: Two surprises this week: *el día* is masculine.
replacement: A few surprises this week: *el día* and many words in *-ma*, like *el problema* and *el idioma* (language), are masculine. *La mano* (hand) and *la foto* are feminine.

problem: None of the six examples shows agreement with a thing, though the title promises "people and things". Swap one in so the rule above is demonstrated.
reason: All six examples are about people although the title promises things, and this swap shows the pair used in the rule by LA1-002. Both the es and en fields of examples[3] change; yourTurn[4] is still derivable from the rule.
quote: ¿Estás ocupada, Vale?
replacement: El pan está listo y la leche está lista. = The bread is ready and the milk is ready.

problem: Here the learner writes es alta and esta cansada side by side, and the Personal task asks for both, yet the es/esta split with adjectives waits until g:ser-estar-adjectives in u15. For thirteen units the only guidance is the "lasting stuff" line in p:es-tiene-lleva. One sentence of the portrait/snapshot model now prevents the permanent/temporary folk rule from filling the gap.
reason: Overstated: g:estar-location-states already gives "how someone is right now" two days earlier, and the Personal task names it. The gap is real only for es with a describing word; amended because es alta never appears in this script, while es amable and está cansada both do. The model matches the title of g:ser-estar-adjectives.
quote: Teachers call this adjective agreement: an adjective agrees in gender and number with its noun.
replacement: Teachers call this adjective agreement: an adjective agrees in gender and number with its noun. You'll notice *es amable* but *está cansada*: *es* says what someone is like, *está* how they are right now. That gets its own lesson later.

problem: The example is the classic case where the progressive is natural. "I'm working at a café these days" is exactly Estoy trabajando en un cafe, a temporary state of affairs; Latin American speakers use it freely. The learner is taught to reject good Spanish, and the course itself breaks the rule: u14-0056 Estoy aprendiendo espanol, por eso escribo mensajes largos; u08-0235 No estoy trabajando hoy.
reason: Right: Estoy trabajando en un café is the normal reading for a temporary situation (teaching sources agree; Butt and Benjamin from memory), and the graph note itself says right-now/temporary. Amended to add -iendo, because the example that follows is aprendiendo; the form is met in u08-0210.
quote: For what you do in general, use the plain present: I'm working at a café these days is *Trabajo en un café*. Plans too: I'm going to Medellín tomorrow is *Mañana voy a Medellín*. Keep *estoy* plus *-ando* for right now, as you speak.
replacement: For what you do in general, use the plain present: I work at a café is *Trabajo en un café*. Plans too: I'm going to Medellín tomorrow is *Mañana voy a Medellín*. Keep *estoy* plus *-ando* or *-iendo* for something in progress: right now, or going on around now for a while, like *Estoy aprendiendo español*.

problem: Same over-narrow test as g:estar-gerund, stated as the decision rule for the whole contrast. It rejects Estoy leyendo un libro muy bueno said at lunch, or Estoy aprendiendo espanol. The real trap is habits, timetables and plans, which is what the English -ing wrongly invites.
reason: The test wrongly rejects Estoy leyendo un libro muy bueno said at lunch, and u14-0056. Amended to the shorter habit, timetable or plan test, which says the same thing without "around now" clashing with "right as you speak" one paragraph above.
quote: Ask yourself: is it happening at this very moment? If not, drop the *estoy*.
replacement: Ask yourself: is it a habit, a timetable or a plan? If so, drop the *estoy*.

problem: False as stated. Indirect objects are often things: A la sopa le falta sal, Le puse sal a la sopa, Le cambie el aceite al carro. The course itself teaches this in p:le-falta-sal and p:quedar-faltar-sobrar, so a later band has to undo the word "only". The same fact would also block the everyday ponle sal.
reason: False as stated: A la sopa le falta sal, which p:le-falta-sal teaches later in the course. For now keeps the A1 guidance and drops the absolute that a later band would have to undo.
quote: The new ones are *le* and *les*, and they ignore gender: *le* is a man, a woman or *usted*. They are only ever for people.
replacement: The new ones are *le* and *les*, and they ignore gender: *le* is a man, a woman or *usted*. For now, use them for people.

problem: Not always. With hay que the pronoun cannot go in front (Hay que hacerlo, never Lo hay que hacer), and the same holds for me gusta verla and after a preposition (para verte). A learner told "always safe" will generalise. Corpus check: "lo/la hay que" occurs 0 times in scripts, story, scenes, bank and writing; "hay que" plus enclitic occurs 78 times.
reason: DPD, pronombres personales átonos: Hay que pedírselo, not *Se lo hay que pedir (seen in a search extract; rae.es refused direct fetch), and the course has 0 lo/la hay que. The claim's gustar and para examples are weak, but hay que alone decides it, and with estar the fronted position is safe, as the replacement says.
quote: In front of the first verb is always safe: *¿Me estás…?*
replacement: In front of *estás* is the safe spot here: *¿Me estás…?*

problem: The rule says any verb plus infinitive gives a free choice. Hay que is a verb plus infinitive the learner has used since u03, and it allows only the glued position. Add the one exception they will actually hit.
reason: The rule offers a free choice for any verb plus infinitive and hay que does not allow it (DPD as in LA1-010). Moved to the end of the rule, since right before "The same goes for estoy" it would read as if that carried the restriction; dropped "you already know", because the learner knows hay que but not this exception.
quote: *No lo puedo creer*, *No puedo creerlo*.
replacement: *No lo puedo creer*, *No puedo creerlo*. One exception to all this: *hay que* gives no choice. It always glues on: *Hay que hacerlo*.

problem: Bogotanos say el TransMilenio or just TransMilenio, never la. The corpus has el TransMilenio 16 times, al TransMilenio 6, del TransMilenio 2, and la TransMilenio only here.
reason: This is the only feminine use against 24 masculine ones (el, al, del) in the corpus, and the bare form also occurs; the system is el sistema and Bogotá usage is masculine. The English needs no change.
quote: Siga derecho dos cuadras. Tome la TransMilenio. Pasen, sigan.
replacement: Siga derecho dos cuadras. Tome el TransMilenio. Pasen, sigan.

problem: Calling fue "a description" collides with the next lesson, g:imperfect-states: "For describing, use *era*" and "*El sábado fue un desastre* sums up an event". The learner gets contradictory labels for the same sentence two units apart.
reason: The contradiction is real: g:imperfect-states says fue sums up an event and "for describing, use era". The claim's wording collides again, because yourTurn[4] of that script says "What someone was is era", so amended to the next lesson's own phrase.
quote: *Fue un desastre*: a description, so was.
replacement: *Fue un desastre*: it sums up an event, so was.

problem: The rule and its test ("if the answer is a place... reach for estar") have no exception, and the Your Turn line says "A place is a where, so it's está, not es." reason: The exception is needed: the bank has ¿La fiesta es en el café o en el parque? at u03-0442, while p:event-ser-en waits until u17 d6. Amended only to remove the double colon.
quote: Teachers call this *estar* for location and states.
replacement: Teachers call this *estar* for location and states. One exception you'll meet soon: an event takes *es* even when you name a place, as in *La fiesta es en el café*.

problem: Stated as an absolute and false for events, which the same unit range practises: u05-0933 La fiesta fue en casa de mi tio; u09-0691 Hoy el almuerzo es en casa de Gloria. A2 has to undo the word "never".
reason: False for events: u05-0933 La fiesta fue en casa de mi tío, u09-0691 Hoy el almuerzo es en casa de Gloria. The replacement keeps the point for places and things and is compatible with LA1-014.
quote: And location is never *es*.
replacement: And a place or a thing never takes *es* for where it is.

problem: Tagged g:hace-ago, but this is hace with a present verb meaning "for" (duration). replacement: Vine aquí hace un rato. = I came here a while ago.

problem: This and readAndPick[0] (Me gusta Tomas) model the crush reading as the neutral "like". Replace both with places or things that still test who pleases whom. A person is not needed to test direction.
