A person is what makes the reversal distractor (Tomás likes me) credible, so swapping in places weakens the direction test, and the claim offers no replacement.
quote: ¿Te gusta Mariana?

problem: The test fails on the commonest sentences: I feel bad is Me siento mal, That's good/fine is Esta bien, That's bad/wrong is Esta mal. The script's own card gives Estoy mal as "I'm not doing well", and u02-0314 uses esta mal for "wrong". The learner who follows the test produces me siento malo. The model should be what the word modifies, not what English says.
reason: The test yields *me siento malo and fails on the script's own Estoy mal and Está bien. The replacement keys on what the word does, and Estoy mal rather than Me siento mal is correct for this level, because u02 d8 precedes the reflexives at u09.
quote: A quick test: if English says good or bad, use *bueno* or *malo*. If English says well or badly, use *bien* or *mal*.
replacement: A quick test: if it describes a thing or a person, use *bueno* or *malo*. If it says how something is done, or how someone is doing, use *bien* or *mal*. So I feel bad is *Estoy mal*, even though English says bad.

problem: A learner will apply this to the job sentences they most need and produce Soy un profesor de ingles, Soy un ingeniero civil. Classifying additions keep the bare noun: Soy profesor de espanol (bank u01-0242, same unit), Es ingeniero civil, Es profesor universitario. The article returns with opinion or description: Es un medico muy bueno, Es un medico excelente.
reason: Only when you add something wrongly bans Soy profesor de español (u01-0242). Sources agree that an evaluative brings un back (Es un médico muy bueno); bare classifying additions rest on the Nueva gramática from memory. Es un médico colombiano in the examples still fits a description of the person.
quote: *Un* or *una* comes back only when you add something about the person, because then you're describing what kind: *Es un médico colombiano.*
replacement: *Un* or *una* comes back when you add an opinion or a description of the person: *Es un médico muy bueno.* Saying what kind of job keeps it bare: *Soy profesor de español.*

problem: Marked wrong, but it is acceptable Spanish in the ordinary biographical frame (Es escritor colombiano, Es medico colombiano). The real error is the bare noun with an evaluative: Es medico muy bueno. Also accept Es ingeniero colombiano in yourTurn[6].
reason: Es médico colombiano is the bio-style bare attribute (Nueva gramática from memory, not settled by search), so marking it wrong overreaches, while Es médico muy bueno is wrong beyond dispute and fits LA1-022. Replace the whole pitfalls[2] object, and also add Es ingeniero colombiano. to yourTurn[6].accept.
quote: Es médico colombiano.
replacement: {"wrong":"Es médico muy bueno.","right":"Es un médico muy bueno.","why":"With an opinion about him, *un* comes back."}

problem: Over-broad. Es dificil de aprender is correct when "it" is the thing being learned: El ruso es dificil de aprender. The course says so later: u39-0263 Es dificil de aprender?, u39-0271 Este tema es dificil de explicar. The rule only applies when the verb has its own object, as the pitfall shows.
reason: Es difícil de aprender is correct when the thing learned is the subject: u39-0263, u39-0271 and x:dificil-de-es-dificil. The replacement narrows the warning to the verb with its own object, matching pitfalls[0].
quote: No to: the verb follows straight on. Not *es difícil de aprender*.
replacement: No to: the verb follows straight on. Not *es difícil de aprender idiomas*.

problem: False for the course's own city. Coger is ordinary and clean in Colombia: coger el bus, coger un taxi, coger TransMilenio. It is rude in Mexico, Argentina and elsewhere, so tomar is a sound recommendation for neutral Spanish, but the reason given is wrong and Cojo el bus should not be presented as an error a Bogotano would hear as foreign.
reason: False for the course's own city: an El Tiempo headline reads "paseo millonario tras coger taxi en Zona T", and the vulgar sense in Mexico and Argentina is well documented. The strike-through stays because the course produces neutral tomar, but the why is now honest; p:dar-un-rodeo and p:agarrar-velocidad carry the same overclaim.
quote: In Latin America you *tomar* the bus. *Coger* is the Spain word, and best avoided here.
replacement: *Tomar* works everywhere. Colombians say *coger* too, but in Mexico and Argentina it's a rude word, so *tomo el bus* is the safe habit.

problem: True only as an option for yes/no questions. Spanish does invert: the same script accepts Es usted de Cali, g:present-ar readAndPick[8] is Trabaja usted en Bogota, and p:question-word-order requires the verb before the subject (Donde vive Vale). The first lesson plants a blanket claim the learner must unlearn in the next unit.
reason: False for question-word questions (Dónde vive Vale needs the verb before the subject) and contradicted by this script's own accepted ¿Es usted de Cali? The replacement limits the claim to what is true and keeps the example.
quote: Questions don't swap the words round the way English does. *¿Eres de Bogotá?* is the statement with question marks, and the first one is upside down.
replacement: A yes-or-no question doesn't have to swap any words round. *¿Eres de Bogotá?* is the statement with question marks, and the first one is upside down.

problem: Glossed as a pure "should", then in the next paragraph no debes is "mustn't", which is stronger than the positive. The bank uses it for all of them: u09-0439 No debo comer pan = shouldn't, u10-0908 debo pagar = have to, u10-1118 Debemos cerrar = have to. Deber expresses duty; the softer "should" of advice properly belongs to deberias, which comes later.
reason: g:deber-modal readAndPick[1] marks must correct and should wrong for the exact sentence glossed should here, and the bank uses debo for have to (u10-0908). Must or should fits both ends, and the wording echoes x:tener-que-deber ("a duty or what is right"). Butt and Benjamin from memory.
quote: *deber*: should, the advice word. *Debes ir al médico.*
replacement: *deber*: must or should, what's the right thing to do. *Debes ir al médico.*

problem: As stated the rule produces *page from pagar and *busce from buscar. The script shows only cruzar, in a pitfall, yet bank u13-0680 has Pague en la caja. The spelling fix is already known from g:preterite-spelling-stem (pague, busque, empece), so one clause ties it together.
reason: As written the rule yields *page and *busce, while the bank has Pague at u13-0680. g:preterite-spelling-stem at u11 d3 comes before this script at u13 d3 and its yourTurn already has Pagué, so the pointer is to known material.
quote: *-ar* verbs take *e*: *toma* becomes *tome*, *espera* becomes *espere*.
replacement: *-ar* verbs take *e*: *toma* becomes *tome*, *espera* becomes *espere*. Spelling keeps the sound, as in *pagué*: *pague*, *busque*, *cruce*.

problem: Y alone or word-final is a vowel. The learner has already met y (and), soy, muy, hay, and the Read and Pick line in this script contains Y Vale. The rule as written predicts "yeh" for and.
reason: Conjunction y and word-final y are vowels, and the current rule predicts "yeh" for the ¿Y Vale? line in this very script. The replacement matches the soy/boy tip in g:ser-identity; it takes the rule to about 165 words, over the 150 guideline, which no gate enforces.
quote: *ll* and *y* sound like the y in "yes".
replacement: *ll* and *y* sound like the y in "yes", but *y* alone or at the end of a word is a vowel: *y* (and) is "ee", and *soy* rhymes with "boy".

problem: Omits lo/la/los/las as "you" for usted and ustedes. The only statement in the whole course is at B1 (p:perdona-que-interrumpa), yet A1 uses it: bank u13-0701 Esperen un momento, ya los atiendo, and the chunk Que pena molestarlo. In a course where usted is everywhere this is the reading a learner most needs and cannot derive.
reason: The forms are correct and usted is everywhere in the course, yet lo, la for usted are unstated until B1 while u13-0701 has ya los atiendo. It parallels the usted line in g:indirect-objects. The quote spans line breaks in the rule, which is why the machine check missed it.
quote:
*lo*: him, or it for an *el* word (*el contrato*)
*la*: her, or it for a *la* word (*la cuenta*)
*los*: them (men, mixed groups, *los* words)
*las*: them (women, *las* words)
replacement:
*lo*: him, you (a man you call *usted*), or it for an *el* word (*el contrato*)
*la*: her, you (a woman you call *usted*), or it for a *la* word (*la cuenta*)
*los*: them or you all (men, mixed groups, *los* words)
*las*: them or you all (women, *las* words)

problem: No reusable model. The title and node promise me levanto, te duchas, se acuesta, but no example or practice item uses them; the rule says "You'll get those verbs later this week". What is drilled is irse, sentirse, encontrarse, parecerse, none of which shows the core idea that the action comes back on the doer. The contrast that creates the model (lavo el carro / me lavo; acuesto al nino / me acuesto) never appears, nor voy versus me voy. The learner gets "some verbs have a little word". Needs a rewrite so the first examples are true reflexives with a non-reflexive partner, which means introducing lavar, levantar or similar before this script.
reason: Nothing here is false, but the title promises me levanto, te duchas, se acuesta, no script item uses them, and bank u09-0004, 0007 and 0030 drill them unmodelled. The fix needs a new example set and moving l:levantarse, l:ducharse and l:acostarse (priority 80) to or before this script at 76, so no single string solves it.
quote: Some Spanish verbs travel with a little word that points back at whoever is doing them.

problem: Tratarse de is impersonal and takes no subject in the standard: La carta trata de la casa, or Se trata de la casa. La carta se trata de is widespread in casual speech but the Academy rejects it, and a learner should not be taught it as the model. Same defect at u49-t-verbs-prepositions-0003 (outside this band).
reason: DPD s.v. tratar: pronominal tratarse de is impersonal and takes no subject (search extract; rae.es refused direct fetch), and p:se-trata-de teaches exactly this. The replacement keeps the target l:tratarse; u49-t-verbs-prepositions-0003, 0010 and 0022 have the same fault and are outside this batch.
quote: La carta se trata de la casa.
replacement: Se trata de la casa. = It's about the house.

problem: In speech an accidental fall is caerse. Bare cayo reads as journalistic or literary here, and for a person it sounds wrong in a conversational sentence. Natural Spanish beats the lexeme tag: the learner already has se from u09.
reason: A person losing balance, with a source phrase, takes caerse in speech. The grammar is met (se from u09, cayó from u11), but l:caerse sits at priority 206 with first rows at u22, so this row needs a retag or a move of that lexeme; natural Spanish wins per the owner.
quote: Simón cayó de la silla y ahora no habla.
replacement: Simón se cayó de la silla y ahora no habla. = Simón fell off the chair and now he isn't talking.

problem: In speech an accidental fall is caerse. Bare cayo reads as journalistic or literary here, and for a person it sounds wrong in a conversational sentence. Natural Spanish beats the lexeme tag: the learner already has se from u09.
reason: A person who falls over takes caerse; bare cayó en la calle reads as a report, not as someone telling you about their grandmother. The same l:caerse retag as LA1-033 applies.
quote: Mi abuela cayó en la calle, pero está bien.
replacement: Mi abuela se cayó en la calle, pero está bien. = My grandmother fell in the street, but she's OK.

problem: In speech an accidental fall is caerse. Bare cayo reads as journalistic or literary here, and for a person it sounds wrong in a conversational sentence. Natural Spanish beats the lexeme tag: the learner already has se from u09.
reason: Overreach: the claim's argument is about people. An object with a goal phrase takes bare caer without strain, as in El Tiempo's "se le resbaló de las manos y cayó al suelo" and the course's u47-1235. Se cayó is also fine, but the current text is not wrong.
quote: El pan cayó al piso.
replacement: El pan se cayó al piso. = The bread fell on the floor.

problem: In speech an accidental fall is caerse. Bare cayo reads as journalistic or literary here, and for a person it sounds wrong in a conversational sentence. Natural Spanish beats the lexeme tag: the learner already has se from u09.
reason: As in LA1-035, caer en with a goal is normal for an object landing in something. The replacement is no gain: se cayó en el café leans towards the location reading, fell at the café, in a course set in one, and weakens the "into" of the English.
quote: El celular cayó en el café.
replacement: El celular se cayó en el café. = The phone fell into the coffee.

problem: Aguapanela is stressed on the penultimate, so its initial a is unstressed and it takes la, as p:el-agua-fria explains with arepa. Every other occurrence in the course (bank u10, u15, story ch039, the lexeme entry) has la or una aguapanela. A learner could reasonably overgeneralise from el agua.
reason: The first a of a-gua-pa-NE-la is unstressed, so la applies, as the DPD says of aguamala and other agua- compounds (search extract; the DLE entry was inaccessible). The course has 11 feminine forms against this one el, and the English needs no change.
quote: Pido una limonada, pero prefiero el aguapanela.
replacement: Pido una limonada, pero prefiero la aguapanela.

problem: Five days after the unit teaches habits with the imperfect, a chapter in the same unit uses the preterite for a childhood habit. The preterite is defensible as a rhetorical sum of a closed period, but the course marks exactly this as wrong: g:imperfect-habitual pitfalls[1] (Mi abuela cocino todos los domingos) and x:pret-imp pitfalls[1] (Cuando era nino, fui a la playa todos los anos). Comia is the natural form too.
reason: The preterite is grammatical as a bounded sum, so this is not a Spanish error, but it comes five days after g:imperfect-habitual strikes through Mi abuela cocinó todos los domingos, and x:pret-imp names todos los días as an imperfect cue. Comía is just as natural and is available at u11 d6; requires and lexemes are tagger-computed, so run the gate fix after the edit.
quote: Yo comí las almojábanas de Rosa todos los domingos de mi niñez.
replacement: Yo comía las almojábanas de Rosa todos los domingos de mi niñez.

problem: Glossed "have dark hair". That is the Peninsular reading. In Colombia moreno/morena mostly refers to skin tone, and hair colour is said with pelo negro or castano. A Bogotano reads this as "My sisters are dark-skinned". Bank rows u05-0097, u05-0106, u05-0114, u05-0509, u05-0705, u05-0708, u05-1176 and u05-0123 repeat the gloss. Mechanical fix for those rows: change the English to dark, as in tall and dark, which keeps the ambiguity.
reason: Moreno reads as skin tone in Colombia (Cunin's Cartagena study lists it as a colour category and Colombian press treats it the same way; DLE has both senses, from memory), so have dark hair is the Peninsular reading. The claim's sentence needs tener el pelo, taught at u05 d6, in a u05 d3 lesson, so this swap keeps the point (mis plus plural agreement) inside what is taught; the listed u05 rows and u33-1002 keep the gloss and need their own fix.
quote: Mis hermanas son morenas.
replacement: {"es": "Mis hermanas son altas.", "en": "My sisters are tall."}

problem: See previous claim. The main answer to "My sisters have dark hair" should be literal. Also update the why line, which mentions morenas.
reason: Same defect as LA1-039. Changing only the answer would leave the prompt saying dark hair against pelo negro (black hair) and the why naming morenas, so the whole card changes and the old accept entry goes.
quote: Mis hermanas son morenas.
replacement: {"prompt": "My sisters are tall.", "answer": "Mis hermanas son altas.", "accept": [], "why": "More than one sister, so *mis*, and *altas* matches them."}

problem: Peninsular gloss on the wrong sense, with pos adj and band B1. In Colombia mono/mona means blond, as the note in p:es-tiene-lleva itself says, and bank u22 uses el Mono as a nickname from that sense. A learner who taps the word gets "overalls".
reason: Overalls is the Peninsular sense and wrong here: all the u41 rows and ch122 tagged l:mono mean blond, and l:mono sits beside l:mono#blond in u41's lexemes, so a learner meets an overalls card. Title and en are identical across this file, so this claim and VR-033 get one text; blond alone would make an exact twin of l:mono#blond, and merging the two entries is a separate cleanup.
quote: overalls
replacement: blond (Colombia); monkey

problem: The only permanence framing in the A1 band, and the seed of the permanent/temporary rule the course otherwise avoids well: g:ser-estar-adjectives and x:ser-estar-adj explicitly reject it (portrait or snapshot). "Lasting" will not survive es joven, esta muerto, esta casado.
reason: x:ser-estar-adj rejects permanent against temporary outright and g:ser-estar-adjectives already says what someone is like, which also matches ¿Cómo es...? in this script. Lasting fails on es joven and está muerto.
quote: *Es* for what someone is, the lasting stuff: *es alto*, *es simpática*.
replacement: *Es* for what someone is like: *es alto*, *es simpática*.

problem: Contradicts the rule in the same script ("add an accent to keep the stress where it was"). The stress does not move. The word grows, so the unchanged stress now falls three syllables from the end.
reason: It contradicts "keep the stress where it was" in the same script: the stress stays on -chán- and the word grows. The wording matches the soundTip of g:imperfect-states.
quote: Gluing a word on moves the stress, so *escuchándote* needs its accent.
replacement: Gluing a word on doesn't move the stress. It now falls three syllables from the end, so *escuchándote* needs its accent.

problem: The story fixes the opening at 1978 and the app year at 2026: bank u06-0159 says hace cuarenta y ocho anos, and p:mas-de-number says mas de cuarenta. The en field needs the same change: forty-eight years ago.
reason: Right: p:dates-years has 1978 and bank u06-0159 is this exact sentence with cuarenta y ocho. Amended to include the en field, which the claim left out and which must match. The node es is only a fallback and look-up text, and other rows still give 40 or 47 years or a 1960s opening, so the canon needs its own pass.
quote: Llegué hace dos semanas. Mi abuela abrió el café hace cuarenta años.
replacement: Llegué hace dos semanas. Mi abuela abrió el café hace cuarenta y ocho años. = I arrived two weeks ago. My grandmother opened the café forty-eight years ago.

problem: Treats the local form as something merely to recognise, then the course demands it: g:imperfect-habitual yourTurn[3] answer is Jugabas futbol, g:estar-gerund readAndPick[2] is Estan jugando futbol, and the A1 bank has 19 rows without al against 27 with it. The dialect decision is Latin American, so the model should state both as right.
reason: DPD s.v. jugar, read through search because rae.es refused the fetch, calls jugar fútbol valid for its roots in American Spanish, and the course already demands that form. I could not verify most people for Colombia, so the text drops the frequency claim and still states both as right.
quote: You'll often hear *juego fútbol* with no *al* in Latin America, and that's fine to understand. Saying *juego al fútbol* is always right.
replacement: In Colombia and across Latin America people also say *juego fútbol*, with no *al*, and that's just as right. Use either.

problem: Grammatical. No ... ya is an established variant of ya no, though less frequent. Presenting it as an error is a false correction. Better to drop this pitfall and keep the two real confusions (todavia no versus ya no, ya versus todavia).
reason: No tengo carro ya is grammatical, since no ... ya is a recognised order (Butt and Benjamin and the literary record, from memory; search found only learner sites), and the UI strikes it through under Almost everyone slips here. The fix is to delete pitfalls[2], which is not a string swap; the schema sets no minimum and the rule's advice to keep ya no together can stay as the default.
quote: No tengo carro ya.

problem: Soler exists and the course says so two units earlier: p:soler-inf smallPrint gives "a past form, *solía* (I used to)". The point of the pitfall is that usar does not work this way.
reason: The contradiction is real: p:soler-inf at u09 gives solía (I used to). The claim's text misreads as the way English used to work, so the wording keeps *used to* marked and unambiguous.
quote: Almost. Spanish has no word for *used to*; the ending does that job: *vivía*.
replacement: Almost. *Usar* can't do the job of *used to*. The ending does it: *vivía*.

problem: The card asks a friend "Where were you"; estabas is you, not she.
reason: The prompt is Ask a friend and estabas is tú; yourTurn[7] in the same script already uses Where you were.
quote: Where she was is the scene (*estabas*); the power cut is the event (*se fue*).
replacement: Where you were is the scene (*estabas*); the power cut is the event (*se fue*).

problem: See the deber gloss above. The trap with no tienes que stays intact if the gloss admits both strengths, and it matches bank u09-0439.
reason: Matches u09-0439 and the "bad idea" gloss in x:tener-que-deber, and is compatible with LA1-027. The trap with no tienes que stays intact, since both readings still differ from don't need to.
quote: *No debes venir* means you mustn't come.
replacement: *No debes venir* means you mustn't come, or you shouldn't.

problem: Ser, saber, estar and dar also break it (sea, sepa, este, de). "One" invites building *soya or *esta from soy and estoy.
reason: One that breaks the trick means an example, not the only exception; the claim reads One as Only. Sea, esté, dé and sepa are not taught until g:subj-irregulars at u21, so The main one gives the learner nothing to act on.
quote: One that breaks the trick: *ir* gives *vaya*.
replacement: The main one that breaks the trick: *ir* gives *vaya*.

problem: Mostly true, not absolute. La presidenta, la clienta and la dependienta are standard, and the course uses presidenta 24 times and clienta 6 times.
reason: Mostly true, not absolute: presidenta, clienta and dependienta are standard (DPD as quoted by secondary sources, since rae.es refused direct access), and the course uses presidenta 32 times and clienta 8. A one-word fix that leaves the teaching point intact.
quote: Words in *-ante* or *-ente* don't change, so the article does the job: *el estudiante*, *la estudiante*.
replacement: Most words in *-ante* or *-ente* don't change, so the article does the job: *el estudiante*, *la estudiante*.

problem: Also rolled after n, l and s: Enrique, alrededor, Israel. Low stakes at this level, but the rule claims completeness and Enrique is a common name.
reason: A defensible day-3 simplification, not an error: the hook promises "about a dozen surprises", not completeness. Enrique occurs 0 times in the course, the first such word is alrededor at u21, nothing drills it, and the rule is already at 147 of about 150 words before LA1-029; if wanted it belongs in a soundTip near u21.
quote: One *r* is a quick tap; *rr*, or an *r* that starts a word, is rolled.
replacement: One *r* is a quick tap; *rr*, or an *r* that starts a word or follows *n*, *l* or *s* (*Enrique*), is rolled.

problem: The card translates "enough" and rejects the word most Colombians would use for it, suficiente. Bastante mainly reads as "quite a lot" in current usage, as readAndPick[4] of the same script shows (Tengo bastante tiempo = quite a lot). Add suficiente as accepted here and in any bank row with "enough".
reason: Suficiente is the plain word for enough, and the bank itself uses it from u14, while readAndPick[4] of this script reads bastante tiempo as quite a lot, so rejecting it is wrong on a card that translates enough. Added the equally natural ¿Tienes tiempo suficiente?
quote: ¿Tú tienes bastante tiempo?
replacement: ["¿Tú tienes bastante tiempo?", "¿Tienes suficiente tiempo?", "¿Tienes tiempo suficiente?"]

problem: The rule below says the primer piso is the ground floor, and p:ordinal-floor translates the same phrase "on the ground floor". For a British-English reader this example says one flight up.
reason: The clash with p:ordinal-floor is real, but this string cannot fix it: readAndPick[0] in the same script keeps Vivo en el primer piso = I live on the first floor, so the swap would make the lesson contradict itself, and a dozen bank rows in u07, u40, u48 and u59 also say first floor. Needs one course-wide gloss for primer piso; u07-0442 (primer piso, encima de la panadería) also breaks the Colombian count.
quote: The bathroom is on the first floor.
replacement: The bathroom is on the ground floor.

problem: Same sentence is "I try the jacket on" in the examples and Your Turn. Probarse is for trying on in a shop, so "my jacket" is wrong, and the owner's rule is exact translation. The example also does not show the possessive point well.
reason: Examples[5] and yourTurn[6] both give I try the jacket on for the same sentence, and probarse is trying on, not owning.
quote: Clothes you put on work the same way: *Me pruebo la chaqueta*, I try my jacket on.
replacement: Clothes you put on work the same way: *Me pruebo la chaqueta*, I try the jacket on.

problem: Duermo poco is "I don't sleep much" everywhere else (p:poco-un-poco, g:stem-boot examples). "I sleep little" is not idiomatic English, and the exact-translation rule favours one rendering.
reason: The node's Spanish is Duermo poco., rendered I don't sleep much in p:poco-un-poco and g:se-meaning-change, and I sleep little is not idiomatic English.
quote: Do you want a coffee? I can't today. I prefer tea. I sleep little.
replacement: Do you want a coffee? I can't today. I prefer tea. I don't sleep much.

problem: Comma before y joining two predicates of one subject is an English habit. Spanish punctuation omits it. This is the first long sentence of the -ar lesson, so it is worth modelling correctly.
reason: Ortografía 2010 (from memory; a press note on the RAE rule gives the same cases) keeps a comma before y for a change of subject or a clause closing a list, and neither applies to two short predicates of one subject. Only the Spanish changes; the English comma can stay.
quote: Hablo inglés, y trabajo en un café en La Candelaria.
replacement: Hablo inglés y trabajo en un café en La Candelaria.

problem: Same as above.
reason: Same fix as LA1-042, and the card is about tall and thin, which what he's like covers exactly.
quote: What he is, the lasting stuff, takes *es*.
replacement: What he's like takes *es*.

problem: In the unit that teaches the two pasts, funcionaba is rendered as a simple past. The English should show the scene: "wasn't working". The Spanish is fine.
reason: The row is El reloj no funcionaba y llegamos tarde., so the scene needs wasn't working, in the very unit that teaches the split. The Spanish stands.
quote: The clock did not work and we arrived late.
replacement: The clock wasn't working and we arrived late.

problem: Siento llegar tarde is correct but sounds Peninsular in Bogota, where Perdon por llegar tarde, Disculpa la demora and above all Que pena are the everyday apologies. The ladder leaves out Que pena, which the course teaches on day one and which is the signature Colombian apology. Rework the ladder so Que pena is on it and Siento is the less common option.
reason: Qué pena as Colombia's apology is well attested (Portafolio quoting the Instituto Caro y Cuervo), but nothing settles whether Siento llegar tarde sounds Peninsular in Bogotá or where qué pena belongs on a small-to-big ladder. The claim gives no text, and this node and x:perdon-lo-siento are both built on siento.
quote: Three ways to say sorry, from small to big:

problem: Correct but not the Bogota default. Tengo afan or Estoy de afan is the everyday form, and it does not appear in the course until u32. 13 A1 bank rows use prisa, 0 use afan.
reason: The count holds: 13 A1 rows use prisa and none uses afán. Afán for hurry in Colombia stands (Diccionario de americanismos from memory; search only partly confirmed it), the note changes no answer, and Tengo afán should also go in yourTurn[5].accept.
quote: *tengo prisa*: I'm in a hurry
replacement: *tengo prisa*: I'm in a hurry (in Colombia you'll also hear *tengo afán*)

problem: Teaches the classic false equation long = imperfect, short = preterite. Length does not choose the past; viewpoint does. A learner who absorbs this writes *Hernando era taxista durante cuarenta años* or *Vivía en Toronto diez años*. It also undoes x:pret-imp (u12), which already says llovió toda la noche wraps a whole night up as one finished thing. The app's own content contradicts it: 28 A2 bank sentences, counted by hand from a regex pull, put a stated duration in the preterite (u21-0386 Hernando fue taxista durante cuarenta años; u15-0717 Hernando estuvo casado treinta años; u25-0292 Mi hijo lloró toda la noche), plus p:horas-y-horas (Rosa trabajó años y años en el café) and ch079.
reason: The length rule is false and undoes x:pret-imp, which already says llovió toda la noche wraps a whole night up. The first reviewer's text stands because sets the scene and wraps up are the course's own phrases from g:imperfect-states, g:pret-vs-imperfect and x:pret-imp, where the claim's standing inside the background is new imagery.
quote:
A stretch of time or an old habit takes the describing past: *Cuando era niño, vivía en Toronto.*
One moment takes the event past: *Cuando llegué a Bogotá...*
replacement:
It isn't about how long something lasted. It's about how you tell it.
What sets the scene, or an old habit, takes the describing past: *Cuando era niño, vivía en Toronto.*
An event that moves the story on takes the event past: *Cuando llegué a Bogotá...*
Even a long stretch can be an event, if you wrap it up as one finished thing: *Hernando fue taxista cuarenta años.*

problem: Same length fallacy in the answer feedback, the place a learner reads it right after a success.
reason: Same fallacy at the moment the learner reads it. The scene wording keeps this one idea with LA2-001.
quote: Being a kid is a whole stretch of time, so the describing past: *era*.
replacement: *Cuando era niño* sets the scene for the rest, so the describing past: *era*.

problem: The correction is right, the reason is false: long stretches take the preterite whenever they are presented as finished (u19-0294 Hernando trabajó de taxista durante cuarenta años).
reason: Right correction, false reason. Hernando's forty years match LA2-001, and the claim's ten years in Toronto would jar with Tomás leaving at seven; yourTurn[4].why repeats the fallacy, is unclaimed, and needs: *Cuando eras niña* sets the scene, so *vivías* and *eras*, and *niña* for a woman.
quote: Almost. Childhood isn't one moment, it's a whole stretch, so *era*.
replacement: Almost. *Cuando era niño* sets the scene, so *era*. It isn't about length: *Hernando fue taxista cuarenta años* wraps forty years up as one finished thing.

problem: Labels correct, everyday Spanish as a mistake. When what was said still holds or is still to come, the present stays: Mariana dijo que va a llamar means the call is still expected. English allows the same (Mariana said she's going to call), so the why, the same shift English makes, is also wrong. The bank itself has u26-0033 Vale me dijo que se va para Medellín. The pitfall shows on a card and in Reference, and yourTurn[5] has no accept for this form, so a correct answer is marked wrong.
reason: The strike-through is wrong, since Dijo que va a llamar is fine while the call is pending, and LA2-006 now says so in the rule. But the claim's iba llamar card discards the lesson's central point, the shift; with nunca llamó the plan is closed, so the present really is wrong and the card teaches the boundary, the same shape as LB1-007. yourTurn[5].accept still needs Mariana dijo que va a llamar.
quote: Mariana dijo que va a llamar.
replacement: {"wrong": "Mariana dijo que va a llamar, pero nunca llamó.", "right": "Mariana dijo que iba a llamar, pero nunca llamó.", "why": "Almost. She never called, so that plan is over: *iba a*. *Va a* only works if the call could still come."}

problem: The take-away test fails on the lesson's own hook. I don't drink coffee in general at night, and I drink coffee, in general, every day, both pass the test, yet the script requires No tomo café and marks Tomo el café todos los días as wrong in pitfalls[3]. The real split is the whole category against some of it, not generality. A learner who trusts the test writes Tomo el café and Compro el pan for habits.
reason: The old test fails on the lesson's own hook, as claimed. But all of it is a poor cue (Me gusta el café is not about all the coffee) and the claim drops the in general wording that the whys at yourTurn[0], [2] and [5] still use, so I rebuilt the test on in general and an amount, the rule's own words; it passes every card in the script.
quote: Quick test: if English could add in general, Spanish wants the article.
replacement: Quick test: are you saying what a thing is like in general, or how you feel about it? Spanish wants the article: *Me gusta el café.* Is it just some, an amount you buy, drink or have? No article: *Tomo café.*

problem: Presents the shift as compulsory. Nothing tells the learner that a fact still true or a plan still on keeps its present, so natural speech looks wrong to them.
reason: The shift is not compulsory when the content still holds or is still pending (authorities as in LA2-004, from memory). The addition sits before the next sentence without clashing and fits LA2-004.
quote: So the present becomes the form you use for describing the past (*estaba*, *tenía*, *vivía*), and *voy a* becomes *iba a*.
replacement: So the present becomes the form you use for describing the past (*estaba*, *tenía*, *vivía*), and *voy a* becomes *iba a*. If what they said is still true or still coming, you can keep the present: *Mariana dijo que va a llamar.*

problem: False. After a past verb para que normally takes the past subjunctive. The app's own bank has u41-0127 Llamé para que me explicaran el contrato and u42-0143 Tomás llamó tres veces para que lo comunicaran con el abogado.
reason: The defect is real, but LC-010 fixes the same sentence with a cleaner one-word cut, so this one is refuted only to avoid a double edit. Nothing here stands against the claim's reasoning.
quote: *Para que* always takes the present subjunctive.
replacement: *Para que* always takes a subjunctive form: the present one for now, and a past one in stories, which comes later.

problem: Caer bien or mal with food is ordinary Spanish: it means agree or disagree with you. The same unit's bank has u15-1008 La aguapanela me cae bien en el estómago and u15-1009 Esta comida me cae mal, both tagged g:parecer-quedar. The rule makes those sentences look like errors.
reason: The food sense is ordinary Spanish (SpanishDict and Mexican and Costa Rican sources for caer mal), though the DLE text I could reach did not show it, so that citation is unverified. The quote is narrowed to the second sentence so CX-026 can carry the first; together they read as one paragraph.
quote: For food and things, stay with *me gusta*.
replacement: With food, *me cae bien* means it agrees with your stomach: *Esta comida me cae mal*. To say you like food or things, stay with *me gusta*.

problem: Me cae bien el café is grammatical, with a different meaning. The problem is the meaning, not that it can't be said.
reason: Right for the reason in LA2-008: the sentence is grammatical with another meaning. Your stomach matches the rule, and this claim carries the fix that CX-027 also proposes.
quote: *Me cae bien* is for people. For food and things, use *me gusta*.
replacement: *Me cae bien el café* says coffee agrees with your stomach. To say you like it, use *me gusta*.

problem: Hides the single most useful pattern: a background with mientras, then an event. The bank uses it: u17-t-cuando-indicative-0024 Mientras esperábamos, tomamos un tinto; u18-0075 Mientras esperábamos el bus, dimos una vuelta por el parque; u19-0618 Robaron en la casa de Hernando mientras estaba en el café. A learner told both sides is the norm will write sonaba el teléfono.
reason: The cited rows exist and background plus event is the everyday pattern with mientras, so both sides as the norm is wrong (Butt and Benjamin from memory). Reworded to scene to match LA2-001; yourTurn[1].why (describing past on both sides) needs the same correction.
quote: *Mientras* means while: two things going on at the same time. Both sides usually take the describing past: *Mientras yo cocinaba, él lavaba.*
replacement: *Mientras* means while. The *mientras* side sets the scene, so it usually takes the describing past: *Mientras yo cocinaba...* The other side depends on what you're telling: something else going on (*él lavaba*), or something that happened in the middle of it (*sonó el celular*).

problem: Implies both verbs must be imperfect. Fine as a correction of this sentence, wrong as a generalisation (see u18-0075).
reason: The why overgeneralises: Mientras yo cocinaba, Hernando lavó los platos is fine, so only cociné is wrong in this pitfall. Same text as the claim with scene for background, matching LA2-010.
quote: *Mientras* sets two things side by side as they were going on, so the describing past.
replacement: *Mientras* sets the scene, so here it wants the describing past: *cocinaba*. The other side can be either: *Mientras yo cocinaba, sonó el celular.*

problem: The script's own examples[6] and readAndPick[8], Fue Vale quien hizo el pan, break the rule: no comma, no little word. So do u24-0429 and u24-0894. It also steers learners to quien after a comma where que is at least as natural in speech.
reason: Fue Vale quien hizo el pan in examples[6] and readAndPick[8] has neither a comma nor a preposition, and que is fine after the comma in Mariana, que es periodista. The new text covers all three uses and only says you'll see the last two.
quote: *quien*: who, for people, after a comma or after a little word like *con*: *Mariana, quien es periodista*; *la persona con quien hablé*.
replacement: *quien*: who, for people, after a little word like *con*: *la persona con quien hablé*. You'll also see it after a comma (*Mariana, quien es periodista*, though *que* works there too), and after *fue* or *es* when you point someone out: *Fue Vale quien hizo el pan*.

problem: Contradicted by examples[6] of the same script, Fue Vale quien hizo el pan.
reason: Same contradiction with examples[6]. The pitfall's sentence, Es la persona que trabaja aquí, stays the right correction.
quote: Right after a person, plain who is *que*; *quien* needs a comma or a word like *con* before it.
replacement: Right after a person, plain who is *que*. *Quien* comes after a comma, after a word like *con*, or in *fue Vale quien*.

problem: Two units earlier p:no-se-que-hacer taught No sé qué hacer, a statement with accented qué. Nothing explains hidden questions, so the two lessons look like they conflict. Indirect questions are not taught until u37.
reason: P:no-se-que-hacer, two days before in u17, teaches No sé qué hacer, and this rule leaves the two looking opposed. The added sentence uses only that taught pattern.
quote: In a statement, where it means the thing that, it's *lo que*: *No entiendo lo que dices.*
replacement: In a statement, where it means the thing that, it's *lo que*: *No entiendo lo que dices.* After words like *no sé*, the question word stays, accent and all: *No sé qué hacer.*

problem: The why says the fix is lo que, but No entiendo qué dices is correct Spanish: entender takes an indirect question. Only the preverbal tú is off. The pitfall teaches that a good sentence is wrong.
reason: No entiendo qué dices is correct because entender takes an indirect question, while gustar does not, so No me gusta qué dices is a real error. The example in the why moves to No sé qué hacer, since finite indirect questions wait until u37; No entiendo qué dices. should also go in yourTurn[4].accept.
quote: No entiendo qué tú dices.
replacement: {"wrong": "No me gusta qué dices.", "right": "No me gusta lo que dices.", "why": "You mean the thing you're saying, so *lo que*. *Qué* stays only after words like *no sé*: *No sé qué hacer*."}

problem: Qué is the safe default, but cuál plus a noun is common in Latin American speech, and the app itself uses it: p:el-rojo-la-grande hook ¿Cuál camisa?, p:el-azul examples[2] ¿Cuáles botas quiere?, u16-1112 ¿Cuál camisa le gusta?, u16-1113 ¿Cuáles zapatos le muestro? Seven units later the learner is told, in effect, that those are wrong.
reason: Cuál before a noun is normal in Latin American speech, and the course itself uses it at u13 and u16 (¿Cuál camisa?, ¿Cuáles botas quiere?), so the flat rule contradicts earlier lessons. The DPD entry returned 403 (from memory only); learner grammars agree it is common in LatAm and rare in Spain, and this wording rests on usage, not on that citation.
quote: Right before a noun, use *qué*: *¿Qué documentos?*, *¿Qué color?* Here *qué* means both what and which.
replacement: Right before a noun, *qué* always works: *¿Qué documentos?*, *¿Qué color?* Here *qué* means both what and which. In Colombia you'll also hear *cuál* before a noun when picking from a few: *¿Cuál camisa?*

problem: The wrong sentence, ¿Cuál documentos necesito?, is wrong because cuál doesn't agree with a plural. The why gives a different reason, one the app's own ¿Cuáles botas quiere? contradicts.
reason: The wrong form fails on agreement, and the why states a ban that ¿Cuáles botas quiere? (p:el-azul, u16) contradicts. The replacement names the real fault and keeps qué as the safe choice, in line with LA2-016.
quote: Right before a noun, Spanish uses *qué*, even when English could say which.
replacement: *Cuál* can't sit in front of a plural: it would have to be *cuáles*. Before a noun, *qué* is the safe choice: *¿Qué documentos necesito?*

problem: Always is false for the course's own dialect region. In much of Latin America demasiado is used with no sense of excess, as an intensifier equal to muy or mucho. A learner will hear praise and read it as complaint.
reason: rae.es/dpd/demasiado, read through a search summary because the page returns 403: in much of America, especially colloquially, demasiado has intensive value equal to mucho or muy with no negative sense. A Caracas corpus study agrees, so 'always' is false for this dialect; Colombian frequency is my judgement, but 'usually' holds either way.
quote: *demasiado caro*: too expensive. More than you want, so it's always a complaint.
replacement: *demasiado caro*: too expensive. More than you want, so it's usually a complaint.

problem: Same false absolute. The advice to use muy is sound; the claim is not.
reason: Same false absolute, same DPD evidence. The advice to use muy survives, and está rico is taught in the same unit.
quote: Careful. *Demasiado* is always a complaint, so this sounds like a problem. For praise, use *muy*.
replacement: Careful. *Demasiado* usually means too much, so this can sound like a problem. For praise, *muy* is the safe choice. You'll still hear people use *demasiado* as praise: *está demasiado rico*.

problem: The right-now model fails on states that last: u15-0717 Hernando estuvo casado treinta años, u21-0350 Mis padres están separados desde hace años, and later está muerto. The contrast script's small print has the better model, a portrait or a snapshot, but it is hidden. The learner needs it in the rule.
reason: Overreach: está casado and están separados still describe how they are right now, and the rule never says temporary, so the test does not fail at this level. LC-034 adds the portrait or snapshot model, and that small print shows on the same Why? tap as this paragraph, so the rule can stay plain.
quote: *Está* + description: how they are right now, or how they seem today. *Hoy está nervioso.*
replacement: *Está* + description: the state they're in, a snapshot rather than a portrait. Usually that's how they are right now, *hoy está nervioso*, but a state can last: *está casado*.

problem: Past also goes with hace plus que, which means the same as ago. The bank has it in about 14 sentences tagged g:hace-que-desde (u23-0426 Hace diez años que Hernando dejó el taxi; u24-0521 Hace seis meses que me mudé a este barrio) and more untagged (u23-0066). The stated rule makes correct sentences look wrong.
reason: Hace + time + que + preterite is correct Spanish and at least 17 rows tagged g:hace-que-desde use it, so 'past goes with plain hace' is false. I kept the crisp past and present contrast the drill depends on and added the exception after it, instead of folding it in.
quote: So the verb and the little word travel together. Past goes with plain *hace*. Present goes with *desde hace*, or with *hace… que*.
replacement: So the verb and the little word travel together. Past goes with *hace*. Present goes with *desde hace*, or with *hace… que*. A past verb can take *hace… que* too, and it still means ago: *Hace dos años que llegué* says the same as *Llegué hace dos años*.

problem: No que is false. Hace dos años que vine aquí is correct, yet it is not in accept. A correct learner answer is rejected and then told a false reason. Add Hace dos años que vine aquí and Hace dos años que llegué aquí to accept.
reason: Hace dos años que vine aquí is correct, so 'no que' is false. Also add 'Hace dos años que vine aquí.' and 'Hace dos años que llegué aquí.' to yourTurn[6].accept: that is a separate array edit, not part of this string.
quote: Coming is a finished moment, so a past verb and plain *hace*, no *que*.
replacement: Coming is a finished moment, so a past verb with *hace*: *Vine aquí hace dos años.*

problem: About 14 sentences tagged for this node use hace plus que plus a preterite, a pattern the rule never mentions. The learner sees Hace diez años que Hernando dejó el taxi right after being told the verb is present.
reason: Real gap: at least 17 rows tagged for this node use hace que with a preterite, right after the rule says present. In the claim's text 'it' had no clear antecedent after the To ask line, so I named the structure and added the gloss, as the next paragraph of this rule does.
quote: To ask: *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que…?* or *¿Desde cuándo…?*, again with the present.
replacement:
To ask: *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que…?* or *¿Desde cuándo…?*, again with the present.

With a past verb, *hace… que* counts back to a moment instead, like ago: *Hace dos años que llegué*, I arrived two years ago.

problem: English will is most often the I'll of an offer or a decision made as you speak. Spanish uses the plain present there, and the bank does it constantly (u15-1003 Tranquila, yo cierro el café = I'll close the café; u21-0818 Sin problema, yo cierro; u21-0152 No se preocupen, yo pago) without any rule saying why. A learner following this guide says Yo pagaré and Yo cerraré, which sound stilted.
reason: The gap is real: the bank has over 140 rows with I'll in the plain present from u01 on (u01-0419 Llamo mañana), and no rule says why. I added the English glosses CX-032 usefully had, so the line can absorb that claim.
quote: A rough English guide: *voy a* is going to, and *-ré* is will, said like you mean it.
replacement: A rough English guide: *voy a* is going to, and *-ré* is will, said like you mean it. One English will takes neither: the I'll you say on the spot, offering or deciding as you speak. That's the plain present: *Yo pago*, I'll pay. *Te llamo luego*, I'll call you later.

problem: Same gap at the point the -ré forms are taught. No script explains the present for on-the-spot I'll.
reason: Same gap at the point the forms are taught. It sits before 'This future is for promises' without clashing, and the script's own Mañana te escribo (I'll write to you tomorrow) already relies on it.
quote: The catch for English speakers: for everyday plans, Colombians still say *voy a*: *Mañana voy a trabajar.*
replacement: The catch for English speakers: for everyday plans, Colombians still say *voy a*: *Mañana voy a trabajar.* And for the I'll you say on the spot, they use the plain present: *Yo pago.*

problem: The rule opens by equating would or could with -ría, and warns only about would. Could as was able to is the matching trap: I could swim at ten is podía or sabía, I couldn't yesterday is no pude. A search of all 916 scripts found one nearby note only, g:preterite-irregular-strong on no pude; none warns that could as was able to is not podría. Past habit form is also a second name for what every other lesson calls the describing past.
reason: Both gaps are real, but the claim's I could swim is a bad example: the course teaches skill with saber (x:saber-poder), so it would be sabía. I swapped the example and merged CX-033 into one list in the script's own format; pitfalls[3] keeps 'past habit form'.
quote: One trap: when English would means used to (we would go every Sunday), Spanish uses the past habit form: *íbamos*.
replacement:
Three traps, where English would or could is really a past:
would as used to (we would go every Sunday): *íbamos*
wouldn't as refused (he wouldn't sign): *no quiso firmar*
could as was able to (as a kid I could sleep anywhere): *podía*, not *podría*

problem: Five units later g:subj-emotion-intro says Vale really is here; it's a fact, and Spanish still uses the wish form. A model built on not a fact collapses. The reusable idea, already in that later script, is that you aren't reporting the clause.
reason: A hope really isn't a fact yet, so the line is true of its own sentence. g:subj-emotion-intro stages the fact case as 'the surprise', a planned next step and not a contradiction, and pitfalls[3] here uses the same contrast, so the edit would leave the script uneven.
quote: A hope isn't a fact yet, so Spanish uses the wish form, *guste*.
replacement: You're not telling anyone a fact here, you're hoping. So Spanish uses the wish form: *guste*.

problem: Nothing explains stem changes in the we form, and no script contains durmamos, pidamos, sintamos, sirvamos or muramos. The I-form trick gives wrong we forms for boot verbs: pensar gives *piensemos, not pensemos; dormir gives *duermamos, not durmamos. The bank uses these from u22: u22-0118 Ojalá nos divirtamos, u22-1099 Ojalá sigamos juntos.
reason: The gap is real: no script has durmamos, pidamos or sintamos and the bank uses such forms from u22. But the claim's text would crowd the visible trick, so I moved it to the next sentence, behind the Why? tap, and re-worded 'can't do that' so its reference still holds.
quote: Six verbs can't do that, because their I form doesn't end in *-o*:
replacement:
Boot verbs follow their I form too, except in the we form, which goes back to the plain stem (*piense*, *pensemos*). *-ir* boot verbs keep a small change there (*durmamos*, *pidamos*).

Six verbs can't use the I form at all, because theirs doesn't end in *-o*:

problem: Teaches siempre que as the way to say every time and never gives cada vez que, which has no other meaning and does not appear in the bank until u30 (0 of 13,263 A2 sentences). Siempre que with the subjunctive later means as long as (g:subj-conditions, u44), so the learner's first tool for whenever is the ambiguous one.
reason: The count holds: cada vez que first appears at u30, and siempre que turns conditional at u44, so naming it now helps. The one you'll hear most is an unverified frequency claim, so that part goes.
quote: *Siempre que* means whenever, every time.
replacement: *Siempre que* means whenever, every time. So does *cada vez que*.

problem: Tagged g:future-conjecture. ¿Cómo se llamará el nuevo socio? is a guess about now: I wonder what his name is. The English turns it into a prediction about a name he'll have, the exact confusion x:future-prediction-conjecture exists to prevent.
reason: Real mistranslation: tagged g:future-conjecture, and people already have names, so this is a guess about now, not a prediction. I used the 'I wonder' form of the neighbouring rows u20-0622, 0625 and 0626 instead of a new 'do you think'.
quote: What will the new partner be called?
replacement: What's the new partner called, I wonder?

problem: Había un accidente en la Séptima is good Spanish: it sets a scene. The bank has it: u18-0400 Había un accidente en la carretera y esperamos dos horas. Labelling it wrong undoes the scene and event model.
reason: Había un accidente is good Spanish as background, as u18-0400 shows, and calling it an error undoes the scene and event contrast of x:pret-imp from u12. The replacement keeps hubo as the answer and gives the true reason.
quote: For one event that happened and is over, Spanish uses *hubo*.
replacement: *Había un accidente* sets a scene: it was already there when you passed. To report that it happened, use *hubo*.

problem: The rule covers only words in -o and -a. Applied to the script's own Pobrecito Tomás, or to the bank's cafecito and pancito (u23-0518, u23-0550), it gives *pobrito, *cafeíto, *panito. In a story set in a café, cafecito is not optional.
reason: Real gap: the rule fails on the script's own Pobrecito Tomás and on cafecito, and the RAE glossary confirms pancito as the American form. I added -cita, because the script also has Pobrecita Vale, and I avoided flor because the bank has florecitas, not florcitas.
quote: It keeps the word's *-o* or *-a*: *una casita*, *un gatico*, *las velitas*.
replacement: It keeps the word's *-o* or *-a*: *una casita*, *un gatico*, *las velitas*. Words ending in *-e*, *-n* or *-r* add *-cito* or *-cita*: *pobrecito*, *pobrecita*, *cafecito*, *pancito*, *amorcito*.

problem: Qué tan is the Latin American degree question (¿Qué tan lejos?), not an exclamative formula. The script teaches ¡Tan lindo! The title reaches learners through bundle.title in the UI.
reason: The script teaches ¡Tan lindo! and never ¡Qué tan lindo!, the RAE glossary gives ¿Qué tan listo es? as the interrogative counterpart of ¡Qué listo es!, and the bank has no such exclamative. The internal note on the node still mentions ¡Qué tan…! but does not reach learners.
quote: Reacting: ¡Qué bueno!, ¡Qué pena!, ¡Qué tan lindo!, ¡Cuánta gente!
replacement: Reacting: ¡Qué bueno!, ¡Qué pena!, ¡Tan lindo!, ¡Cuánta gente!

problem: In Latin America the indicative is common after qué bueno que, especially for something already past. The bank has u27-0203 ¡Qué bueno que viniste hoy, Hernando! in the same unit as a lesson that says a reaction takes the wish form, with no note.
reason: The indicative is documented in ¡Qué bueno que viniste! (Colegio de México study, for Mexico), and u12-0204 and u27-0203 use it, so a note is needed. I could not verify 'Colombians often', so I dropped the nationality, and I used the course's term plain past.
quote: You'll also hear *Me alegro de que estés bien*, which means the same.
replacement: You'll also hear *Me alegro de que estés bien*, which means the same. And about something already over, you'll often hear the plain past after *qué bueno que*: *¡Qué bueno que viniste!*

problem: Mientras and siempre que have no accented form, and the accent also appears in statements: p:no-se-que-hacer, same unit, No sé dónde dejar el carro.
reason: Mientras and siempre que have no accented form, and p:no-se-que-hacer, two days earlier, keeps accents in statements. Out loud misleads, and No sé cuándo ir uses the infinitive pattern already taught, because finite indirect questions wait until u37.
quote: No accent on any of them unless you're asking a question: *¿Cuándo llegaste?*
replacement: *Cuando* only takes an accent in a question, even one tucked inside a sentence: *¿Cuándo llegaste?* *No sé cuándo ir.*

problem: Same issue: hidden questions in statements keep the accent.
reason: A hidden question is still a question, so only for questions is true, and the amended LA2-035 rule now says so. For asking is no more precise, so nothing changes.
quote: The accent is only for questions. Here *cuando* just joins two ideas.
replacement: The accent is only for asking. Here *cuando* just joins two ideas.

problem: Contradicts p:no-se-que-hacer, No sé dónde dejar el carro, a statement with the accent.
reason: Only for the question ¿Dónde? is too narrow after No sé dónde dejar el carro in u17. Reworded to match the question wording kept in g:cuando-indicative, and it uses the sentence the course already taught.
quote: The accent is only for the question *¿Dónde?*
replacement: The accent is only for questions, even ones tucked inside a sentence: *¿Dónde?*, *No sé dónde dejar el carro*. Here *donde* just links to *el lugar*.

problem: Ser cansado means to be tiring, not to be a tired type.
reason: Ser cansado is the textbook pair for tiring (DLE 'que produce cansancio', from memory; learner grammars agree). The replacement also matches x:ser-estar-adj, which says Soy aburrido means you're a boring person.
quote: *Soy cansado* sounds like tired is your personality.
replacement: *Soy cansado* would mean you're a tiring person.

problem: The lesson title promises es aburrido / está aburrido, the pair English speakers trip on most, but the script never mentions it. It appears only in the next day's contrast.
reason: The node title promises es aburrido / está aburrido and the script never contains aburrido. The added line is taken word for word from the x:ser-estar-adj rule the next day.
quote: *es malo*: bad. *está malo*: gone off, or ill.
replacement:
*es malo*: bad. *está malo*: gone off, or ill.
*es aburrido*: boring. *está aburrido*: bored.

problem: ¿Cuánto tiempo has vivido aquí? is grammatical. The everyday form is the one given, but this is not an error.
reason: ¿Cuánto tiempo has vivido aquí? is grammatical; the present is the everyday form (Butt and Benjamin, from memory). 'Not wrong' has precedent in x:ir-a-future pitfalls[2].
quote: Close. English asks how long have you lived, but Spanish asks with the present: *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que vives…?*
replacement: Not wrong, but the everyday question keeps the present: *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que vives…?*

problem: g:time-sequence teaches luego, después, entonces: then, with ¿Y entonces qué hizo Rosa? = And then what did Rosa do? The two lessons disagree.
reason: g:time-sequence at u26 teaches entonces as then, with ¿Y entonces qué hizo Rosa?, so the flat 'sounds like so' clashes. 'Can sound' keeps the warning and removes the clash.
quote: One trap: in the middle of a story, *entonces* sounds like so, as if one thing caused the next. For plain and then, use *y después*.
replacement: One trap: in the middle of a story, *entonces* can sound like so, as if one thing caused the next. For a plain next step, *y después* is clearer.

problem: Comimos, entonces fuimos a bailar is not an error, and it clashes with g:time-sequence.
reason: Comimos, entonces fuimos a bailar is not an error, and it clashes with g:time-sequence in the same way. The softened why matches LA2-041.
quote: Careful. *Entonces* here sounds like the eating caused the dancing. For one thing after another, say *y después*.
replacement: Not wrong, but *entonces* here can sound as if the eating caused the dancing. For a plain next step, *y después* is clearer.

problem: Talla is also used for shoes in Latin American retail, in my experience of the usage. Número is the safe phrase, but only for clothes is too strong. Lower confidence: no source checked.
reason: Colombian retail does use talla for shoes (Falabella Colombia's 'Guía completa de tallas de zapatos', encarguelo.com's 'Talla Colombia'), so 'only for clothes' is false. The claim's 'the word is número' swaps one absolute for another, so I softened it; it stays compatible with the rule's 'Don't swap them' as advice on production.
quote: Almost. Shoes go by *número*; *talla* is only for clothes.
replacement: Almost. With *calzar*, *número* is the natural word: *¿Qué número calza?*

problem: La chica con los ojos azules is grammatical and understood. De is the more idiomatic way to identify someone, but con is not an error.
reason: La chica con los ojos azules is grammatical and understood; de is the idiomatic way to identify (Butt and Benjamin from memory). The line still steers learners to de, and 'Not wrong' has precedent in x:ir-a-future.
quote: Close. To say which girl, Spanish uses *de*, not *con*.
replacement: Not wrong, but *de* is the natural way to pick someone out: *la chica de los ojos azules*.

problem: He llamado, he escrito, y nada is natural if you're still trying, the same still-open use p:perfecto-still-live teaches. Lower confidence.
reason: He llamado, he escrito, y nada is natural while you are still trying, the open use p:perfecto-still-live teaches, and 'In Colombia' wrongly makes the choice regional. The replacement keeps the plain past for a finished story, which is what the lesson drills.
quote: In Colombia the tries go in the plain past: *llamé*, *escribí*.
replacement: In a finished story the tries go in the plain past: *llamé*, *escribí*. *He llamado* would mean you're still trying.

problem: De is the right default, but el mejor jugador en la historia is common and not wrong. Never overclaims.
reason: The RAE's online grammar lists en as a valid superlative coda (en toda la ciudad, en el mundo), so 'Never' is false. The replacement keeps de as the production rule.
quote: Never *en* here.
replacement: Use *de* here, not *en*.

problem: Pitfalls[2] says the noun comes first, then más and the adjective, but mejor goes before the noun, and no one says so. Peor, the worst, is not given at all.
reason: The omission is real and peor is known from u11, but the claim's text breaks the next sentence: 'The same goes for mayor' would then say mayor goes before the noun, and it follows it (mi hermano mayor). I widened the quote to reword that sentence.
quote: Best is just *mejor* with the article: *el mejor tinto*. The same goes for *mayor*: *el mayor* is the oldest.
replacement: Best is just *mejor* with the article, and it goes before the noun: *el mejor tinto*. Worst is the same: *el peor tinto*. *Mayor* takes the article too: *el mayor* is the oldest.

problem: Momentito is not an error in Colombia. The app's own u23-0555 has Hace un ratito que llegó Mariana. -ico is the strong local tendency, not a rule.
reason: Momentito is correct Spanish and the app's own u23-0555 has ratito beside ratico, so -ico is a strong tendency, not a rule. Bogotá frequency could not be verified, but 'usually' and 'not wrong' hold whatever it is.
quote: People will understand you, but in Colombia a word ending in *-to* takes *-ico*.
replacement: Not wrong, but *momentico* sounds more local: in Colombia a word ending in *-to* usually takes *-ico*.

problem: True of there is, but false of the verb: g:subj-perfect (u34) uses hayas, hayamos, hayan.
reason: One form holds only for there is; hayas, hayamos and hayan arrive at u34. 'Never changes' also usefully warns off plural hayan.
quote: *Haya* has just the one form: *Quiero que haya café.*
replacement: For there is, *haya* never changes: *Quiero que haya café.*

problem: This lesson is u17, and the -ré forms arrive at u20, so the learner can't read the wrong form or make this mistake. x:si-clause-no-future covers it at the right moment. Delete this pitfall.
reason: True: this is u17, -ré forms arrive at u20, and x:si-clause-no-future covers the slip then. But the fix deletes a whole pitfalls element, not a string, and it leaves two where all 916 scripts have at least three, so add a level-appropriate third or accept two.
quote: Si tendrás tiempo, ven al café.

problem: Si meaning whether can take the future: No sé si lloverá. Learners who over-apply this rule will reject correct sentences.
reason: English really does say I don't know if it will rain, so the note earns its place, and No sé si is known from u17. The claim's spot would interrupt the visible trick, so I moved it after 'trust your English', where the whether case is the real exception.
quote: So trust your English here: the half with if gets the present, and the will goes in the other half.
replacement: So trust your English here: the half with if gets the present, and the will goes in the other half. (The *si* of whether is different, in English too: *No sé si lloverá*, I don't know if it'll rain.)

problem: Sino follows any negative: nunca, nadie, ni, and no solo … sino también at u44.
reason: Sino follows any negative, such as nunca or nadie. The claim's no solo example does contain no, but the general point stands, and the fix costs nothing.
quote: So *sino* only ever comes after a *no*.
replacement: So *sino* only ever comes after a negative, nearly always *no*.

problem: Frequency usually takes al or a la: cuatro veces al día, used in the bank in A2.
reason: 'Always' is false: learners have had tres veces al día since u09. But the slip here is para for por, so I kept that contrast, and 'Per a person or a night' read awkwardly.
quote: Per is always *por*: *por persona*, *por noche*.
replacement: Per is *por*, not *para*: *por persona*, *por noche*. For how often, Spanish usually says *al*: *dos veces al día*.

problem: Leaves out you, although this script's own node example is ya se la empaco, addressed to usted.
reason: The list leaves out a reading this unit drills: u16 rows targeting g:double-pronouns such as u16-0346 Se lo doy en un momento = I'll give it to you (polite). The cited node example is not itself shown in the lesson, but the bank settles it even with x:le-se-lo a day later.
quote: *se la di* is I gave it to him (or to her, or to them).
replacement: *se la di* is I gave it to him (or to her, to you as *usted*, or to them).

problem: Learners in Latin America will meet se los dije for I told them, with the plural moved onto lo. The script says this se has no plural, which is right, but it gives no warning about a form they'll hear and misread as several things.
reason: RAE grammar (via search summary) calls se los digo frequent in colloquial speech across broad areas of America, and Moreno de Alba 2013, read directly, documents it, including an El Tiempo example, and quotes advice to avoid it in careful speech. The note says Latin America, so the Bogotá frequency I could not establish does not affect it.
quote: Teachers sometimes call this the false *se* (*se espurio*): it's just *le* or *les* in disguise, nothing to do with the *se* in *se llama*.
replacement: Teachers sometimes call this the false *se* (*se espurio*): it's just *le* or *les* in disguise, nothing to do with the *se* in *se llama*. In Latin America you'll also hear *se los dije* for I told them: the plural slips onto *lo*. Understand it, but say *se lo dije*.

problem: x:ser-event-estar-location pitfalls[1] gives the same pair with the honest note you'll hear está in casual speech. This script doesn't.
reason: x:ser-event-estar-location pitfalls[1] carries this exact caveat for the same pattern two lessons later, so the earlier card should not be stricter. The added sentence is copied from the course and creates no conflict.
quote: You're asking where it happens, not where a thing sits: *es*.
replacement: You're asking where it happens, not where a thing sits: *es*. You'll hear *está* in casual speech, but *es* is always right.

problem: Estoy alegre de que and estoy feliz de que are fine. The error in the wrong sentence is the missing de.
reason: Estar feliz or contento de que is standard and the bank has it from u30 (u30-0360, u47-0357), so the real slip is the missing de. The replacement says so and keeps me alegra as the main route.
quote: Spanish turns it around like *me gusta*: the news gladdens you, so *me alegra*.
replacement: Spanish usually turns it around like *me gusta*: the news gladdens you, so *me alegra*. If you start with *estoy*, it needs *de*: *Estoy feliz de que Vale esté aquí.*

problem: Seguir plus gerund isn't in this lesson. p:seguir-gerundio arrives at u32.
reason: g_gerund-ways never uses seguir, no u26 bank row has seguir plus gerund, and p:seguir-gerundio has priority 309 against 244 here; llegó cantando is in the rule. Follow-up: the node's es and en fields still carry Sigue lloviendo and It's still raining and need the same change.
quote: By doing, while doing: aprendí leyendo, sigue lloviendo, va mejorando
replacement: By doing, while doing: aprendí leyendo, llegó cantando, va mejorando

problem: Four paragraphs later the verb goes plural. No model links the two, so se venden carros looks like an exception. The verb agrees with the thing.
