problem: Gives the wrong cause. A change of subject explains *que* versus the infinitive. It does not explain the mood: *Llamo porque vienes* has a change of subject and takes the indicative. The mood comes from the second action being not yet real.
reason: A change of subject explains que, not the mood, as Llamo porque vienes shows. But 'hasn't happened yet when you plan it' fails for sin que (Hernando entra sin que nadie lo note), and the claim dropped the course's name for the form, so this is reworded.
quote: The second action belongs to someone else, so its verb takes the wish form: *veas*, *note*, *salgas*, *llegue*.
replacement: The second action belongs to someone else, so you need *que*. And it isn't a fact: it hasn't happened yet, or it doesn't happen at all. So its verb takes the wish form: *veas*, *note*, *salgas*, *llegue*.

problem: *No conozco a nadie que sepa* is not wished for. The test the script itself uses is better.
reason: *No conozco a nadie que sepa* involves no wish, and the replacement repeats the script's own opening test, do I know this thing exists.
quote: The verb after *que* tells your listener whether the thing is real or only wished for.
replacement: The verb after *que* tells your listener whether you know the thing exists.

problem: Contradicts the rule, which says *quizás* and *tal vez* take either form.
reason: The hook contradicts the rule, since *quizás* and *tal vez* take either form, and *can* fixes that. *Almost never* keeps the second half true to the DPD and compatible with the LB1-070 rewrite.
quote: two take the wish form, one never does.
replacement: two can take the wish form, one almost never does.

problem: Struck through as wrong, but this script's readAndPick[2] teaches the same shape as correct: *Busco a una abogada que sabe de arriendos* means a particular lawyer. x:relative-ind-subj also says the article does not decide. Indefinite plus indicative is correct when you have one in mind.
reason: This script's readAndPick[2] teaches indefinite plus indicative as correct for a particular lawyer, so the sentence is wrong only on the any-one reading. Only the why changes, so the quote now targets that string and wrong and right stay as they are.
quote: Almost. You haven't found it yet, so the verb after *que* takes the wish ending: *tenga*.
replacement: Almost. If you haven't found it and any one will do, use the wish ending: *tenga*. *Que tiene* would mean you already have one in mind.

problem: Ties the mood to the article. That contradicts x:relative-ind-subj ("The article helps... but it doesn't decide") and will collide with *el que quiera* at u50 (g:subj-free-relatives).
reason: *Busco el apartamento que tenga balcón* can be grammatical for whichever one has a balcony, and x:relative-ind-subj says the article doesn't decide. The replacement ties the mood to what the speaker knows, matching the rule.
quote: Almost. *El apartamento* is one you already know about, so the verb is ordinary: *tiene*.
replacement: Almost. If you mean one particular apartment you know, the verb is ordinary: *tiene*.

problem: Personal *a* signals a specific person, which pulls against the subjunctive reading this item teaches ("any lawyer, if there is one"). The bank mostly gets this right: 7 rows drop the *a* (u33-0039, u33-0054, u33-0055) against 2 that keep it (u33-0523, u33-0960). Dropping it also shows a second cue for the same idea.
reason: RAE's usage page gives *Busco un camarero que sepa inglés* without *a* for a non-specific person, and the DPD ties *a* to a person in mind (both through search snippets; rae.es refuses fetches). The old line is not ungrammatical, but this item teaches exactly that reading, and the replacement is the textbook form.
quote: Busco a una abogada que sepa de arriendos.
replacement: Busco una abogada que sepa de arriendos.

problem: The node title and example promise *siento que*, but the script never uses it and no script teaches the meaning switch. *Siento que estés triste* is I'm sorry you're sad; *Siento que estás triste* is I sense you're sad. Both moods are in the bank (u30-0037, u30-1135, u25-0392), and p:sentir-lo-de strikes the indicative through as wrong. This is the sharpest mood contrast in the emotion family and English speakers will not guess it.
reason: The gap is real and the contrast is standard; both forms are known at u30. I gave it its own paragraph because it is not one of the later-this-week phrases, and put the English in double quotes like this rule's own "buys"; LB1-043 fixes the matching card in p:sentir-lo-de.
quote: Later this week you'll add *me da pena que*, *me da rabia que* and *me da miedo que*. Same shape.
replacement:
Later this week you'll add *me da pena que*, *me da rabia que* and *me da miedo que*. Same shape.

One trap: *siento que* changes meaning with the verb. With the wish form it means "I'm sorry": *Siento que estés triste.* With the plain verb it means "I feel" or "I sense": *Siento que estás triste.*

problem: *Siento que tienes que irte* is correct Spanish with a different meaning. Keep the pitfall but say why.
reason: Siento que tienes que irte is correct Spanish meaning I feel you have to leave, so the old why misdescribes it. English in this file goes in double quotes, not italics (see the rule's "what happened with"), so I changed the markup and shortened one phrase.
quote: Feelings about someone else call for the *tengas* form, not *tienes*.
replacement: To say you are sorry, use the *tengas* form. *Siento que tienes que irte* means "I feel you have to leave".

problem: The bank drills 18 rows with *no es cierto que* or *no es verdad que* and 14 with *es imposible que* in u29, for example u29-0600 and u29-0624, tagged g:subj-doubt. No script in the course names either frame. x:fact-value teaches that *es verdad que* takes the plain verb and never says that denying it flips the mood.
reason: Verified: 18 no es cierto or no es verdad rows and 14 es imposible rows, u29 tagged g:subj-doubt, no script names either frame, and x:fact-value covers only the positive es verdad que. Both examples are standard, u29-0600 uses pierda, and the line fits between the frames and the idea paragraph.
quote: *Puede que* + wish form
replacement:
*Puede que* + wish form

The same goes when you deny a fact or rule it out: *No es cierto que el café pierda plata.* *Es imposible que lo sepa.*

problem: The bank drills *después de que* (u32-0103 to u32-0107) and *tan pronto como* (u32-0100) under this node, but the script names neither, and no script in the course teaches *después de que*. *Apenas*, the everyday Colombian as soon as, is also missing.
reason: Checked: no script in the course contains despues de que, while the bank drills it (5 rows) plus tan pronto como (2) and apenas (1) under this node. Apenas as as soon as is licensed since u26-0401, so it is not a sequencing problem; I added tan pronto como because the claim's own problem names it but its replacement left it out.
quote: The same goes for *en cuanto* (as soon as) and *hasta que* (until).
replacement: The same goes for *en cuanto*, *apenas* and *tan pronto como* (as soon as), *después de que* (after) and *hasta que* (until).

problem: *Irse* takes a destination all the time: *Me voy a la playa* (u22-0109), *se fue a Santa Marta* (u25-0274). The contrast x:ir-irse says it better: it looks back at where you are leaving.
reason: Me voy a la playa (u22-0109) and se fue a Santa Marta (u25-0274) are normal, so "the place no longer matters" is false. The replacement matches what x:ir-irse teaches the next day (irse looks back at where you are leaving).
quote: *irse* is leaving, and the place no longer matters: *Me voy*.
replacement: *irse* is leaving. It looks back at where you are leaving from, so you can say just *Me voy*, or add where you're off to: *Me voy a Medellín*.

problem: The title promises *quedar* and *quedarse*, but the script gives only *quedarse*. The contrast is never shown. It replaces it with *parecer* and *parecerse*, and the closing question ("just doing it, or leaving, or starting it?") does not fit *parecerse*.
reason: Of 39 rows targeting the node, 6 are parecerse and 0 are bare quedar; the script gives no quedar and p:quedar-en only arrives at u32, so the title fix is honest. Loose ends for the owner: graph forms[3] (Quedamos en vernos), the x:ir-irse line naming quedar and quedarse, and the script's closing question still need tidying.
quote: When "se" changes the meaning: ir and irse, dormir and dormirse, quedar and quedarse
replacement: When "se" changes the meaning: ir and irse, dormir and dormirse, parecer and parecerse

problem: *Ponerse* also marks lasting visible changes, and the bank tags these to this node: u30-0550 *Mi tío se puso muy gordo*, u30-0582 *La situación se puso fea*. The learner is taught that the change passes and then drilled on one that does not.
reason: The contradiction is real: u30-0550 se puso muy gordo and u30-0582 se puso fea are drilled under a rule saying the change passes. The cited chapter is wrong (verbs of becoming is Butt and Benjamin ch. 27 from memory, not 16), and "visible" is wrong for moods such as nervioso, so I reworded to stay compatible with LB1-049.
quote: *Ponerse* + a word for a mood or colour: it hits you, then passes. *Me puse rojo. Se puso contento.*
replacement: *Ponerse* + a word for a mood, colour or look: a change you can see or feel, usually quick. *Me puse rojo. Se puso contento.*

problem: Same as above, and it excludes *volverse famoso*, which is in the node title and in the bank (u30-0589, u30-0596).
reason: Volverse famoso is in the node title and in u30-0589 and u30-0596, and the current why wrongly excludes it, while "only for quick moods and colours" repeats the fault of LB1-048. The replacement is compatible with the amended LB1-048 text.
quote: Fame is a status you reach over time, so *hacerse*; *ponerse* is only for quick moods and colours.
replacement: Fame is a status you reach over time, so *hacerse* or *volverse*; *ponerse* is for a change in how someone looks or feels.

problem: *Vale quiere volverse famosa* is natural, is what the node title says, and is marked wrong because accept lists only *Vale se quiere hacer famosa*.
reason: Vale quiere volverse famosa is natural and matches the title, and it is wrongly rejected today. The accept list already allows the pronoun in front for hacerse, so the same variant belongs here for volverse.
quote: Becoming something through effort uses *hacerse*.
replacement: Add to accept: "Vale quiere volverse famosa." and "Vale se quiere volver famosa."

problem: Spanish does not say *for arriving*, it says *por llegar*. pitfalls[1] says the opposite: "Unlike English *for arriving*, Spanish uses the infinitive."
reason: Spanish does not say for arriving, and pitfalls[1] of the same script says "Unlike English", so the line contradicts itself. The replacement is accurate and shares the sentence with LB1-069 without overlapping it.
quote: English says *for arriving*, and so does Spanish: no *porque*, no changing the verb.
replacement: English says *for arriving*; Spanish says *por llegar*: no *porque*, and no *-ando* form.

problem: Untrue on both sides, in this script's own translations: *Debes descansar* is You must rest and *Debe de estar cansada* is She must be tired, so English uses *must* for both, and *debe* versus *debe de* differ by a word, not an ending.
reason: The script's own glosses give must for both debes and debe de, and debe versus debe de differs by a word, not an ending. This file puts English in double quotes ("would", "shouldn't"), so I changed the italics; the Spanish point stands as claimed.
quote: English uses different words for each job. Spanish keeps one verb and changes the ending.
replacement: English uses "must" for two of these jobs and "should" for the third. Spanish keeps one verb: the ending, or the little *de*, tells you which job it is doing.

problem: Not a fast speech effect. Educated written usage also allows *deber* without *de* for probability.
reason: RAE's own answer (RAEinforma on X, quoting the DPD; rae.es refused direct access) says deber + infinitive for probability "está extendido en la lengua culta", so this is not a fast speech effect. The script already accepts Vale debe estar en la cocina, so the replacement matches the checker.
quote: In fast speech people often drop the *de* from a guess, so listen to the meaning.
replacement: People often drop the *de* from a guess, even in careful writing, so go by the meaning.

problem: Not regional. Spanish has no present subjunctive for a finished past, so *hayas venido* corresponds to both *viniste* and *has venido* everywhere.
reason: Right that the mapping of hayas venido to viniste is not regional, but the claim overreaches: "any finished action" ignores me alegra que vinieras, and it is not true that Spanish has only this form for a finished past. Dropping the words In Latin America fixes the false implication and keeps the sentence's accurate "often".
quote: In Latin America it often covers a recent finished action too, where English says simply *you came*.
replacement: It often covers a recent finished action too, where English says simply *you came*.

problem: Addressed to a friend about an arrival still to come, this needs the subjunctive, by the rule learned at u32 ("is it still in the future?"). The indicative reads as a general truth about arrivals. Translation yourTurn[4] should make *llegues* the answer and keep *llegas* in accept.
reason: A specific arrival still to come takes the subjunctive, exactly as the u32 test says, and llegas only works as a general truth; proportional clauses pattern with temporal ones here (from memory, a web search found no direct authority). The same sentence also stands in the rule, so apply this at every occurrence and see LB1-117 for the answer, accept and why.
quote: Mientras más temprano llegas, mejor.
replacement: Mientras más temprano llegues, mejor.

problem: The title and the node sentence (*Ganamos el doble que el año pasado*) promise *el doble* and *más de la mitad*. The rule, examples and exercises teach neither. *El doble* has 0 rows in B1. *Mientras más* has 0 rows in u36 to u41 and 1 in the whole bank. Of 121 rows tagged to this node, 67 are plain *más de* or *menos de*.
reason: Measured: el doble has 0 rows before u54, mitad 0 in the 121 node rows, mientras más 1 row in the whole bank (u45), so the title and the node sentence promise what the lesson does not teach and the taught pattern is barely drilled. My loose count of plain más de or menos de rows is 83, not 67, but the point stands; the fix is a choice between trimming the title or adding content and rows.
quote: Comparing in numbers and degrees: el doble, más de la mitad, cada vez más, cuanto más…

problem: Grammatical Spanish, struck through under "Almost everyone slips here", and g:passive-ser teaches this exact construction two units later. It is a register note, not an error. Delete it or move it to the rule.
reason: The why is already a register note ("in everyday Spanish, se does the job"), and g:passive-ser says the same two units later: "In everyday talk people usually say... Se vendió el edificio, so expect to read this more than to say it." The course is consistent, and overusing the ser passive is the classic English calque, so the pitfall earns its place.
quote: Fueron vendidos todos los almuerzos.

problem: Adds "to make sure". The Spanish is *Joaquín le pidió a Eulalia que la familia hiciera las paces.*
reason: The owner's exactness rule covers translation cards, and the hook is a display gloss with no expected answer (teach.tsx). Pedirle a X que Y haga has no literal natural English, and the replacement is a garden path (asked Eulalia for the family...), while the existing English keeps the meaning and matches the story's own gloss in ch122.
quote: Joaquín asked Eulalia to make sure the family made peace.
replacement: Joaquín asked Eulalia for the family to make peace.

problem: When the order is still pending, Latin American speakers commonly keep the present subjunctive: *Me dijo que la llame mañana*. This is accepted usage and the learner will meet it in Bogotá.
reason: A present subjunctive after a past verb is grammatical when the ordered event still lies ahead of the moment of speaking, and it is well documented in Latin America (Carrasco Gutiérrez 1999 and Suñer and Padilla-Rivera 1987, from memory; web search did not surface them). It is a recognition note only, so the production rule is untouched.
quote: Teachers call this reported (indirect) commands: the order moves into the past, so the past subjunctive follows *dijo* or *pidió*.
replacement: Teachers call this reported (indirect) commands: the order moves into the past, so the past subjunctive follows *dijo* or *pidió*. If the order still stands, you will also hear the present: *Me dijo que la llame mañana.*

problem: Presents *ojalá* as new at u41. The learner met it at u22 and spent u40 d1 (g:imperfect-subj) on this exact content, with the same sentences: *Ojalá pudiéramos quedarnos*, *Ojalá tuviera*, *Ojalá fuera*. Use this day for what u40 did not cover, such as *ojalá* with a person other than I, or merge the nodes.
reason: Confirmed: g:subj-wishes taught ojalá at u22, and g:imperfect-subj at u40 d1 has the same hope against wish contrast and the same sentences (Ojalá pudiéramos quedarnos, Ojalá tuviera, Ojalá fuera). Rewording the hook would hide the symptom only: the day needs new content or a merge of the two nodes.
quote: You need *ojalá*, the Spanish way to say "I wish" and "if only".

problem: Wrong dialect, presented as Bogotá speech. The DPD marks *igual* for *maybe* as colloquial Spain. In American Spanish a sentence-initial *igual* is documented as concessive, *anyway*, *regardless*: *Igual voy* is I'm going anyway. So the 21 bank rows likely mean something else in the setting they are written for: *Igual hace frío en la noche, lleva chaqueta* would read as It's cold at night anyway, not It might be cold. *De pronto* for maybe is correct Colombian usage and should stay. The rest of the rule, the examples, pitfalls[1] and the bank rows need rewriting with it.
reason: Unresolved: ask a Bogotá speaker what Igual no viene, no sé means. From memory Colombian *igual* is anyway and the DPD snippet confines maybe to colloquial Spain, but no source covers Colombia and web search was unavailable in this pass; if maybe is rejected, drop it from production as a rewrite, because the claim's string alone would contradict the next paragraph, the pitfalls, yourTurn and personal.
quote: *Igual* at the start also means *maybe*, in casual talk.
replacement: *Igual* at the start of a sentence usually means something else in Latin America: *anyway*. *Igual voy* is I'm going anyway. In Spain it can mean maybe, so don't be surprised if a Spanish friend uses it that way.

problem: Same issue.
reason: Stands or falls with LB1-061. The line makes a positive claim about Bogotá speech that no source supports, but *usually means anyway* is equally unverified for Bogotá, so neither wording ships before a native answers; *de pronto* as maybe is not in doubt.
quote: Listen to people in Bogotá for an afternoon and you will hear *de pronto* and *igual* all the time, and neither means what the dictionary says. In everyday speech, both mean *maybe*.
replacement: Listen to people in Bogotá for an afternoon and you will hear *de pronto* and *igual* all the time. *De pronto* means *maybe*. *Igual* usually means *anyway*.

problem: *Confiar en que* also takes the future indicative, which may be the more usual choice: *Confío en que todo saldrá bien*. A learner who says this will be marked wrong and told it is not allowed.
reason: Confío en que todo saldrá bien is correct and common, so "it takes the subjunctive" is too strict (NGLE ch. 25 from memory; only a usage example found online). The claim's "usually" is an unproved frequency claim that contradicts its own problem statement, so I removed it; yourTurn answers worded with will should also accept the future, for example Confiamos en que el negocio crecerá este año.
quote: Teachers call this a hope or expectation phrase. Like other wishes, it takes the subjunctive.
replacement: Teachers call this a hope or expectation phrase. Like other wishes, it takes the subjunctive, but you will also meet the future: *Confío en que todo saldrá bien.*

problem: *Ser de* is common with measurements: *La mesa es de dos metros*, *El apartamento es de 70 metros*. What is wrong is *es dos metros* with no *de*.
reason: "Spanish has no ser for size" is false as written: la mesa es de dos metros, el apartamento es de 70 metros and plain es grande are all normal. The replacement names the real error, matches pitfalls[0], and leaves the verbs taught unchanged.
quote: Spanish has no *ser* for size or weight. It uses a verb for each question:
replacement: Spanish doesn't say *es dos metros*. It uses a verb for each question:

problem: Struck through as wrong, but *Sí, con gusto* or *Sí, claro* is a normal answer to *¿Te importaría...?* in real speech: the pragmatics of the request win over the literal logic. Keep the advice that *no* is the safe answer, not the claim that *sí* is a mistake.
reason: The why is already hedged ("Strictly... start with no so it is clear") and does not claim sí is impossible; it gives the safe answer for a learner, which holds however often people say Sí, claro. No string is proposed, and whether Bogotá speakers say Sí, con gusto would not change that advice.
quote: Sí, con gusto.

problem: Struck through as wrong. It is correct Spanish, and the owner's policy is that Peninsular forms are accepted. The why is fine; the strikethrough is not. Reframe as a preference.
reason: Unlike LB1-057, this breaks a standing decision: a Peninsular form is struck through as a slip at B1, and yourTurn[2] has an empty accept list, so it is also rejected as an answer. Delete pitfalls[1], since the rule already says Latin Americans use pareció, and add ¿Qué te ha parecido el restaurante? to yourTurn[2].accept; that is two structural edits, not one string.
quote: ¿Qué te ha parecido el restaurante?

problem: Plain verb means the infinitive here and the indicative elsewhere.
reason: Plain verb is used for the indicative elsewhere in B1 (g:subj-emotion, p:de-pronto-igual), and the pattern's own note says Pensaba / Iba a + infinitive. Infinitive is an established term in the scripts, so the edit is safe.
quote: First, the plan: *pensaba* or *iba a*, in the imperfect, plus a plain verb.
replacement: First, the plan: *pensaba* or *iba a*, in the imperfect, plus an infinitive.

problem: Same collision.
reason: Same terminology collision as LB1-069, and the example right after it shows the form. A safe edit, though three other "plain verb" uses in this script are left for a sweep.
quote: then *importaría*, then the plain verb: *¿Te importaría cerrar la ventana?*
replacement: then *importaría*, then the infinitive: *¿Te importaría cerrar la ventana?*

problem: Same collision. The -r gloss saves it, but the term should be one thing.
reason: Plain verb means the indicative in the mood lessons and the infinitive here (about 170 hits across 73 scripts, both senses), so the collision is real. The fix is safe and touches a different substring from LB1-051; a sweep would be cleaner than line edits, and two "plain -r verb" whys remain in this script.
quote: *Por* + a plain verb ending in *-r*: the reason is an action.
replacement: *Por* + an infinitive, the form ending in *-r*: the reason is an action.

problem: Fine as production advice, but false as a statement about Spanish, and this course is Latin American by decision. The DPD says *a lo mejor* takes the indicative almost always, while the subjunctive is also possible, especially in American Spanish. Keep the plain verb as the answer, drop "classic mistake".
reason: The DPD entry *mejor* (read through search snippets) says *a lo mejor* is almost always indicative but the subjunctive is possible, especially in American Spanish, and one corpus study found 98.3% indicative, so the absolutes are false while the plain verb stays the right thing to teach. This text alone would contradict rule line 2, smallPrint, yourTurn[0].why, yourTurn[6].why and pitfalls[0].why, plus p:seguramente-probablemente and p:de-pronto-igual, so they must move together.
quote: *A lo mejor* has no choice: plain verb, every time. *A lo mejor tengas razón* is a classic mistake.
replacement: *A lo mejor* takes the plain verb almost every time. You may hear the wish form in Latin America, but the plain verb is always right.

problem: Same issue.
reason: *Only choice* is the absolute the DPD contradicts, and the replacement stays true whatever happens to LB1-070, so it can go in on its own.
quote: Almost. Same rule: with *a lo mejor* the plain verb is the only choice.
replacement: Almost. Same rule: with *a lo mejor*, use the plain verb.

problem: The advice is right but "never" is too strong. The current DPD notes that *deber de* for obligation also occurs in cultivated usage, though much less often.
reason: Verified: the current DPD says deber de, "aunque con frecuencia mucho menor, también se usa en la lengua culta para expresar obligación", with a Mexican example, and an earlier recommendation rejecting it was withdrawn. So never is now too strong, and the replacement keeps the advice unchanged.
quote: Almost. The *de* belongs only to guesses, never to advice.
replacement: Almost. For advice, leave out the *de*. It belongs to guesses.

problem: *Abrió la caja que encontró* is grammatical, and Latin American speakers often leave order to the context. *Había encontrado* is clearer, not obligatory.
reason: Takes había states an obligation that does not exist: the preterite in a relative clause is correct, especially in Latin America. The replacement keeps the lesson's point about order without the false rule, and I prefer it to CX-028, which covers the same text.
quote: He found the box before he opened it, so the earlier event takes *había*.
replacement: He found the box before he opened it. *Había encontrado* makes that order clear.

problem: *Más y más* is grammatical. It is less idiomatic, not wrong.
reason: The why never calls más y más ungrammatical: it says Spanish uses cada vez más, which is true, and it opens with Almost. Steering English speakers off a calque toward the everyday form is a defensible simplification at B1, so nothing needs changing.
quote: Almost. English repeats "more and more", but Spanish uses *cada vez más*.
replacement: Almost. *Más y más* exists, but the everyday Spanish is *cada vez más*.

problem: At u32 it does not come later. The bank has *pienso que* in 7 rows before u32, and the learner has used *creo que* since A2.
reason: p:pensar-en taught pensar que at u28 (Pienso que es un error) and seven rows use pienso que before u32, so "comes later" is false at u32. The replacement is correct and fits the sentence.
quote: *Pensar* here is not about opinions: for those, *pienso que* comes later.
replacement: *Pensar* here is not about opinions: for those, use *pienso que*.

problem: The lesson on this exact point contains a reversed sentence. *Este* is the nearer item and must agree with *mi prima*, so it should be *esta*; *aquel* points to the earlier *mi hermano*. As written, gender forces *este* onto the brother and *aquella* onto the cousin, which reverses the rule and contradicts the English ("the latter brought bread").
reason: *Este* can only be the brother, so the Spanish reverses the rule and the English; the fix is right. The first reviewer's accept change is essential: accept holds semicolon fragments, including the old wrong clause este trajo pan y esta trajo jugo.
quote: Mi hermano y mi prima llegaron tarde; este trajo pan y aquella trajo jugo.
replacement: {"es": "Mi hermano y mi prima llegaron tarde; esta trajo pan y aquel trajo jugo.", "accept": []}

problem: The lesson on this exact point contains a reversed sentence. *Este* can only be Simón, the first named, so *este* is pointing at the former, and the English says "the latter talks". Two proximal demonstratives in a row also defeat the contrast. To match the English: Vale (latter) talks, Simón (former) listens.
reason: *Esta* is Vale, the last named, and *aquel* is Simón, so the Spanish now matches the latter talks and the former listens, exactly as g:referring-back teaches.
quote: Simón y Vale están en la sala. Este habla y esta escucha.
replacement: Simón y Vale están en la sala. Esta habla y aquel escucha.

problem: The lesson on this exact point contains a reversed sentence. The last named is *un hermano*, so the latter must be *este*. *Esta* can only be the sister, the first named. Spanish and English disagree on who lives where.
reason: *Este* is the brother, last named, and *aquella* the sister, which matches the English and the rule.
quote: Vale tiene una hermana y un hermano. Esta vive en Cali y aquel vive en Bogotá.

problem: Negation does not force the switch here. Unlike no creo que, these verbs leave a choice, and the choice carries meaning. No vi que estabas ahí says you were there and I missed it. No vi que estuvieras ahí says I saw no sign that you were. No dijo que era urgente says it was urgent and he left that out. The rule erases the distinction and the model the learner needs, and the course already teaches the indicative after no sabía que and no me di cuenta de que.
reason: The forced switch is false (NGLE 25.7c via the first reviewer). I kept that text with two changes: plain *-r* verb becomes infinitive, the term LB1-030 settles on, bridged by *la vi salir* from u46 d4, and the link to *no creo que* comes back. Ship with CX-004, CX-005, CX-006, LB2-013, LB2-014 and LB2-016; also unclaimed: hook.line needs can change, yourTurn[5] and [6] need the indicative in accept and softer whys, and examples[4].en should read I saw no sign that Vale was angry.
quote:
Put *no* in front and you are no longer vouching, so the verb after *que* switches to the past form that ends in *-ra*: *estaba* becomes *estuviera*, *era* becomes *fuera*, *tenía* becomes *tuviera*, *llegó* becomes *llegara*, *sonó* becomes *sonara*.

*No vi que estuviera enojada.* *No dijo que fuera urgente.* It is the same switch as after *no creo que*.

So does *No es que no quiera, es que no puedo*: the first half is the thing you deny.

English keeps one verb for both. Spanish changes it.
replacement:
Put *no* in front and you now have a choice, and it says who is vouching.

Keep the ordinary verb and you still vouch for it: it was true, and someone missed it or left it out. *No vi que estabas ahí.* You were there, and I missed you. *No dijo que era urgente.* It was urgent, and he left that out.

Switch to the *-ra* form, as after *no creo que*, and nobody vouches: *estaba* becomes *estuviera*, *era* becomes *fuera*, *tenía* becomes *tuviera*, *llegó* becomes *llegara*, *sonó* becomes *sonara*. *No dije que fuera urgente.* I never claimed that. *No vi que estuviera enojada.* I saw no sign of it.

Three cases leave no choice. With *nadie* or *nada*, use the *-ra* form: *No vi que llegara nadie.* After *no veo que*, use the wish form: *No veo que esté enojada.* *No es que* denies the idea, so it takes the wish form too: *No es que no quiera, es que no puedo.*

If you missed something that did happen, you can also use the infinitive, as in *la vi salir*: *No oí sonar el teléfono.*

English keeps one verb for both. Spanish tells you who stands behind the claim.

problem: Marks correct Spanish as wrong. This is the natural sentence when she was angry and I failed to notice, as in the everyday Perdón, no vi que estabas ahí. The English of the same card, I didn't see that Vale was angry, normally presupposes she was.

The slot must still change, through CX-004, which uses a firm error.

problem: English I didn't hear the phone ring reports missing a real event. Spanish says that with perception verb plus infinitive, taught four days earlier in p:la-vi-salir at u46 d4. Oír que with the -ra form means I did not hear that it rang, leaving open whether it did. Same sentence at readAndPick[4] and yourTurn[3].

If it rang and you missed it, *No oí que sonó* and *No oí sonar el teléfono* work too."}

problem: Marks correct, indeed the commoner, Spanish as wrong, and directly contradicts g:subj-doubt pitfalls[1], which marks the subjunctive wrong after the same words. A learner is penalised in opposite directions at B1 and B2.

problem: Presented as a forced choice between sea and es, with es rejected (accept is empty). Both are fine. Accept should include No dudo que el plan es bueno, pero es caro.

problem: B1 file, flagged because it conflicts with B2. p:concede-pero and nine bank rows at u44 use this construction as correct. Marking it wrong sets up the contradiction.

problem: True as the default, but stated as an absolute that a later lesson breaks.

replacement: *No dudo que* is certainty, so the indicative is the natural choice, but the subjunctive is also correct, especially when you grant a point before a *pero*.

problem: Everything is too strong. If the content still holds, Spanish keeps the tense (Dijo que viene mañana, when tomorrow has not come), and the preterite is often retained, especially in Latin America (Dijo que ya habló con ellos). A learner taught total backshift will mark normal Colombian speech as an error and misjudge what speakers imply.
reason: Everything is false, and u25 already says a past stays put. The first reviewer's text gives the two exceptions in plain words without a new absolute; it needs LC-029, LB2-024 and LB2-025 in the same commit, because pitfalls[3] and yourTurn[1] would otherwise reject forms this paragraph allows.
quote: When you retell a conversation after the fact, everything takes one step back, in time and in place. Spanish does it as faithfully as English.
replacement: When you retell a conversation after the fact, most things take one step back, in time and in place, just as in English. Two things can stop that. If what was said still holds right now, the verb can stay: *Dijo que Bogotá es fría*, or *Dijo que viene mañana* if tomorrow has not come yet. And a plain past often stays as it is: *Dijo que ya habló con ellos.*

problem: Correct Spanish when Simón is still missing. Marked wrong without context, and the why claims the question must step back.

quote: Vale preguntó dónde está Simón.

The replacement is the whole yourTurn[1] object with habló in accept; the prompt keeps *hablé*, which stays wrong here because it would mean I spoke.

problem: The rule says vengo becomes venía, and the source line is Mañana vengo, so the rule points to venía. The card asks the learner to pick and rewards vendría, while silently accepting venía.

replacement: Both work here. *Venía* steps back from *vengo*, and *vendría* steps back from the future idea. For a promise, *vendría* is clearer. *Mañana* becomes *al día siguiente*.

problem: The lesson moves tenses, times and places but not persons, which is where reported speech most often goes wrong: Tengo tu libro must become Dijo que tenía mi libro. It also teaches allí while the examples and Your Turn use the Colombian allá.
reason: The person shift is missing from the rule, and the script's own cards use *allá*. Changed only so the quoted Spanish is in italics, as the file does for direct speech (*"Mañana vengo."*).
quote: *aquí* → *allí*
replacement:
*aquí* → *allí* or *allá*

Who is speaking shifts too: *"Tengo tu libro"* becomes *Dijo que tenía mi libro*.

problem: Correct Spanish when the arrival is still ahead of the speaker now: He told me he will call when he gets here, and he has not arrived yet. Marked wrong without context.
reason: Me dijo que me llamará cuando llegue is correct while the arrival is still ahead, the same retained-tense case as LB2-024, and the why states a blanket rule. The replacement adds the context in which the step back is needed.
quote: Me dijo que me llamará cuando llegue.
replacement: {"wrong": "Me dijo que me llamará cuando llegue. (he arrived last week)", "right": "Me dijo que me llamaría cuando llegara.", "why": "The arrival is already behind you, so both parts step back. If it is still ahead of you now, this sentence is fine."}

problem: Marks correct Spanish as wrong. A present judgement about a past act is exactly what this sentence says: I think it is wrong that you left yesterday. Present matrix with imperfect subjunctive is standard.
reason: Me parece mal que te fueras ayer is correct: a present judgement on a past act takes the past subjunctive (NGLE from memory, and everyday usage). The new pair tests a real error, the indicative after the judgement.
quote: Me parece mal que te fueras ayer.
replacement: {"wrong": "Me pareció mal que te vas.", "right": "Me pareció mal que te fueras.", "why": "Almost. After *me pareció mal que*, the verb takes the *-ra* form."}

problem: The past of the action alone is enough. The rule implies Me parece mal que te fueras is impossible.
reason: Same point as LB2-029: the rule ties *-ra* to the judgement alone, when a past action also brings it. The replacement fixes that in one clause and fits the new pitfall.
quote: The *-ra* verbs (*fueras, dijeras, avisaran*) follow because the judgement is in the past.
replacement: The *-ra* verbs (*fueras, dijeras, avisaran*) follow because the judgement or the action is in the past: *Me parece mal que te fueras ayer* works too.

problem: Both forms are natural, and the indicative is at least as common, as with no sabía que. The bank row tagged to this very pattern, u45-0790, uses the indicative: Mi hermana no tenía ni idea de que yo vivía en Bogotá.
reason: Both moods are natural and bank u45-0790 uses the indicative, so a flat usually misleads. The claim's indicative at least as common is not shown (Ngrams has ni idea de que estaba ahead of estuviera, but estabas level with estuvieras and fuera ahead of era), so the replacement stands because it makes no frequency claim.
quote: In the past, the next verb is usually in the "-ra" form: *No tenía ni idea de que estuvieras aquí.*
replacement: In the past, the next verb can be the ordinary past or the "-ra" form, and both are natural: *No tenía ni idea de que estabas aquí*, *No tenía ni idea de que estuvieras aquí.*

problem: The correction implies only the -ra form is possible, and the why says Spanish uses it. Estabas is fine. The sentence with estás is itself acceptable while the person is still here.
reason: Follows from LB2-031: *estabas* is fine, and *estás* is fine while the person is still here, so the card cannot correct to the *-ra* form. Dropping *de* before *que* is a genuine standard error, and the replacement tests that instead.
quote: No tenía ni idea de que estás aquí.
replacement: {"wrong": "No tenía ni idea que estabas aquí.", "right": "No tenía ni idea de que estabas aquí.", "why": "Keep the *de* before *que*."}

problem: Grammatical, and common as a more tentative question. It differs in force rather than being an error. The why is fine as far as it goes, but the card presents it as wrong.
reason: The why already scopes the card to the nudge (In this question you believe it is expensive) and the rule sets that frame, so nothing false is claimed. Teaching sources tie the indicative to expecting a yes, and in Ngrams *no crees que es mejor* is present while *no crees que sea mejor* falls below the data threshold, so the taught contrast is fair here.
quote: ¿No crees que sea muy caro?
replacement: {"wrong": "¿No crees que sea muy caro? (you are sure it is expensive)", "right": "¿No crees que es muy caro?", "why": "You believe it is expensive, so keep the indicative. With *sea* you are really asking, and you lean less hard."}

problem: False for the as long as sense, and the bank proves it at u50-1602: Dijimos que no firmaríamos nada mientras hubiera dudas. See also u50-1610 mientras no tuviera sus cosas.
reason: Always is false, but the claim's example needs g:subj-future-in-past (u50) and this drill is u45, so it uses the script's own car sentence, which needs only the -ra forms of u41. *Always* is dropped for while too (Dijo que esperaría mientras yo comiera), and yourTurn[6].why repeats the old line and should become: A past "while" takes an ordinary verb.
quote: In the past it is always an ordinary verb: *Mientras estudiaba, trabajaba.*
replacement: A past "while" takes an ordinary verb: *Mientras estudiaba, trabajaba.* A past "as long as" takes the *-ra* form: *Me dijo que podía usar el carro mientras lo cuidara.*

problem: Marked wrong under the claim that both halves need the same time frame. That is false: a lasting condition with a past result is standard (Si fuera más paciente, no habría dicho eso). This sentence is only wrong if the money is about that past moment.
reason: Both halves need the same time frame is false: with a lasting condition, *si* + imperfect subjunctive + conditional perfect is standard (todoele: Si fueras más puntual, no te habrías perdido el inicio), and UDEP's objection covers only a condition placed in the past. Wording changed because *tuviera* is not about what is true.
quote: Si tuviera plata, habría viajado.
replacement: {"wrong": "Si tuviera plata el año pasado, habría viajado.", "right": "Si hubiera tenido plata el año pasado, habría viajado.", "why": "*El año pasado* is over, so the *si* half needs *hubiera tenido*. *Tuviera* only fits now or always, as in *Si fuera más paciente, no habría dicho eso.*"}

problem: Only one of the two mixed patterns is allowed. Learners need the other to understand ordinary sentences like Si no fuera tan terco, habría aceptado.
reason: Same evidence as LB2-035: the script allows one mix when both are in ordinary use. Follow-on: yourTurn[1] (*Si ___ plata, habría viajado.*) has no time word and rejects *tuviera*, so it should gain *el año pasado*.
quote: Keep the two halves in the same time. A word like *ayer* or *el año pasado* tells you to go to the second pair. You may also mix them on purpose: a past "if" with a result about today, as in *Si hubiera aceptado, hoy viviría en Toronto.*
replacement: The two halves usually share a time. A word like *ayer* or *el año pasado* tells you to go to the second pair. You can also mix them on purpose. A past "if" with a result about today: *Si hubiera aceptado, hoy viviría en Toronto.* A lasting "if" with a result in the past: *Si fuera más paciente, no habría dicho eso.*

problem: Wrong only in the intended sense of finding out at the time. Si supiera nadar, habría venido is correct. The lesson title promises mixed conditionals and gives only one direction.
reason: Bare *supiera* here reads as finding out, and the why rightly says it imagines now and that the past needs *hubiera sabido*, so nothing false stands. The other mixed direction arrives one day later in x:si-past-present-unreal through LB2-036.
quote: Si supiera, habría venido.
replacement: {"wrong": "Si supiera, habría venido. (you mean: if I had found out at the time)", "right": "Si hubiera sabido, habría venido.", "why": "*Supiera* is about now or always. For finding out back then you need *hubiera sabido*. *Si supiera nadar, habría venido* is fine, because knowing how to swim is a lasting fact."}

problem: The learner met the same form at u29 in g:conditional-past-guess for guessing about the past: tendría veinte años means he was probably twenty. Now La policía tendría pruebas means the police reportedly have evidence. The script never mentions the collision or how to tell them apart.
reason: The collision with the u29 guess is real and unmentioned, since both are the same form (RAE glossary lists them apart, from memory). Moved to the end of the paragraph, because in the claim's spot *It lives in news* would point at the guess.
quote: It lives in news and formal reports, and a *según...* often names the source.
replacement:
It lives in news and formal reports, and a *según...* often names the source.

Careful: you have met this form before, for guessing about the past. *Tendría veinte años*: he was probably twenty. A named source or a news report points to the rumour. A story about the past points to the guess.

problem: The rule says this form lives in news and formal reports, then asks for neighbourhood gossip, where it would sound odd.
reason: The script's own examples are neighbour talk (Según un vecino, Altamira ya habría comprado tres edificios), so the prompt practises what was taught. A newspaper prompt would also sit badly with LC-039's advice to be careful writing this form.
quote: Write two harmless bits of gossip you have heard about a neighbour or a famous person. Start each one with *según...* and put the verb in the conditional.
replacement: Write two short news items, in the style of a newspaper, about your town or a famous person. Start each one with *según...* and put the verb in the conditional.

problem: By g:conditional-rumour, the simple conditional reports now or later, and a past claim needs habría habido. So reportedly were breaks the rule this pattern requires. With no source and a past reading, Habría unas cien personas is the B1 guess: there must have been about a hundred. Same text at the Read and Pick option.
reason: The simple conditional also passes on a past state, as *había* maps to *habría*: Colombian press writes of a past crash that *el conductor estaría borracho* (Publimetro 2025), and bank u45-0144 reads the same way. The rule's conditional perfect holds for events, the hook is a past protest, and *There are* would pull the Spanish from its natural reading; this rests on press usage, not a grammar.
quote: There were reportedly about a hundred people in the square.
replacement: There are reportedly about a hundred people in the square.

problem: Rumour of a past fact would be Habría habido unas cincuenta personas under the course's own rule. The answer given, Habría unas cincuenta personas, reports the present.
reason: Same as LB2-040: *Había cincuenta personas* to *Habría unas cincuenta personas* is a past state passed on, which is the right mapping, and *Hay* would fit a live report only. If the overlap with the u29 guess is a worry, name a source in the Spanish as bank u45-0144 does.
quote: Make it a rumour, "there were reportedly about fifty people": *Había cincuenta personas.*
replacement: Make it a rumour, "there are reportedly about fifty people": *Hay cincuenta personas.*

problem: Llegarán pronto is a plain future. Probably is not in the Spanish, and the conjectural future refers to now, not later (the script itself says Estará en casa is about now). Teaches a wrong link between future tense and probability about the future, and breaks the exact-translation rule.
reason: *Llegarán pronto* is a plain future and *probably* is not in the Spanish, so the option breaks the exact English rule and suggests the future of probability points ahead. The answer index stays 1.
quote: They will probably arrive soon.
replacement: They will arrive soon.

problem: The script's own examples use could have. Can have is rare in this meaning.
reason: The script's own lines say could have (Where could I have left my keys?, Who could have left this cup here?), and can have is rare in this sense.
quote: English says "must have", "will have" or "can have".
replacement: English says "must have", "will have" or "could have".

problem: Sino before a finite verb needs que. This row targets the structure being taught, so the learner is drilled in the error.
reason: *Sino* before a finite verb needs *que* in this register (DPD, via the first reviewer's search summary). It depends on LB2-046, because without that line nothing teaches *sino que* before u46.
quote: ¿No solo estudias español, sino también trabajas en español?
replacement: ¿No solo estudias español, sino que también trabajas en español?

problem: As u44-t-argument-markers-0028.
reason: Same point and same dependency on LB2-046 as LB2-044.
quote: ¿Tus vecinos no solo hablan mucho, sino también ayudan?
replacement: ¿Tus vecinos no solo hablan mucho, sino que también ayudan?

problem: g:pero-sino promised sino que comes later, and this is where it is needed. Without it, learners extend sino también to finite verbs, as two bank rows do.
reason: g:pero-sino's smallPrint promises *sino que* for later, and nothing teaches it before p:no-es-que-sino-que at u46, while this lesson's rows need it (LB2-044, LB2-045). The example is correct and uses no new grammar.
quote: *No solo… sino también…*: not only this but also that. After a *no solo*, English "but" becomes *sino*.
replacement: *No solo… sino también…*: not only this but also that. After a *no solo*, English "but" becomes *sino*. If a whole new verb follows, add *que*: *No solo vende pan, sino que también enseña a hacerlo.*

problem: Here implies actualmente sometimes means actually. It never does, as p:actualmente says plainly. And correcting someone takes en realidad, not de hecho.
reason: *Here* wrongly implies *actualmente* sometimes means actually, against p:actualmente at u32, which also taught *en realidad* for correcting. The replacement matches that lesson.
quote: English "actually" is not *actualmente* here; use *de hecho*.
replacement: *Actualmente* never means "actually": it means "nowadays". For "actually", use *de hecho* to add proof and *en realidad* to correct something.

problem: Sentence-initial En cambio, nosotros queremos quedarnos is equally correct.
reason: *En cambio, nosotros queremos quedarnos* is standard, so sits right after is too narrow. The fix corrects only that and keeps the point about the article.
quote: Almost. *En cambio* has no article, and it sits right after the thing you contrast.
replacement: Almost. *En cambio* has no article. It can open the sentence or sit right after the thing you contrast.

problem: ¿Será que me puedes ayudar? with tú is ordinary Colombian. g:softening in the same unit says it works with any person. Será que softens, and it does not fix the pronoun. It needs testing with a native Colombian.
reason: García Rodríguez (Diálogo de la lengua, 2012, abstract only) finds *será que* + *poder* across hierarchical, commercial and very intimate relations, and g:softening yourTurn[6].why says any person, so *usted* belongs to this card and not to the form. The replacement says exactly that.
quote: *¿Será que…?* is the extra-courteous Colombian opener, followed by *usted* forms.
replacement: *¿Será que…?* is the gentle Colombian opener. It takes *usted* forms here because the request is formal. With a friend it goes with *tú*.

problem: Placing it above podría as a higher formal rung is doubtful. It is a softener, orthogonal to formality, as ch125 says better: La cuarta es muy bogotana: pides sin pedir.
reason: *Very courteous* is not false, since that study calls this *tratamiento cortés*, yet it also finds the form in intimate talk, so whether it sits above *¿Me podría…?* on a formality ladder is a usage question. The replacement does not move the rung anyway; a Bogotá speaker should rank the two.
quote: Literally "could it be that you can…". Very Colombian and very courteous.
replacement: Literally "could it be that you can…". Very Colombian: you ask without quite asking.

problem: Misdiagnoses the fault. The real error is tú with señor. Páseme la sal, por favor is perfectly polite, and the same unit teaches Llámeme lo antes posible as a formal command.
reason: The fault in the wrong line is *pásame* with *señor*, not that it is a command: *Llámeme lo antes posible* is taught as polite in this band. The replacement names the real error and keeps *¿Me podría…?* as the gentler option.
quote: Almost. *Por favor* does not change the grammar, so a command to a stranger stays blunt.
replacement: {"wrong": "Pásame la sal, por favor, señor.", "right": "Páseme la sal, por favor, señor.", "why": "Almost. *Señor* calls for *usted*, so the command is *páseme*. To be gentler still, ask: *¿Me podría pasar la sal?*"}

problem: False. Usted has its own commands, taught at A2 and used politely in this unit. Teaches that usted commands are impolite.
reason: *Usted* has its own commands (u13), so the why is false. Changed *gentlest* because rungs 4 and 5 of this ladder sit above *podría*.
quote: A command becomes a *podría* question as soon as you say *usted*.
replacement: To a notary you use *usted*, and a *podría* question is a polite way to ask. The plain command would be *Llámeme mañana*.

problem: Quisiera, the central Spanish softener, is not in this script. 106 of the 120 bank rows targeting g:softening contain it. Measured: only 3 of 916 scripts mention quisiera, all incidentally, none explains it, and no chunk holds it. It first appears in the bank at u40. An unexplained past subjunctive with no trigger undermines everything the learner was told about the subjunctive.
reason: The omission is real. Politest of all goes because *le agradecería* sits above it on this unit's own ladder, and past wish form is the term g:register-ladder already uses. The lesson still has no example or Your Turn with *quisiera* though 93 of 120 rows use it, so one of each should follow, unclaimed.
quote: English softens with "I was wondering…", "could you possibly…" and "I imagine…". Spanish has four matching moves.
replacement:
English softens with "I was wondering…", "could you possibly…" and "I imagine…". Spanish has five matching moves.

*Quisiera* ("I would like") is the classic polite opener. It looks like the past wish form, but here it stands alone with no *que* in front: *Quisiera saber si hay mesa.*

problem: False claim about register. Rosa, que abrió el café, era la abuela de Tomás is standard in any newspaper. Learners will over-use el cual and sound stilted, which the story itself jokes about in ch155.
reason: *Que* is the default relative in print too, so too chatty for print is false (Butt and Benjamin from memory), and ch155 treats heavy *cual* as comic. The replacement keeps the story beat and the lesson's purpose.
quote: Mariana is writing about the café for her newspaper, and *que* alone sounds too chatty for print. She needs the more careful "who" and "which" that writers use to add a detail about someone.
replacement: Mariana is writing about the café for her newspaper. *Que* is still correct in print, but she also wants the more careful "who" and "which" that writers use to add a detail about someone.

problem: False after a preposition. El hombre con quien hablé (taught at u33) and la razón por la cual have no commas, and the bank drills this: u48-0006, u48-0016, u48-0060, u48-0068. The true constraint, never stated, is that a bare subject without commas cannot be quien: el vecino quien es doctor is wrong.
reason: After a preposition, no-comma *quien* and *el cual* are normal (bank u48-0006, u48-0068 checked), so the old line is false. The RAE Libro de estilo rejects *El niño quien vino ayer* and exempts prepositions and comma clauses (via search summary), which is what the replacement says.
quote: With no commas, plain *que* picks out which one.
replacement: With no commas, a plain subject or object takes *que*: *El vecino que es doctor trabaja mucho*, never *El vecino quien es doctor*. After a preposition, *quien* and *el cual* work with no commas: *el hombre con quien hablé*, *la razón por la cual*.

problem: The script never says what el cual is for. Its real job is after heavy prepositions and quantifiers, and to mark which noun is meant. The bank has all of this (u48-0012, u48-0041, u48-0064) with no explanation, so the learner meets it as an unexplained pattern.
reason: The script never says what *el cual* is for, and the bank drills exactly these uses (u48-0012, u48-0041, u48-0064 checked). The description matches standard accounts (Butt and Benjamin from memory) and follows LB2-055's new text cleanly.
quote: Tomorrow you will meet *lo cual*, for commenting on a whole situation.
replacement:
*El cual* really earns its place after a long preposition (*según la cual*, *a lo largo de la cual*) or a number (*dos de las cuales*), and to show which noun you mean when two are close.

Tomorrow you will meet *lo cual*, for commenting on a whole situation.

problem: A subject la cual for a simple description is stilted even in writing. The comic use in ch155 relies on exactly that. Also at rule, readAndPick[3] and yourTurn[2].
reason: *La puerta, la cual es muy vieja* is grammatical but stilted for a plain description, where a writer would use *que*, and ch155's joke rests on that. Swapping examples[4] alone fails, as the sentence is also in rule, readAndPick[3], yourTurn[2] and pitfalls[2] (plural), so rework them together around uses where *cual* earns its place; bank u48-0012 is good material.
quote: La puerta, la cual es muy vieja, no cierra bien.
replacement: {"es": "El edificio tiene dos escaleras, una de las cuales está cerrada.", "en": "The building has two staircases, one of which is closed."}

problem: As examples[4]. Natural Spanish is Las mesas, que compró Rosa, son de madera. Also at rule and readAndPick[1].
reason: Same as LB2-057: *Las mesas, que compró Rosa* is the natural form. The sentence is also in rule and readAndPick[1], and the *los proyectos, los cuales* items share the fault, so it needs the same coordinated rewrite; bank u48-0006 fits once LB2-055 allows *cual* with no commas.
quote: Las mesas, las cuales compró Rosa, son de madera.
replacement: {"es": "Hay una grieta por la cual entra agua cuando llueve.", "en": "There is a crack through which water comes in when it rains."}

problem: English cannot drop whom in this clause, and the a is personal a, not a stranded preposition. Your Turn explains it correctly.
reason: English cannot drop *whom* in a comma clause, and this *a* is the personal *a*, as yourTurn[1].why already says.
quote: English drops "whom", but Spanish keeps the preposition: *a quien*.
replacement: You meet a person, so Spanish needs the personal *a*: *a quien*.

problem: Omits el que and la que, the commonest spoken form, and the preposition repeat. The bank uses both unexplained: u47-0096 Fue Simón el que dijo, u47-0107 Fue Rosa la que me enseñó, u47-0148 Fue con Vale con quien hablé primero, u47-0146 Es por esto por lo que no firmé. English speakers will write Fue con Vale que hablé.
reason: Both this and LC-037 are right: the bank uses *el que*, *la que* and the repeated preposition unexplained (u47-0096, u47-0107, u47-0148), and plural *son* is in no script. Merged here with the quote extended so the plural note follows *lo que*, *even more common* dropped as an unproven frequency claim, and *Fue Tomás el que llamó a Vale.* should join yourTurn[3].accept.
quote: So the recipe is *ser* + the highlight + *quien* / *donde* / *cuando* + the rest. With things, flip it: *lo que* + the rest + *es* + the highlight.
replacement:
So the recipe is *ser* + the highlight + *quien* / *donde* / *cuando* + the rest. In everyday speech, *el que* and *la que* do the same job as *quien*: *Fue Vale la que encontró la carta.* If the highlight has a preposition, say it twice: *Fue con Vale con quien hablé.*

With things, flip it: *lo que* + the rest + *es* + the highlight. If the highlight is plural, *es* becomes *son*: *Lo que necesito son vacaciones.*

problem: A bare noun with no article takes no pronoun. The bank does this at u47-0275: Ni agua nos ofrecieron. Colombian speech uses it all the time: Plata no tengo.
reason: A noun with no article takes no pronoun (*Ni agua nos ofrecieron*, bank u47-0275 checked; NGLE from memory), so the note helps, but *the one exception* overclaims: u60 teaches fronted *Mucho ha cambiado el barrio*, also with no pronoun. Reworded to avoid that.
quote: English does this with stress or "as for". Spanish needs the pronoun: never *El contrato firmé yo.*
replacement: English does this with stress or "as for". Spanish needs the pronoun: never *El contrato firmé yo.* A bare noun with no article is different and takes no pronoun: *Plata no tengo.*

problem: The gerund belongs to the speaker, while the main subject is don Hernando, against the rule in the same script. It works in speech as a speaker comment, but it is a poor model for a lesson on formal compact clauses. Don should be lower case mid-sentence.
reason: *Conociendo a don Hernando, va a llegar tarde* is idiomatic with the speaker as the one who knows him, and the script's rule says *usually*, so it breaks nothing; no grammar I reached covers this exact case, so that is judgement. *Sé que* would also force a change to options[0], so only the capital changes: *don* is lower case mid-sentence.
quote: Conociendo a Don Hernando, va a llegar tarde.
replacement: Conociendo a don Hernando, va a llegar tarde.

problem: The commonest gerund error of English speakers, the gerund describing a noun, is warned against nowhere in the course: the man wearing a hat, a box containing letters. Checked here and in g:gerund-ways.
reason: The gap is real: no script warns against it, and the RAE rejects the gerund as a noun modifier (DPD from memory). Changed the italics on the English to double quotes, since the file keeps italics for Spanish.
quote: Never use the gerund for something that happens afterwards.
replacement: Never use the gerund for something that happens afterwards. And never use it to describe a noun, the way English does: "the man wearing a hat" is *el hombre que lleva un sombrero*, not *el hombre llevando un sombrero*.

problem: Misanalysis. Envío is the verb, and two finite verbs cannot stand side by side without a link. The DPD describes this invariable adjunto as an adverbial use common in administrative language, so the formula itself is acceptable and must NOT be flagged as an error. The rule's gloss "I attach and send you" repeats the mistake.
reason: The DPD (via search summary, rae.es returned 403) gives invariable adverbial *adjunto* as frequent in administrative language, especially at the start of a sentence, so *a verb form* is wrong. *Never changes* overreaches, because the agreeing adjective also exists, so it now reads *here it does not change*.
quote: In *Adjunto les envío*, *adjunto* is a verb form: "I attach".
replacement: In *Adjunto les envío*, *adjunto* works like an adverb, so here it does not change: "attached, I send you". With no other verb, as in *Les adjunto mi hoja de vida*, it is the verb *adjuntar*: "I attach".

problem: Does not say that it cannot take a subject. English It's about prompts El libro se trata de, which the DPD rejects. It is common in Latin American speech, so the note should be calm.
reason: The line is true, and p:se-trata-de (u39 d6) already teaches this exact point, with the same calm note in its pitfalls[0] and the same rule that a named thing takes trata de, so the omission overreaches; Academia Chilena via search and the DPD from memory confirm the norm. The real defect is in the bank, not this note: u11-0205 and u49-t-verbs-prepositions-0003 drill La carta se trata de, and those two rows should become La carta trata de.
quote: *Tratarse de* is only used as *se trata de*.
replacement: *Tratarse de* is only used as *se trata de*, with no subject in front. For a book or a film, say *El libro trata de la guerra*. You will hear *El libro se trata de la guerra* in speech, but it is not careful Spanish.

problem: Taught as the way to say what an object is made of, it pushes learners to Esta mesa está fabricada con madera where anyone says Esta mesa es de madera.
reason: Calling fabricado con the way to say what an object is built from oversells a register-marked form, since the learner has had es de since p:ser-de-material (A2) and p:estar-hecho-de (B1). The fix keeps the drill intact and suits the hook, where Vale is reading labels.
quote: For what an object is built from, use *estar fabricado con* plus the material: *está fabricada con madera*.
replacement: For what an object is made of, the everyday choice is *ser de*: *La mesa es de madera.* *Estar fabricado con* is the label or catalogue version: *está fabricada con madera*.

problem: Omits the subjunctive that grants a known fact and waves it aside. The bank has it, and English even if mistranslates it: u44-0052, u44-0062. Learners cannot understand Aunque seas mi hermano from this rule.
reason: *You don't care whether it's true* does not reach a fact the speaker knows, and the use is real: the subjuntivo polémico, with *Aunque sea mi hijo* as the textbook case (Pacagnini 2019 via search; Butt and Benjamin not checked). The example changes to *Aunque sea mi hermano* because *Aunque seas el dueño* can be read as open (see LB2-069), and the wording fits the *may ... but* renderings in x:aunque-ind-subj.
quote: When the thing is only possible, or you don't care whether it's true, the verb changes ending: *Aunque llueva, saldré.* In English that is even if.
replacement: When the thing is only possible, or you don't care whether it's true, the verb changes ending: *Aunque llueva, saldré.* In English that is even if. The same form can admit a known fact and wave it aside: *Aunque sea mi hermano, está equivocado.* In English that is "he may be my brother, but".

problem: He is known to be the brother, so even if is wrong. The Spanish concedes a fact.
reason: A speaker cannot be unsure of his own brother, so *even if* breaks the lesson's own mapping, and *may ... but* is how x:aunque-ind-subj already renders this subjunctive. The English stands as claimed, with accept and acceptEn added because both checkers are strict: *Puede que sea* is right for the new prompt, and *even if* is what the lesson has just taught.
quote: Even if he's my brother, he's wrong.
replacement: {"en": "He may be my brother, but he's wrong.", "accept": ["Puede que sea mi hermano, pero está equivocado."], "acceptEn": ["Even if he's my brother, he's wrong.", "Even though he's my brother, he's wrong."]}

reason: Not *as u44-0052*: whether the listener owns a place can be unknown or beside the point to the speaker, which is what *you don't care whether it's true* covers, and *even if you're the owner* is natural English for both readings. The current text is correct, so LB2-067 no longer uses this sentence as its example.
quote: Even if you're the owner, you have to obey the law. (to a man)
replacement: You may be the owner, but you have to obey the law. (to a man)

problem: Present subjunctive under a past habitual main verb, in a row targeting the structure, with no subject for llegue. The English has someone and arrived, so the two sides do not match either. It is the only such row my scan found in the 14,063 B2 rows.
reason: *Llegue* cannot hang on habitual *guardaba* and has no subject, while the English has someone. The fix matches u44-0080 and u44-0081, and the row's requires must add g:imperfect-subj.
quote: Aunque llegue tarde, Rosa siempre guardaba una mesa.
replacement: {"es": "Aunque alguien llegara tarde, Rosa siempre guardaba una mesa.", "en": "Even if someone arrived late, Rosa always kept a table."}

problem: False, and the same unit drills the exception: u50-0233 ¡Que bajes ya!, u50-0793 ¡Que te quedes quieto!. Good wishes also go to the listener: u51-0754 Que te vaya muy bien. The lesson title promises wishes, but no example is one.
reason: Rows u50-0233 ¡Que bajes ya! and u50-0793 ¡Que te quedes quieto! drill que to the listener in this same unit, and c:que-te-vaya-bien has been known since A2, so nothing changes is false as written. The lesson title promises wishes and the rule had none; ¡Que bajes ya! anticipates p:que-subj-repeated-order by one day, but it uses only forms and a frame the learner already has.
quote: To the person in front of you, nothing changes: *Entra*, *no entres*.
replacement: To order the person in front of you, nothing changes: *Entra*, *no entres*. But *que* can go to them in two cases: a good wish (*Que te vaya bien*) and repeating an order that was ignored (*¡Que bajes ya!*).

problem: Que le digan means have them tell him. The English gives an order to the listener, the very confusion this lesson removes.
reason: Que le digan is third person plural, so Tell him is Dile, the very mix-up this lesson exists to remove. Have them matches the script's own Have Vale do it today, and the row is the only one with this English.
quote: Tell him I'm not here.
replacement: Have them tell him I'm not here.

problem: Whatever follows is false: se venden casas, se produjeron dos explosiones, as the course teaches. The singular is right because a clause follows, as pitfalls[1] says correctly.
reason: Read literally the line contradicts g:passive-se (u36), where the verb after se is plural: se vendieron. The replacement states the real reason in the same terms as pitfalls[1] of this script.
quote: The verb after *se* stays singular, whatever follows.
replacement: The verb stays singular, because a whole *que* clause follows.

problem: A woman speaking of herself can say una. Not stated anywhere in the course. Women also say uno, so this is a note and not a rule.
reason: Women use both forms: the NGLE treats the pronoun as uno/una, and De Cock and an Argentine corpus study (via search) document una alternating with uno, so 'can also' is the right strength. It adds a true fact without touching the rule, and no script states it; the NGLE chapter number itself was not verified.
quote: *Uno* plus a normal verb: "one" or "you" in general, often including yourself.
replacement: *Uno* plus a normal verb: "one" or "you" in general, often including yourself. A woman can also say *una*.

problem: Wrong sound. Spanish éis sounds like English ace. Eyes matches áis. The learner would say co-MICE and confuse it with -áis.
reason: Plain phonetics: -éis is /eis/, English ace, while eyes is the sound of -áis, which the script's own soundTip gives correctly, so the pitfall teaches co-MICE and merges the two endings. This text is also the final one for LC-008.
quote: The accent marks the stress on *é*, which sounds like *eyes*: *co-MEIS*.
replacement: The accent marks the stress on *é*, and *-éis* rhymes with English *ace*: *co-MEIS*.

problem: A recognition lesson that misses what learners will read. Hablasteis, hablabais and teníais fit none of these endings, and the bank uses such forms (14 rows in -steis, 7 in -bais or -íais, e.g. u51-0114, u51-0154). Vuestro appears in 0 scripts and 2 bank rows.
reason: Measured: 14 bank rows in -steis, 7 in -bais or -íais and 2 with vuestro, all in u51, and no script names vuestro, while none of those forms fits the three endings given. All the forms in the replacement are correct, and they are for recognition only.
quote: Look for the ending *-áis*, *-éis* or *-ís*.
replacement: Look for the ending *-áis*, *-éis* or *-ís*. Past forms give it away too: *hablasteis*, *comisteis*, *hablabais*, *teníais*. And *vuestro*, *vuestra* mean "your" to a group of friends.

problem: Your Turn items 0, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 make the learner type vosotros forms, against the owner's decision of no vosotros in production and the script's own line You will not say these yourself. g:spain-pasts yourTurn 0, 2, 3 and 5 do the same while saying You do not need to produce this. Better: convert Spain forms into Colombian ones, or read and choose.
reason: Six of seven Your Turn items require a typed vosotros form with no ustedes answer in accept, against the standing decision and the script's own You will not say these yourself; only item 4 goes the permitted way. g:spain-pasts items 0, 2, 3 and 5 do the same, so both lessons need new items that convert to Colombian forms or read and choose, which is not one string.
quote: Say it as a friend from Madrid would: Have you all eaten yet?

problem: Hoy no he comido nada means I haven't eaten anything today, with the day still running, and Colombians say it too, so it does not illustrate a Spain-only habit. The bank has the right English at u51-t-spain-pasts-0024. Same text at readAndPick[1].options[2].
reason: With hoy still running the exact English is I haven't eaten, the row's sibling u51-t-spain-pasts-0024 says so, and this is the not-yet use the script keeps for Colombia too. Replace both occurrences in the script (examples[3].en and readAndPick[1].options[2]) and the same English in bank row u51-t-spain-pasts-0009.
quote: I didn't eat anything today.
replacement: I haven't eaten anything today.

problem: The forms do not alternate when -ra stands for the conditional: polite quisiera, pudiera and debiera cannot become quisiese. The polite-form case is my inference from the general rule.
reason: Castellano Actual (UDEP), via search, cites NGLE 24.2c: the endings do not alternate when -ra equals the conditional, its example being una película que no quisiera perderme, and Quisiera un vaso de agua is the polite case; the source page itself refused automated access. This wording keeps the colon leading into the list of forms, so it is the final text for LC-009 too.
quote: It has a twin ending in *-se*, with exactly the same meaning and uses:
replacement: It has a twin ending in *-se*, with the same meaning in almost every use (polite *quisiera* is the exception, and stays in *-ra*):

problem: They are two forms, not spellings, and they differ in sound and history. Also at yourTurn[5].why.
reason: They differ in sound and origin, so spellings is false, but 'forms are two forms' reads badly, so the sentence is reworded. Make the matching edit at yourTurn[5].why: *Hubieran* and *hubiesen* are two forms of one tense.
quote: The *-ra* and *-se* forms are two spellings of one tense.
replacement: The endings *-ra* and *-se* give two forms of one tense.

problem: Marks correct Spanish as wrong, and contradicts the script's own rule that with al the first event can set off the second. The RAE's own example of temporal al + infinitive is Al vernos, se acercó.
reason: Al firmar, se fue is correct: the RAE's own example is Al vernos, se acercó (via search), and with a punctual verb al gives immediate sequence. But Al firmar, volvió a Medellín un mes después is more odd than wrong and its right form is redundant, so the swap uses a verb that takes time, where al really does mean during (aspect point from memory); replace the whole pitfalls[2] object.
quote: Al firmar, se fue.
replacement: {"wrong": "Al almorzar, volvió a la oficina.", "right": "Tras almorzar, volvió a la oficina.", "why": "Almost. Lunch takes a while, so *al* puts going back in the middle of it. For one thing and then the next, use *tras*."}

problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
reason: Grammatical, so this is a register call and not an error, but once LB2-005 says por si for a precaution this card would expect the opposite; in Ngrams por si hace frío appears and en caso de que haga frío falls below the threshold. Keep g:subj-conditions in requires so por si stays behind its lesson; u44-0195, 0198, 0201, 0205, 0215, 0228 and 1494 are the same pattern and unclaimed.
quote: Llévate un abrigo en caso de que haga frío en la audiencia.
replacement: Llévate un abrigo por si hace frío en la audiencia.

problem: Grammatical, but this is a precaution, where a Colombian says por si. Depends on adding por si to g:subj-conditions. The tagger must retarget this row, because it stops being subjunctive practice.
reason: Same case as LB2-082: a precaution taken now, grammatical as it stands but contradicting the rule once LB2-005 lands. In Ngrams por si se pierde is at 3.5e-9 and en caso de que se pierda falls below the threshold.
quote: Guarda una copia de la carta en caso de que se pierda.

quote: The imperfect is for the past; for a plan, use the present.
replacement: For a fixed plan, use the present. *Viajaba* would sound as if the plan has fallen through.

problem: Quise + infinitive normally means "tried to", often unsuccessfully: quise llamarte pero no pude. Nothing need have happened.

quote: The imperfect softens the request; the preterite would say it already happened.
replacement: The imperfect softens the request; *quise* would report an attempt in the past, not a request now.

quote: It's going to be expensive, but it's worth it.
replacement: It isn't expensive, but it's worth it.

problem: Qué va rejects what was just said, so after a negative question it opens a yes: ¿No te gustó? ¡Qué va, me encantó! A learner told it is always a no misreads that reply.
reason: DEA and DUE (via a journal article found by search) call it an emphatic negative reply, Alarcos says it rejects what was stated, and its origin is ¡qué va a + infinitive!, so it negates the previous claim, not always the answer. u24-0917 already shows it rejecting a negative question; the exact sentence ¿No te gustó? ¡Qué va, me encantó! was not found in a search and rests on my judgement that it is natural.
quote: *¡Qué va!* on its own means "not at all". It is always a no.
replacement: *¡Qué va!* rejects what was just said. After *¿Estás cansado?* it means "not at all". After *¿No te gustó?* it can open a yes: *¡Qué va, me encantó!*

problem: Same point. The pitfall sentence is still wrong, but for a different reason.

replacement: Almost. *Qué va* rejects what was just said, and here you are saying yes to it.

problem: Por mucho que and por más que take the indicative for something that really happened: Por más que lo intentó, no pudo. No script and no row of the 72,693 shows this, so a learner will force the subjunctive on factual past effort and misread the indicative in every novel. u52-0266 Por mucho que lo negase, acabó por admitirlo and u44-0092 Por más que Tomás se esforzara, la palabra no le salía both narrate real events, where the indicative is the normal choice.
reason: Same string as LC-011, which is confirmed and carries the point better: it keeps por mucho que in its example and the file's plain verb label. Applying both would collide; the factual subjunctive rows u44-0092 and u52-0266 are literary, not errors, and can stay.
quote: *Por mucho que* and *por muy… que* take the subjunctive: the speaker grants any degree and the result stays the same.
replacement: *Por mucho que* and *por muy… que* normally take the subjunctive: the speaker grants any degree and the result stays the same. For something that really happened, the indicative is normal: *Por más que lo intentó, no pudo*.

replacement: Remember: *mucho* goes with a verb, *muy* with an adjective or adverb. Before a noun, *mucho* agrees with it: *por mucha plata que tenga*.

problem: False. The tense follows the time of the consequence, not the first clause. The bank itself contradicts it: u56-0203 La ciudad creció sin plan; de ahí que el tráfico sea una pesadilla, and u57-0403 uses the perfect subjunctive hayan sorprendido.
reason: False as stated: u56-0203 pairs a past cause with sea, and the old rule would push the learner to fuera, which changes the meaning. The replacement keeps the lesson's own forms in plain words, and needs LC1-038 and LC1-039 to carry it into the whys.
quote: If the main sentence is in the past, the verb after *de ahí que* is the past subjunctive (*se aplazara*, *oyera*). If it is in the present, it is the present subjunctive (*pueda*).
replacement: The tense follows the result, not the first sentence. A result in the past takes the past subjunctive (*se aplazara*, *oyera*). A result that holds now takes the present subjunctive (*pueda*), even after a past cause: *la ciudad creció sin plan; de ahí que el tráfico sea una pesadilla*.
