replacement: *De manera que* also takes a normal verb when you simply report what happened: *llegó tarde, de manera que perdió el vuelo*. With the subjunctive it names a goal, not a result: *habla despacio de manera que te entiendan* means "speak slowly so that they understand you".

problem: In Colombia apenas is the everyday "as soon as", and it works for the future too. The rule restricts it to the past, while the bank already uses it with the subjunctive from u32 on (u37-0080 Quiero que me llames apenas llegues; u45-0798 Yo te pongo al tanto apenas llegue Mariana; u50-1567). The C1 rule is narrower than what the learner has been reading for 20 units, and the unit then gives 58 rows to nada más + infinitive instead.
reason: The rule is narrower than the course: the DPD gives apenas as en cuanto, and u32-0102, u37-0080 and u45-0798 use it with the subjunctive. No source backs 'the everyday choice in Colombia', so that became very common in Latin America, the forward reference to en cuanto is softened, and this text also carries LC-025.
quote: *Apenas* + past: "barely had we... when". It is quick and sudden.
replacement: *Apenas*: "as soon as", and very common in Latin America. About the past, use a past verb: *Apenas abrimos, llegó Hernando* ("we had barely opened when Hernando arrived"). About the future, use the "wish" form, as with *en cuanto*: *Apenas llegue, te aviso*.

problem: Nada más + infinitive leads this lesson with 58 C1 rows and no regional note, yet it is chiefly a Spain construction and is not how a Bogotá speaker would say it (Nada más terminar la viga, llámame; ¿Vas a llamar nada más llegar?). It is fine for recognition and writing, but the course presents it as the default.
reason: The regional point is right but belongs to LC-026, which puts it in the rule where the learner meets the form, so the two would repeat each other. 'And formal writing' is also unsupported: the NGLE Manual calls the construction characteristic of European Spanish, not of formal style.
quote: Teachers call these temporal conjunctions.
replacement: Teachers call these temporal conjunctions. *Nada más* + infinitive is mostly Spanish from Spain and formal writing; in Bogotá people say *apenas* or *en cuanto*.

quote: *La mitad* (half) behaves like *la mayoría*: *la mitad se fue* or *se fueron*.
replacement: *La mitad* (half) behaves like *la mayoría*: *la mitad se fue* or *se fueron*. *El resto de* works the same way. If you belong to the group, the verb can say so: *la mayoría de los vecinos votamos en contra*.

problem: The title says "at the edges" but the four frames are mostly B1 phrases, and La mesa es de madera is A2. Nothing here deals with actual C1 ser and estar: resultative estar versus passive ser (la tienda está cerrada, fue cerrada), estar + adjective for a perceived change (estás muy joven), estar que + verb, es para tanto, estar en (el problema está en que...), ser de + infinitive (es de esperar).

The true gaps are ser de + infinitive (es de esperar, no rows at all) and estar en (el problema está en que, no script), and extending the lesson is a content job, not a string.

problem: With verbs of arriving, appearing and remaining, the subject normally follows: se fue la luz, llegó Vale, queda poco. The lesson's own examples (Poco queda del edificio) have no subject to move. This is the last word-order lesson in the course and the only one a C1 learner gets; subject after the verb when the subject is the news is taught nowhere.
reason: A simplification rather than an error, and 'taught nowhere' overstates it (g:topic-fronting says new information lands at the end, g:parecer-quedar puts the thing after the verb). Presentational verbs do favour the subject after the verb (faltan agujas, Meyer-Hermann via Borzi), but nearly all verbs allow both orders, so 'usually' becomes 'often, when it is the news', and I keep the words Normal order because the last paragraph refers back to them.
quote: Normal order puts the subject first: *El barrio ha cambiado mucho.*
replacement: Normal order puts the subject first with most verbs: *El barrio ha cambiado mucho.* With *llegar*, *quedar* and *faltar* it often comes after, when it is the news: *llegó Vale*.

problem: No limit is given, so a learner will build Caminado el parque or Trabajada la mañana. The construction needs a verb with an end point: transitive or unaccusative, perfective in meaning.
reason: The limit is real: only transitive and unaccusative verbs form absolute participles, and unaccusatives need a terminative reading (UAB thesis citing Hernanz and De Miguel, and an RFE review, both from search extracts; NGLE from memory). Every example in the script and topup has a finish line, and llegado el momento fits the list.
quote: It is a shortcut for "once that was done".
replacement: It is a shortcut for "once that was done", so it needs a verb with a finish line: *firmar*, *aprobar*, *terminar*, *llegar*. Open-ended verbs like *caminar* or *trabajar* do not work here.

problem: The first example has a doer and the second has a thing done, and the rule treats them as one. When both are named, Spanish needs a second marker. Por parte de, the formal device this register depends on, is in no script, and it occurs in only 2 bank rows, neither with a noun of action.
reason: The gap is real: por parte de is the normal formal marker of the doer with an event noun (everyday press Spanish; NGLE from memory). Pasted as proposed, it would cut off the next sentence, The English "Yesid's arrival" turns around, from its example, so the quote is widened and the new sentence moved after it.
quote: Who or what the action belongs to follows with *de*: *la llegada de Yesid*, *la venta del edificio*. The English "Yesid's arrival" turns around.
replacement: Who or what the action belongs to follows with *de*: *la llegada de Yesid*, *la venta del edificio*. The English "Yesid's arrival" turns around. When you name both the thing done and the doer, the doer takes *por parte de*: *la compra del edificio por parte de Altamira*.

problem: Coger is vulgar in Mexico, Central America and the River Plate, but it is ordinary in Colombia, the story's setting: coger un taxi, coja la Séptima. "Never" is false there, and the bank never shows it (0 rows), so a learner is warned off a word they will hear daily in Bogotá and may think it obscene. Avoiding it for neutral production is defensible; the blanket claim is not.
reason: Never is false in the story's own city: a Publimetro Bogotá headline reads cuánto cuesta coger Transmilenio, and the vulgar sense in Mexico and Argentina is well documented (learner references; Diccionario de americanismos from memory). Agarrar stays the neutral production choice, and the replacement says exactly that.
quote: In Latin America, *agarrar* is very common here. Never *coger*.
replacement: In Latin America, *agarrar* is very common here. Avoid *coger* in Mexico or Argentina, where it is vulgar. In Colombia it is ordinary and you will hear it all the time.

problem: Same point. Cojo el bus en la 72 is normal Bogotá Spanish, and it is listed as wrong.

quote: In Latin America you *tomar* the bus. *Coger* is the Spain word, and best avoided here.
replacement: Across Latin America you can always *tomar* the bus. *Coger* is fine in Colombia but vulgar in Mexico and Argentina, so *tomar* is the safe choice.

problem: Same point, more mildly put.
reason: Same evidence as LC1-087: the old why implies coger is out across Latin America, while the new one keeps agarró as the safe answer without that claim. Follow-up, not covered by this claim: the rule in the same script still says where Spain says *coger*. Avoid *coger* here, which needs the same softening.
quote: Almost. In Latin America *coger* is best avoided, so say *agarró* (or *tomó*).
replacement: Almost. *Coger* is vulgar in some countries, so *agarró* (or *tomó*) is the safe choice.

problem: False as stated. "Not to pay attention to" is an established meaning in the DLE and the everyday one: me ignoró. The course's own bank uses it (u43-1103 Ignoré el aviso y salí sin abrigo; u43-1104 no quiero ignorar tus ideas). A learner who believes this misreads ordinary Spanish and sees a contradiction with u43.

replacement: Watch out: *ignorar* can mean "to take no notice of" (*me ignoró*), but in a formal text like these it means you lack the information.

problem: Asumir for "suppose" is an English calque, widespread but still avoided in careful Spanish, and this is the unit teaching dar por sentado.

The claimed Fundéu position could not be found, a bilingual dictionary marks the sense as Latin American, and the row targets nothing, so correct text stays.

problem: Negating a perception or speech verb does not force the subjunctive. The mood carries meaning. Indicative: the speaker takes the content as true and someone missed it (No vi que había un escalón, there was a step and I missed it). Subjunctive: no evidence for it (No vi que hubiera un escalón). The rule also clashes with correct bank rows: u26-0741 'Tomás no sabía que Rosa tenía una deuda', u42-0585 'yo no sabía que era hoy'. A learner who applies the rule writes No sabía que estuvieras aquí for the everyday No sabía que estabas aquí.
reason: The diagnosis is right, but this is the same string as LB2-010, which carries the change. Its added line on no sabía que is not needed: LB2-010's test, true and someone missed it, already gives No sabía que estabas aquí.
quote: Put *no* in front and you are no longer vouching, so the verb after *que* switches to the past form that ends in *-ra*
replacement: Put *no* in front and you can choose. If you are not vouching for it, the verb after *que* switches to the past form that ends in *-ra*: *No vi que estuviera enojada* (I saw no sign of it). If it was true and someone just missed it, the ordinary verb stays: *No vi que estaba enojada* (she was, and I didn't notice). *No sabía que* nearly always keeps the ordinary verb: *No sabía que Rosa tenía una deuda.*

problem: True for people, false as stated. El día en que, la forma en que, la manera en que, la casa en que vivo are standard, and the bank uses them (u34-1118 'la forma en que habla Hernando', u43-0532 'el día en que Joaquín volviera'). The learner meets sentences the rule calls wrong.

replacement: With a person, a preposition needs an article or *quien*, not a bare *que*. With things and times, bare *que* is fine after *en*: *el día en que llegó*, *la forma en que habla*.

problem: Este último / esta última is the most common written way to say the latter, because it removes ambiguity. Telling the learner Spanish does not say it is false and takes away a form they will read daily.

quote: Almost. Spanish does not say 'the last one' for 'the latter'; *esta* does the pointing.
replacement: Almost. On its own *la última* can sound loose. Say *esta última*, or just *esta*: both do the pointing.

problem: -éis does not sound like eyes. The diphthong ei rhymes with English case or day. Eyes is the sound of ai, the -áis ending (habláis). The pitfall mixes up the two endings it is teaching.

replacement: The accent marks the stress on *é*, and *-éis* rhymes with English *ace*: *co-MEIS*.

problem: False once the main verb is past: Te dejé la llave para que abrieras. The learner is told always at A2 and has to unlearn it at u41. Dropping one word keeps the point and stops the later contradiction.

replacement: *Para que* always takes the subjunctive.

problem: Por mucho que also takes the indicative for a real event: Por mucho que insistí, no me hizo caso. A C1 learner told it takes the subjunctive will force an unnatural form for past facts or read correct prose as wrong.

All 23 bank rows use the subjunctive, so the gap is real; this also carries LC1-034, and the file's plain verb label is kept.
quote: *Por mucho que* and *por muy… que* take the subjunctive: the speaker grants any degree and the result stays the same.
replacement: *Por mucho que* and *por muy… que* usually take the subjunctive: the speaker grants any degree and the result stays the same. For a real past event the plain verb is normal too: *Por mucho que insistí, no me hizo caso.*

problem: Siempre que is one of the four, and at u17 g:cuando-indicative taught it with the indicative for whenever: siempre que llueve, vendemos más. No contrast node separates the two meanings (x:mientras-ind-subj does this job for mientras). The always contradicts an earlier lesson.
reason: The diagnosis is right, but this is a duplicate of LB2-003 on the same string, which carries the change with the file's own term, ordinary verb.
quote: They always take the subjunctive.
replacement: With these meanings they always take the subjunctive. *Siempre que* with the plain verb is the one you already know, whenever: *Siempre que llueve, vendemos más.*

problem: No hay que + infinitive has two readings. It often means one mustn't, and the bank translates it that way: u52-0691 'No hay que olvidar...' = We mustn't forget; u56-0104 'no hay que perder la esperanza' = we mustn't lose hope. The rule gives only one reading, so the learner misreads warnings in B2 and C1 prose.
reason: Both readings are real: u56-0104 and u52-0691 show mustn't, and learner sources agree context decides (the Butt and Benjamin citation could not be checked). *Perder la esperanza* is known from u26, and the no-need reading stays first, as the exercises drill it.
quote: *No hay que pagar* says there's no need to.
replacement: *No hay que pagar* says there's no need to. With a warning it can also mean you mustn't: *No hay que perder la esperanza.* Context decides.

problem: Si meaning whether takes the conditional freely: Preguntó si vendría, and the bank has 8 such rows (u42-0370 'preguntó si sería posible'). The learner met this at u25 and u37. No node contrasts if-si and whether-si, so never will be read as covering both.
reason: Bank rows and the u25 and u37 teaching show whether-*si* with the conditional, and no node separates the two. The replacement fits the sentence and uses only forms already taught; the rule's own "After *si*" line is framed by the imaginary *if*, so it can stay.
quote: Almost. Never use the *would* form after *si*; that spot always takes the *ra* form.
replacement: Almost. In an *if* half, never use the *would* form after *si*; that spot takes the *ra* form. (*Si* meaning whether is different: *Preguntó si vendría.*)

problem: Same overgeneralisation as g:si-hypothetical. It is true of como si, false of si in general.
reason: Same fix and same text as LB1-022: true of *como si*, false of *si* in general.
quote: The *would* form never follows *si*; this spot takes the *ra* form.
replacement: The *would* form never follows *como si*; this spot takes the *ra* form.

problem: Struck through as a slip, but momentito is correct everywhere, including Colombia, where -ico after t is the frequent regional preference and not a rule. The dialect target is neutral Latin American. Move this to smallPrint as a tip and delete the pitfall.
reason: Overreach: momentico is the lesson's headline local form and the pitfall still teaches it. LA2-048 removes the false rule by softening the why, with precedent in x:ir-a-future ('Not wrong, just stiff'), so deleting the pitfall is unnecessary.
quote: Espérame un momentito.

problem: A correct sentence (Of course I went!) is struck through as a slip with no context, and the why only says the sentence means something else. It teaches nothing about the structure. Delete it.
reason: The card is headed 'Almost everyone slips here' and strikes through correct Spanish, and the slip is only a tense choice with no link to the structure, unlike the calque in LB1-057. Delete pitfalls[2], which leaves three, inside the 3 to 5 the brief allows; that removes an array entry, so it is not a string replacement.
quote: ¡Pues claro que fui!

problem: y must become e before the sound i: e hizo. This is a spelling rule of the standard language, and the sentence is a model the learner copies.
reason: y before the sound i is e (Ortografía 2010, from memory), but this sentence sits in the file four times: examples[2], rule, readAndPick[0] and yourTurn[1].answer. Replace every occurrence; the quote drops the final period so it also catches the rule, where an asterisk comes before it.
quote: Don Hernando vio el error y hizo la vista gorda
replacement: Don Hernando vio el error e hizo la vista gorda

problem: The expected answer has the same error and accept is empty, so a learner who writes the correct e hizo is marked wrong. The prompt's gap 'vio el error y ___' must change too, to 'vio el error ___', because the conjunction depends on the option chosen: y pasó por alto, e hizo la vista gorda.
reason: LC-018's replace-all fixes the answer, so this carries the yourTurn[1].prompt the claim says must change: the old gap makes the learner type y hizo, which the checker rejects with "y" isn't the word here, check the meaning (tested), a misleading hint for a spelling rule. No script teaches y to e, so the options show the conjunction, and lo makes the wrong option grammatical; yourTurn[1].why could add one clause on it.
quote: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Don Hernando vio el error y ___.* (*pasó por alto* or *hizo la vista gorda*)
replacement: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Don Hernando vio el error ___.* (*y lo pasó por alto* or *e hizo la vista gorda*)

problem: Same spelling error in a reading item.
reason: Same rule as LC-018 in a reading item, and no other field of the item depends on the conjunction.
quote: Don Hernando vio el error y hizo la vista gorda.
replacement: Don Hernando vio el error e hizo la vista gorda.

problem: y before hi- should be e. Repetition does not suspend the rule.
reason: The y to e rule depends only on the sound that follows and has no exception for repeated words; its only exceptions are diphthongs like hierro and some interrogatives (Ortografía 2010, from memory and search extracts). Historias e historias is the regular form.
quote: Mariana escuchó historias y historias en el barrio.
replacement: Mariana escuchó historias e historias en el barrio.

problem: internet starts with the sound i, so y becomes e. A translation card built on this row teaches the error and the checker expects it.
reason: Internet is said with the sound i in Spanish, so the rule applies, and a translation card built on this row would teach y as the expected answer. The English stays exact.
quote: Para el teletrabajo solo necesito una computadora y internet.
replacement: Para el teletrabajo solo necesito una computadora e internet.

problem: o becomes u before the sound o: luminosa u oscura. Six instances across all 103,451 Spanish strings miss this rule (three bank rows, three fields of one script) and no script teaches it.
reason: Oscura begins with o, so o becomes u (Ortografía 2010, from memory and search extracts). My scan of bank and scripts found seven misses, not six, because of the rule field noted under LC-018.
quote: ¿La cocina es luminosa o oscura?
replacement: ¿La cocina es luminosa u oscura?

problem: In Latin America cuál before a noun is widespread: ¿Cuál libro quieres? Spain prefers qué. The target dialect is Latin American, so the absolute is too strong, and the checker should accept the form. Qué stays the safe production choice.
reason: Duplicate of LA2-017 on the same string, whose wording is cleaner; 'never with a singular cuál before a plural noun' is tangled. The substance stands through LA2-017, so nothing else changes.
quote: Right before a noun, Spanish uses *qué*, even when English could say which.
replacement: Right before a noun, *qué* is the safe choice. In Latin America you will also hear *cuál* there, but never with a singular *cuál* before a plural noun.

problem: Latin American apenas means as soon as and is at least as common about the future: u37-0080 'Quiero que me llames apenas llegues', u45-0798 'apenas llegue Mariana'. The rule restricts it to the past and gives only a literary gloss, in a course whose dialect is Latin American.
reason: The substance is right, but it is the same string as LC1-055, which carries the merged text with a past example and a gloss. Nothing to apply here.
quote: *Apenas* + past: "barely had we... when". It is quick and sudden.
replacement: *Apenas*: "as soon as". It works like *en cuanto*. About the past: *Apenas abrimos, llegó Hernando.* About the future, with the wish form: *Apenas llegues, me llamas.*

problem: Nada más + infinitive is mainly Peninsular. A Colombian speaker would normally use apenas or al + infinitive. The dialect rule says Peninsular material is for recognition from B2 and should be labelled. It leads the lesson with no label.
reason: The NGLE Manual, as quoted in a Caracas corpus study, calls this characteristic of European Spanish and says it is rare in America, so a label is due under the dialect rule. 'In books' is dropped as unsupported and the note goes after the explanation it would otherwise interrupt; whether 58 rows and a production card should stay is a separate owner question.
quote: the infinitive carries it.
replacement: the infinitive carries it. This one belongs mainly to Spain, so learn to recognise it. In Colombia you will more often hear *apenas llegó Tomás*.

problem: The stem list omits saber (sup-), though the bank uses it 41 times from u06 (u06-0102 'Ayer supe la verdad'). More important, no script in the course explains that the preterite changes the meaning of state verbs: supe is found out, conocí is met, no quise is refused. Read and write cards use these meanings with no explanation. The English speaker will say Sabía la verdad ayer for I found out, or read conocí as knew. g:imperfect-subj then builds supiera from a form that was never taught.
reason: The gap is real, with supe in the bank from u06 and no script explaining it, but the flat glosses fail later: 26 of 35 no quise or no quiso rows read didn't want (u29-0479 no quise molestar), and 16 of 73 supe rows read knew (u47-1076 no supe qué decir). I hedge with usually and can, and drop in the past because the imperfect is also a past, met at u06 d1.
quote: *No pude* is more than I couldn't: it means I tried and it didn't happen.
replacement: *No pude* is more than I couldn't: it means I tried and it didn't happen. *Saber* joins this group (*supe*, *supo*), and it usually means found out, not knew: *Ayer supe la verdad.* In the same way, *conocí* is usually I met, and *no quise* can mean I refused.

problem: This is the core Latin American use of the perfect, yet it first appears at u52 (C1), 44 units after g:perfecto-experience. Meanwhile that A1 script says He is for ever, never and not yet, which excludes Siempre he vivido aquí and Últimamente he estado cansado. A learner has no way to talk about a situation that continues up to now for most of the course, and writes siempre viví aquí or hace que. Move the node to A2, near u23 (g:hace-que-desde) or u26 (g:acabar-de-ya-todavia).
reason: The gap is real: the A1 script calls the perfect a narrow job with only life so far and not yet, and only about 8 rows before u51 use siempre he or este año he, so Siempre he vivido aquí goes untaught for 50 units. But do not move this node: it requires g:tense-modal-uses and teaches a C1 split (siempre he pensado que fue); add a short new A2 node near u23 to u26 by hand in the unit data, and widen the A1 line.
quote: The *he* + participle form is for what is still open: a view you still hold (*siempre he pensado*, *nunca he entendido*) or a stretch of time you are still in (*este año*, *esta semana*).

problem: Presented as obligatory, against u25, which says Something already in the past stays put (Dijo que Joaquín se fue). Both are correct. Also missing anywhere in the course: no backshift when the content is still true or still ahead (Dijo que Bogotá es fría, Dijo que viene mañana). A learner following the rule mechanically will backshift everything, which sounds stilted in Latin American speech.
reason: Right that the list line overstates and contradicts u25 (Dijo que Joaquín se fue). The second line about *Dijo que Bogotá es fría* moved into LB2-023 so the two replacements do not repeat each other.
quote: *hablé* → *había hablado* (I spoke → had spoken)
replacement: *hablé* → *había hablado* (I spoke → had spoken), or it can stay *hablé* when the order is clear

problem: The script teaches ¡Tan lindo!, not ¡Qué tan lindo!. Qué tan is the Latin American interrogative (¿Qué tan lejos es?). The exclamative has 0 bank rows.
reason: Duplicate of LA2-033, identical replacement on the same string. Nothing else changes.
quote: Reacting: ¡Qué bueno!, ¡Qué pena!, ¡Qué tan lindo!, ¡Cuánta gente!
replacement: Reacting: ¡Qué bueno!, ¡Qué pena!, ¡Tan lindo!, ¡Cuánta gente!

problem: The title promises siempre y cuando, but the script's rule, examples and pitfalls teach con tal de que instead. Either teach it or change the title.
reason: Duplicate of LC1-044, same edit: siempre y cuando is absent from this script and already taught at u45, so changing the title beats adding it here.
quote: Conditions with style: de haberlo sabido, como no llegues, a no ser que, siempre y cuando
replacement: Conditions with style: de haberlo sabido, como no llegues, a no ser que, con tal de que

problem: Haya has a full paradigm (hayas, hayamos, hayan), taught at u34 in g:subj-perfect. Just the one form is true only of the there-is use.
reason: Duplicate of LA2-049 on the same string, which carries the fix. Nothing else changes.
quote: *Haya* has just the one form: *Quiero que haya café.*
replacement: For there is, *haya* is the only form you need: *Quiero que haya café.*

problem: The rule gives -o masculine and -a feminine as the guess, with only día and agua as surprises. No script in the course names the -ma family (el problema, el idioma, el sistema, el tema, el programa) or la mano, la foto, la moto. These are high-frequency, and an English speaker who trusts the rule says la problema. The app relies on the article in each word card.
reason: The gap is real but LA1-004 now fixes it in the rule, where the learner meets the guess; refuted to avoid teaching it twice. smallPrint is the slot for the technical term, and the proposed list mixes in el mapa, which is not a -ma word.
quote: Grammar books call this grammatical gender. *El*/*la* are the definite articles; *un*/*una* are the indefinite articles.
replacement: Grammar books call this grammatical gender. *El*/*la* are the definite articles; *un*/*una* are the indefinite articles. Watch for a few everyday breakers: *el problema*, *el idioma*, *el tema*, *el mapa*, *la mano*, *la foto*.

problem: The rule's test, how they are right now, fails on está muerto and está casada, which the bank uses (u15-0199 'Mi hermana está casada con un médico'). No script mentions either. The contrast script's portrait or snapshot model is the better reusable model, and it is never shown in a lesson. State here that estar names a state reached, not a temporary one.
reason: A state need not be temporary, and drills show only the rule's trick, so the portrait or snapshot small print in x:ser-estar-adj never reaches a lesson. The claim's 'no script mentions either' is slightly off (p:enamorarse-de has one), but that does not change the fix.
quote: Teachers call this the difference between a characteristic (*ser*) and a state (*estar*).
replacement: Teachers call this the difference between a characteristic (*ser*) and a state (*estar*). A state need not be temporary: *está casada*, *está muerto*. Think portrait or snapshot, not permanent or temporary.

problem: The rule says the forms change after little words, with no exceptions. Entre and según keep yo and tú: entre tú y yo, según tú. English speakers say between you and me, and a transfer of the rule gives *entre ti y mí. No node covers it.
reason: The omission is real and the DPD (pronombres personales tónicos, via search) confirms entre and según take subject forms, but Two words is false: the bank itself drills todos menos yo at u46 and u53, and excepto and salvo behave the same (from memory). Amended to A few words and added the English; separately, u15-0626 drills the wrong Entre ti y yo and must become Entre tú y yo.
quote: Teachers call *mí*, *ti*, *conmigo* and *contigo* prepositional (or tonic) pronouns.
replacement: Teachers call *mí*, *ti*, *conmigo* and *contigo* prepositional (or tonic) pronouns. A few words keep *yo* and *tú* instead, above all *entre* and *según*: *entre tú y yo* (between you and me), *según tú* (according to you).

problem: The most useful generalisation is missing: the preposition also stays before que (me acuerdo de que, confío en que, sueño con que, insisto en que), and verbs without one take none (pienso que, not pienso de que). Queísmo is named once, in p:estar-convencido-de, and dequeísmo only as a one-line pitfall in g:impersonal-register. The node also arrives at u49, after about 60 patterns whose id ends in a preposition (A1 to B1) have already been taught.
reason: The omission is real: the preposition before que is stated nowhere as a rule, queísmo appears once, and the Spanish examples are correct (DPD dequeísmo, from memory). Changed the last sentence because pensar does have small words, which the course itself teaches (pensar en, ¿Qué piensas de...?), so 'a verb with no small word' is false of the very verb it cites.
quote: The small word stays when a pronoun follows: *Depende de ti*, *Cuento contigo* (*con* + *ti*).
replacement: The small word stays when a pronoun follows: *Depende de ti*, *Cuento contigo* (*con* + *ti*). It stays before *que* too: *Me acuerdo de que llovía*, *Confío en que vendrá*. A verb that takes plain *que* never gains one: *Pienso que*, never *pienso de que*.

problem: Two things an English speaker needs are missing. The everyday form el que / la que (Fue Vale la que encontró la carta) is not offered. With a preposition, it appears on both sides: Fue con Vale con quien hablé; English It was Vale I spoke to transfers as Fue Vale con quien hablé. Copular agreement is also untaught in the whole course: Lo que necesito son vacaciones, Lo importante son los niños (0 bank rows, 0 scripts).
reason: Duplicate of LB2-060 on the same string. Its content (*el que*, the repeated preposition, plural *son*) is carried there, with the plural note placed after *lo que*, where it makes sense.
quote: So the recipe is *ser* + the highlight + *quien* / *donde* / *cuando* + the rest.
replacement: So the recipe is *ser* + the highlight + *quien*, *el que* or *la que* / *donde* / *cuando* + the rest. If the highlight has a preposition, it comes twice: *Fue con Vale con quien hablé.* And *ser* follows a plural highlight: *Lo que necesito son vacaciones.*

problem: No script teaches the anterior form como si + hubiera (Sigue como si no hubiera pasado nada), though 12 bank rows use it. The learner has no rule for as if it had happened.
reason: Real gap, smaller than claimed: 7 of the 12 rows are the anterior form (u41-0280, u43-0085), and 5 are just *hubiera* of *hay* (u40-0295). It belongs as a new line in g:pluperfect-subj at u43, not in this u40 rule where *hubiera* + participle is untaught, and the u40 and u41 rows that use it early need review.
quote: *Como si* means *as if*. It describes something that is not true, or not known to be true, so the verb after it is the *ra* form you just learned: *fuera*, *tuviera*, *conocieras*, *pudieran*.

problem: Spanish-language style guides discourage this use as a gallicism. A C1 writer should recognise it but not imitate it in formal prose. The script presents it as neutral.
reason: Press style books do push back: El País has an entry on it, a study reports a Catalan daily rejecting it outright, and an Español urgente column warns against overuse (all via search summaries). I saw no Fundéu text calling it a gallicism and the NGLE and RAE glossary only describe it, so the note is narrowed to newspaper style guides.
quote: Teachers call this the conditional of rumour, or *condicional de rumor*, and in journalism it is a way of reporting without taking responsibility for the claim.
replacement: Teachers call this the conditional of rumour, or *condicional de rumor*, and in journalism it is a way of reporting without taking responsibility for the claim. Many newspaper style guides discourage it, so learn to read it and be careful about writing it.

problem: Tapping the name Ana in the reader shows "anus". Bundle.gloss("Ana") returns es "el ano", en "anus": looseLemma turns final a into o, and l:ano exists. Doña Ana Rita has 20 tokens in the reader (ch214), and the chapter gloss does not cover her. Save word then stores it. The tagger makes the same slip: ch214.lexemes lists l:ano.
reason: Reproduced through the real Bundle: gloss('Ana') returns el ano, anus, with and without ch214 passed in. The fix is code in looseLemma: no a to o guess on a capitalised word or onto a noun.
quote: const cands = [d, d.replace(/(os|as|a|es|s)$/, 'o'), d.replace(/as$/, 'a'), d.replace(/(es|s)$/, ''), d.replace(/(a|as|es)$/, 'e')];
replacement: Do not apply the a to o guess to capitalised words, and do not apply it when the guess is a noun: only adjectives in the graph inflect that way. See also LG-002 and LG-003.

problem: A C1 frequency-list word no lesson needs. It has no bank row, and its only appearance is the false hit in ch214.lexemes, where the tagger read Ana as ano. Keeping it makes every future name in -a one guess away from this gloss.
reason: The gloss is a correct dictionary sense, so the string is not the defect. The false hit comes from looseLemma (LG-001) and the tagger (LG-003), l:ano occurs only in lexemes.json and ch214, and once those two are fixed nothing reaches it.
quote: anus

problem: The chapter is tagged as using the word anus because the tagger read the name Ana as a form of ano. Reading the chapter logs an exposure to that lexeme.
reason: ch214.lexemes does list l:ano, but removing it alone fails the gate: a scratch run reports lexemes differs (+l:ano), because the tagger recomputes it from sentence-initial Ana. Ana must be registered as a name first (castNames reads only storyArc), and then --fix drops the entry.
quote: l:ano
replacement: Remove "l:ano" from the lexemes array, and add proper names to the tagger's skip list.

problem: Names of the main cast gloss as verbs or nouns. Tapping Tomás shows "from tomar, to take (you, present)", which is a voseo reading in a course with no voseo: 1,347 taps in the 219 chapters. Tapping Vale shows "from valer, to be worth": 894. Gloria shows "glory": 347. The chapter gloss rescues a small share of these and only by accident (see LG-005).
reason: Reproduced: Tomás gives tomar, you, present; Vale gives valer; Gloria gives glory. One correction: the Tomás reading is the unaccented tú reading with accentExact false, not voseo, which the target filter removes; the name note still has to go in Bundle.gloss.
quote: const viaVerb = this.verbGloss(word, w);
replacement: Keep a cast list (Tomás, Vale, Gloria, Ana, Simón, Mariana, Hernando and so on) and return a name note for those words before any lemma or verb lookup, when the token is capitalised and not sentence-initial, or is always a name.

problem: A tap on a common word returns the first phrase gloss of the chapter that contains that word anywhere, even when the tapped occurrence is not in that phrase. Tapping de in "tres clases de salsa" (ch046) shows "La última vez gritó gol en un gol de Millonarios". Tapping Y in ch006 shows "And a parrot". Of 87,034 tokens in the 219 chapters, 38,007 return a phrase gloss and 26,198 of those are not at that position, so 30 percent of all taps in the reader show an unrelated sentence. Worst: la 3,361, de 2,707, el 2,061, en 1,324, a 1,306, y 1,288.
reason: Reproduced: de in ch046 returns the Millonarios sentence and Y in ch006 returns And a parrot. A scan of the first 40 chapters found 22.6 percent of tokens landing on a phrase gloss away from that phrase, and gloss() receives no position, so this is a code change.
quote: if (!phrase && toks.includes(w)) phrase = g;
replacement: Pass the tapped word's position, and use a phrase gloss only when that position falls inside an occurrence of the phrase. Otherwise fall through to the single-word path.

problem: There is no lexeme for the articles la, las, los. Tapping them gives lemma lo, "him, it; the thing that is" (los directly, la and las through the a to o guess). The most frequent word in Spanish glosses as "him" whenever the chapter has no phrase to misfire on: la 339, las 522, los 315 taps. Una and unas go to uno, "one", which is merely weak.
reason: Reproduced: la, las and los all return lo, him, it; the thing that is, and the graph has no l:la, l:los, l:las or l:una. This takes new nodes or a closed-class table in Bundle, not a string edit.
quote: him, it; the thing that is
replacement: Add closed-class lexemes: la "the", los "the", las "the", una "a, an", unos and unas "some". Keep l:lo for the pronoun, and give pronoun la and las a second sense only in the chapter gloss.

problem: The loose lookup ignores accents and swaps endings with no check that the two words are related. Real results: calla and callas give "street" (la calle, 20 uses across story and bank); lentes gives "slow"; pera gives "but"; aceras gives "steel"; Cuba gives "bucket"; perdida gives "la pérdida, loss"; mama (in mamar gallo) gives "mom"; carné gives "meat"; dañó and daña give "el daño, damage"; cuántas gives "cuanto, as much as"; cuarta gives "room, bedroom"; dicha gives "saying"; arrienda, odia, engaña, insultó, clavó, choqué, reprocha give the noun. Each one shows as "X from Y", which states a false derivation as fact.
reason: Reproduced for calla, lentes, pera, aceras, Cuba, perdida, mama, carné, dañó, cuarta and dicha: each returns an unrelated lemma as a stated derivation. The fix is code in looseLemma plus new verb lexemes.
quote: const lex = c ? this.plain.get(c) : undefined;
replacement: Remove the accent-blind step and the a to o swap for anything but known adjectives. Showing "No note for this word yet" is better than a wrong derivation. Add a verb lexeme where the noun is catching verb forms: dañar, callar, arrendar, odiar, engañar.

problem: An adjective stored as a noun with an article, so the lexeme card asks for "alleged" and expects "el presunto". The same corruption, pos noun with an adjective gloss: el presunto = alleged; el comunitario = community (adj.); el biológico = biological; el orgánico = organic; el tóxico = toxic; el bendito = blessed; el químico = chemical; el físico = physical; el egoísta = selfish; el apasionado = passionate; el tierno = tender, affectionate; el discreto = discreet. "el físico" means physicist or physique, not "physical". Tapping "la presunta culpable" shows "el presunto".
reason: All twelve nodes are pos noun with an adjective gloss, and tapping presunta shows el presunto. The fix changes es, pos and gender on twelve nodes (egoísta is invariant), so it is more than one string.
quote: el presunto
replacement: presunto, with pos "adj" and no gender. Apply the same to the other eleven.

problem: The course uses the adjective (lo gruesas que son, w-u48-03) but the lexeme is the rare noun "el grueso, width, breadth". Tapping gruesas gives "width, breadth".
reason: Every bank use is the adjective (paredes gruesas, papel grueso) and gruesas glosses as width, breadth. The title repeats the gloss so it changes too; the gate passes once --fix adds g:adjective-agreement to two rows.
quote: width, breadth
replacement: es: grueso | en: thick | title: thick | pos: adj | gender: removed

problem: mono is glossed "overalls" with pos adj, a Spain work-clothes sense that the pos does not even match. No lexeme in the graph means monkey, the sense every learner needs, and l:mono#blond covers Colombian mono.
reason: Overalls is wrong, but monkey is not a safe paste: every course use of mono is the Colombian blond (u41-0682 to u41-0687, ch122), both nodes sit in u41, and Bundle resolves mono to the first node, so Mi sobrino es mono would gloss as monkey. Retire l:mono or make the tap and the u41 day resolve to l:mono#blond; everyday Colombian for monkey is mico (from memory).
quote: overalls
replacement: monkey (es: el mono, pos: noun, gender: m)

problem: Spelling superseded in 2010: guion takes no accent. The bank and chapters already write guion, so the reader shows "guion from el guión", and a lexeme card expects the accented form.
reason: The 2010 Ortografía writes guion without an accent (from memory, the search budget ran out), and this also clears guion from el guión. The claim's premise is only half true: bank and story still have 17 uses of guión against 9 of guion, and those need the same edit.
quote: el guión
replacement: el guion

problem: In Bogotá la inseguridad means street crime and lack of safety. English insecurity reads as an emotion or as food or job insecurity. "There's insecurity in this area at night" (u28-0410) is not English, and sc-u28-d t2 has "there is a lot of insecurity". Eight bank rows in u28 carry the same word: u28-0407 to u28-0412, u28-0961, u28-1079.
reason: The false friend is real: There's insecurity in this area at night is not English. But crime first collides with l:crimen and l:delito, both glossed crime, so the safety sense leads; the title repeats the gloss, and the eight u28 bank rows need their own edits.

problem: States as a rule that negation forces the subjunctive. With negated verbs of seeing and saying both moods are correct and they mean different things: No dijo que era urgente (it was urgent, he failed to mention it) against No dijo que fuera urgente (he made no such claim). The usual meaning of English "I didn't see that she was angry" is the first, so the course steers the learner to the wrong Spanish for what they mean.
reason: The diagnosis is right, but this is the same string as LB2-010, whose fuller version also gives the cases that leave no choice, and applying both would collide.
quote: Put *no* in front and you are no longer vouching, so the verb after *que* switches to the past form that ends in *-ra*: *estaba* becomes *estuviera*, *era* becomes *fuera*, *tenía* becomes *tuviera*, *llegó* becomes *llegara*, *sonó* becomes *sonara*.
replacement: Put *no* in front and you have a choice. If you aren't vouching for the idea at all, the verb after *que* switches to the past form that ends in *-ra*: *estaba* becomes *estuviera*, *era* becomes *fuera*, *tenía* becomes *tuviera*, *llegó* becomes *llegara*, *sonó* becomes *sonara*. If you know it was true and someone just missed it or left it out, keep the ordinary verb: *No dijo que era urgente* means it was urgent and he didn't mention it.

problem: Same over-claim as the rule.
reason: Same over-claim as the rule, and this was the closest wording, changed only to replace 'usually', which sources do not settle. Shared final text with LB1-003, LB2-022 and LC-005.
quote: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it takes the indicative.
replacement: *No dudo que* is certainty, so the indicative is the natural choice, but the subjunctive is also correct, especially when you grant a point before a *pero*.

problem: The test fails on the future. "While you're in Bogotá next week, come and see me" is plainly while, and Spanish needs the subjunctive: Mientras estés en Bogotá, ven a verme. Mientras follows the same future rule as cuando (u32), and the test tells the learner the opposite.
reason: *Mientras* about a time still to come takes the subjunctive even when it means while, like *cuando* at u32 (Butt and Benjamin and NGLE from memory), so the test does give the wrong answer. The replacement is correct and fits LB2-034.
quote: Test: can you say "while" in English? Ordinary verb. Does "as long as" fit better? Wish form.
replacement: Test: does "as long as" fit? Wish form. Does "while" fit, about now, about every day or about the past? Ordinary verb. A "while" about a time still to come works like *cuando*, so it takes the wish form too: *Mientras estés en Bogotá, ven a verme.*

problem: "English says even if it will rain" is false about English and contradicts x:si-clause-no-future ("Nobody says if it will rain"). The learner loses the helpful parallel.
reason: Even if it will rain is not what English says, and it contradicts x:si-clause-no-future, so the claim holds. The claim quoted a whole JSON object; only the why string changes, so quote and replacement are narrowed to it with the same new text.
quote: Almost. English says even if it will rain, but after *aunque* a possible event takes the present subjunctive, not a future.
replacement: Almost. English says even if it rains, with no will in it, and Spanish doesn't use the future here either: a possible event takes the present subjunctive.

problem: The test fails on the script's own example: Les pregunté la hora is "I asked them the time", and English cannot say "asked the time to them". It also fails on everyday le with for and from (le compré flores, le robaron el celular), so learners who trust it write *la pregunté.
reason: The test fails on the script's own Les pregunté la hora, so it needs fixing. Changed the time to a question in the replacement, because in that sentence the time comes from them and it is the question that goes to them, which keeps the test honest at A1.
quote: And there's a quick test: if English could add to (gave the keys to him, told the truth to her), it's *le*.
replacement: And there's a quick test: if something passes to the person (the keys, the truth, a question), or English could add to (I wrote to him), it's *le*.

problem: The first test fails on the rule's own third case: "Thanks for to come" is not English, yet the answer is venir. The second gives the wrong answer on "I'm going to Medellín tomorrow", which x:present-progressive teaches on the same day as plain present.
reason: Both tests fail as claimed: Thanks for to come is not English, and am, is, are wrongly catches I'm going to Medellín tomorrow, taught the same day in x:present-progressive. The new test works on every case in the script; the only change is "it" and "that" in quotation marks, matching "to" in this rule, because asterisks here mark Spanish.
quote: A quick test: can you put "to" in front instead? I like to cook works, so *cocinar*. Is there an am, is or are in front? Then it's *estoy*, *está* and so on, plus *-ando*.
replacement: A quick test: can you swap the -ing word for "it" or "that"? I like cooking, I like it: it's an activity, so *cocinar*. Thanks for coming, thanks for that: *venir*. Is someone in the middle of doing it right now? Then it's *estoy*, *está* and so on, plus *-ando*.

problem: There is a third job with no warning anywhere in 916 scripts: -ing as a describing word (a boring class, an interesting idea). The matcher answers *un libro aburriendo with "Check the spelling."
reason: No script warns about -ing adjectives, Es un libro aburriendo does get Check the spelling (probe run), and aburrido is known from u02. Added *-iendo* because the very error in question, aburriendo, is not an *-ando* form; the bank has no adjectival gerund such as agua hirviendo, so never does not clash at this level.
quote: English uses -ing for two very different jobs. Spanish gives each one its own form.
replacement: English uses -ing for two very different jobs. Spanish gives each one its own form. (A third -ing never takes *-ando* or *-iendo*: a describing word. A boring class is *una clase aburrida*.)

problem: x:muy-mucho says to use muy before a describing word, so *muy mejor follows from the rule, and nothing corrects it. The only mucho mejor in any script is an unexplained example at u35.
reason: Muy before mejor is ungrammatical (DPD s.v. mucho and muy, from memory), and x:muy-mucho at u07 tells learners to use muy before a describing word, so the slip is invited. Mucho is known by u11 and the addition is short.
quote: Two words skip *más*: *mejor* (better) and *peor* (worse). Say *mejor*, not *más bueno*.
replacement: Two words skip *más*: *mejor* (better) and *peor* (worse). Say *mejor*, not *más bueno*. And much better is *mucho mejor*, never *muy mejor*.

problem: x:tener-que-deber taught "you must not" as no debes seven units earlier. Está prohibido que + tú is notice language; said to a guest's face it is stilted, and the common form is Está prohibido fumar, with an infinitive, which this script never shows.
reason: The register point holds: x:tener-que-deber already gave no debes for you must not, and está prohibido que with tú sounds like a notice. But the proposed text drops "You mustn't", which is the English trap this paragraph exists for and which pitfalls[1] still names, so that wording is kept and the register note added to it.
quote: Watch the English trap. "You don't have to" is *no hace falta*. "You mustn't" is *está prohibido*.
replacement: Watch the English trap. "You don't have to" is *no hace falta*. "You mustn't" is *está prohibido*, which sounds like a sign on the wall. Face to face, *no puedes* or *no debes* is more natural.

problem: p:hay-que-tener-en-cuenta (u45) says the opposite: add no and it means "we shouldn't". Both happen and context decides (No hay que perder la calma = we mustn't). Since the course makes "don't have to" against "mustn't" a headline English trap, stating two opposite rules for no hay que undoes it.
reason: Right that u35 and p:hay-que-tener-en-cuenta state opposite absolutes. *Usually* is unproven, so this takes the LC-013 text and quote; the u45 line saying *no* makes it "we shouldn't" needs a matching softening outside this batch.
quote: *No hay que pagar* says there's no need to.
replacement: *No hay que pagar* says there's no need to. With a warning it can also mean you mustn't: *No hay que perder la esperanza.* Context decides.

problem: Contradicts g:impersonal-obligation, which says no hay que means there is no need.
reason: No hay que covers both readings: no hay que subestimar is must not and no hay que ser millonario is need not (SpanishDict examples; NGLE from memory). The old line says only one, against g:impersonal-obligation's *No hay que pagar* says there's no need to, and the replacement is true of both.
quote: Add *no* in front and it means "we shouldn't": *no hay que tener en cuenta los rumores*.
replacement: Add *no* in front and it can mean "there's no need" or "we shouldn't", depending on the context: *no hay que tener en cuenta los rumores*.

problem: "Even if the coming is still in the future" states the rule exactly where it is weakest. Present subjunctive after a past main verb, when the event is still ahead or still relevant, is widespread in Latin American Spanish (Le dije que venga mañana). A learner in Bogotá will hear it daily. Note quería here can also be the softened present.
reason: The old why is too absolute: over half of Peruvian tweets used present under past, and one dissertation reports 30% in Argentina, 6% in Mexico and 3% in Spain, with Quería que me ayudes as its example. No source covers Colombia, so the amended text says parts of Latin America, keeps the -ra rule firm for production, and narrows the quote to the why string.
quote: A past first verb needs the *-ra* form after it, even if the coming is still in the future.
replacement: After a past first verb, use the *-ra* form. In parts of Latin America you'll also hear *vengas* when the coming is still ahead, but *vinieras* is always right.

problem: Marks as simply wrong a form that is normal in the course's own dialect, where the request still holds.
reason: Same evidence as CX-019: the Peruvian pattern is conditioned by whether the action can still continue, exactly this case, so griten is not simply wrong, yet Colombian frequency is unproven. The amended text drops in Colombia, keeps gritaran as the production form, and narrows the quote to the why string.
quote: *Pedí* is past, so *gritaran* follows it.
replacement: *Pedí* is past, so use *gritaran*. In parts of Latin America you'll also hear *griten* when the request still stands.

problem: Cuál + noun (¿Cuál libro quieres?, ¿Cuáles documentos?) is normal across much of Latin America, Colombia included, and is not an error. In a course whose dialect is Latin American, the rule teaches learners to hear local speech as wrong and the checker rejects it. Qué remains the safe default.
reason: Duplicate of LA2-016 on the same string. The substance stands and LA2-016 carries it, so nothing else changes here.
quote: Right before a noun, use *qué*: *¿Qué documentos?*, *¿Qué color?* Here *qué* means both what and which.
replacement: Right before a noun, use *qué*: *¿Qué documentos?*, *¿Qué color?* Here *qué* means both what and which. (In Colombia you'll also hear *¿Cuál color?* and *¿Cuáles documentos?*. That's fine, but *qué* works everywhere.)

problem: The real error in the wrong form is the singular cuál, not cuál before a noun. The why teaches a false prohibition.
reason: Duplicate of LA2-017 on the same why; the claim's quote was a JSON object, so it is corrected to the why string. Nothing else changes.
quote: Right before a noun, Spanish uses *qué*, even when English could say which.
replacement: {"wrong": "¿Cuál documentos necesito?", "right": "¿Qué documentos necesito?", "why": "Almost. *Cuál* has to match the plural: *¿Cuáles documentos?* But right before a noun, *qué* is the safest choice everywhere: *¿Qué documentos necesito?*"}

problem: Al firmar, se fue is correct, natural Spanish: on signing, he left. Al + infinitive covers immediate sequence (Al llegar a casa, se acostó) as well as overlap. Tras + infinitive is the formal, written form; everyday Spanish says después de firmar, which the script only mentions in passing.
reason: Right that Al firmar, se fue is good Spanish, but Tras firmando only repeats pitfalls[1] and drops the al versus tras contrast this drill exists for. Aligned to the LB2-081 text, so only one edit lands; the quote was inexact only because the object spans several lines.
quote: Al firmar, se fue.
replacement: {"wrong": "Al almorzar, volvió a la oficina.", "right": "Tras almorzar, volvió a la oficina.", "why": "Almost. Lunch takes a while, so *al* puts going back in the middle of it. For one thing and then the next, use *tras*."}

problem: The model breaks in the same unit: es posible que and es probable que can lean yes and still take the subjunctive, and x:impresion-vs-no-estoy-seguro later says "a doubt does not lean". The reusable model is whether the speaker puts the idea forward as true.
reason: The leaning model breaks on es posible que llegue, met the day before in g:subj-doubt, and on x:impresion-vs-no-estoy-seguro (A doubt does not lean), so the assertion model is the right fix. Reworded to g:subj-doubt's own phrase, putting it on the table, so the two neighbouring lessons use one image.
quote: So the choice is not about how sure you are, it is about which way you lean. Leaning yes: plain verb. Leaning no: wish form.
replacement: So the choice is not about how sure you are, it is about what you are doing with the idea. Putting it on the table as what you believe: plain verb. Not putting it on the table: wish form. That's why *es posible que llegue* takes the wish form too, even when it may well happen.

problem: In Colombia me da pena very often means I'm embarrassed. The bank uses it that way (u34-1029, u22-0369), and p:me-da-pena-que notes it, but this contrast, set in Bogotá, presents sadness as the whole story.
reason: In Colombia pena often means embarrassment (Caro y Cuervo linguist quoted in Infobae; press and learner sources), and the bank uses it that way at u34-1029 and u22-0369. The note is short, true, and agrees with p:me-da-pena-que two days earlier.
quote: *Me da pena que...* is sadness: a loss, a pity, something you wish were different.
replacement: *Me da pena que...* is sadness: a loss, a pity, something you wish were different. (In Colombia *pena* can also mean embarrassment, so the context matters.)

problem: Nowhere does the course warn that me gusta about a person means attraction: "me gustas" and "te gusto" appear in 0 scripts and 0 bank sentences. The natural English transfer of "I like you / I like Hernando" is exactly this. The line also over-claims: the bank itself has La aguapanela me cae bien en el estómago (u15-1008).
reason: The omission is real: me gustas appears nowhere, and learner references agree it reads as attraction. Usually replaces the flat means because u03 has rows such as Me gusta Vale. = I like Vale.; the quote is narrowed to this sentence so it and LA2-008 do not overlap.
quote: *Me cae bien* is for people.
replacement: For people, use *me cae bien*: *me gusta* about a person usually means you find them attractive, and *Me gustas* says exactly that.

problem: Bank sentence u15-1008 uses the construction with food correctly, so the flat "is for people" is contradicted by the course.
reason: Same pitfall and same fix as LA2-009, which carries the final text, so this is refuted only to avoid a clashing edit. The quote matches once decoded.
quote: {"wrong": "Me cae bien el café.", "right": "Me gusta el café.", "why": "*Me cae bien* is for people. For food and things, use *me gusta*."}
replacement: {"wrong": "Me cae bien el café.", "right": "Me gusta el café.", "why": "About food, *me cae bien* only means it agrees with your stomach. To say you like it, use *me gusta*."}

problem: The preterite for an earlier event in a relative clause is correct and common in Latin America. It is a style point, not an error.
reason: Same text as LB1-073, which I confirmed, so this is refuted as a duplicate to avoid two edits on one field. The fact is right, but "Not wrong in speech" reads badly under a struck-through line, and its quote was a JSON fragment, not a source string.
quote: He found the box before he opened it, so the earlier event takes *había*.
replacement: {"wrong": "Tomás abrió la caja que encontró y vio una carta.", "right": "Tomás abrió la caja que había encontrado y vio una carta.", "why": "Not wrong in speech, but the order gets lost. He found the box before he opened it, and *había* makes that clear."}

problem: The sentence is grammatical. Labelling it wrong over-teaches; the learning point is preference for the present.
reason: Duplicate of LA2-040, which carries the fix, and its added claim that the perfect 'can sound as if the living is over' is unsupported, because the perfect here reaches up to now. The claim's quote was a JSON object, so it is corrected to the why string.
quote: Close. English asks how long have you lived, but Spanish asks with the present: *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que vives…?*
replacement: {"wrong": "¿Cuánto tiempo has vivido aquí?", "right": "¿Cuánto tiempo hace que vives aquí?", "why": "Not wrong, and you'll hear it, but it can sound as if the living is over. If you still live here, Spanish asks with the present: *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que vives…?*"}

problem: x:tener-que-deber later teaches debo as must and deberías as should. In the same script the pitfall glosses no debes as "you mustn't". English speakers map must and should firmly, so one form with two glosses across the course leaves them guessing.
reason: Right on the problem, but it has the same quote as LA1-027, which carries the fix; refuted to prevent a double edit. The duty word is also the weaker wording, because this script's hook gives your duties to tener que and good advice to deber.
quote: *deber*: should, the advice word. *Debes ir al médico.*
replacement: *deber*: must or should, the duty word. *Debes ir al médico.*

problem: Nobody says Los platos fueron lavados por Vale in a kitchen; everyday Spanish says Vale lavó los platos. Overuse of the ser passive is one of the most persistent English-speaker faults, and this prompt asks for it in the one register where it is wrong. g:passive-ser rightly calls it "the news voice" and g:passive-se warns against it, so this contrast undoes both.
reason: The prompt asks for a news-voice passive in the one setting where nobody uses it, undoing g:passive-ser (the news voice). The replacement moves it to a building, and *fue construido* is in that node's title; the dishes example and exercise elsewhere in the script are a separate matter and this claim does not touch them.
quote: Look at your kitchen. Say one thing that is done with *está* or *están* (for example *Los platos están lavados*), then one thing that someone did with *fue* or *fueron*.
replacement: Look at your kitchen. Say one thing that is done with *está* or *están* (for example *Los platos están lavados*). Then think of a building you know and say what happened to it, the way the news would, with *fue* (for example *Fue construido en 1950*).

problem: Equating will with -ré is the central English transfer error here. Most spoken English "I'll" is neither: decisions on the spot and offers take the plain present (Te llamo luego, Yo pago, ¿Te ayudo?), which the bank uses from u08 without any rule. Nothing states this until "mañana viajo" at C1 (u52). The matcher makes it worse: 0 of 44 bank sentences with I'll + -ré accept voy a.
reason: Same string as LA2-024, which carries the point with the same examples and without the overclaim that most everyday I'll is neither. The missing voy a accepts on I'll rows are real, but that is a data task, not this string.
quote: A rough English guide: *voy a* is going to, and *-ré* is will, said like you mean it.
replacement: A rough English guide: *voy a* is going to, and *-ré* is will, said like you mean it. But most everyday English I'll is neither. A decision on the spot or an offer takes the plain present: *Te llamo luego.* I'll call you later. *Yo pago.* I'll pay. *¿Te ayudo?* Shall I help you?

problem: English would has three Spanish translations and only two are taught. "He wouldn't sign" (refused) is No quiso firmar, and a learner will write No firmaría or No firmaba. The bank uses it (u31-0054) but no script explains it.
reason: Right in substance, but it edits the same sentence as LA2-026, whose final list already includes wouldn't as refused: *no quiso firmar*. Nothing to apply here.
quote: One trap: when English would means used to (we would go every Sunday), Spanish uses the past habit form: *íbamos*.
replacement: One trap: when English would means used to (we would go every Sunday), Spanish uses the past habit form: *íbamos*. A second trap: when English wouldn't means refused (he wouldn't sign), Spanish uses the past of *querer*: *No quiso firmar*.

problem: This one line is the only teaching in the course of the meaning shifts in the preterite. English "knew", "met", "wanted" and "could" do not map one to one: supe is found out, conocí is met, no quise is refused, pude is managed. The bank uses all of them from u06 with the right English (u06-0102 Ayer supe la verdad = found out), so a learner sees the shift and is never told it. Also missing: "could" of past ability (podía, sabía) against managed (pude).
reason: Right on substance, but LC-027 rewrites the same sentence and its second-review text in second-02 already carries supe, conocí and no quise. Both replacements keep the quoted sentence, so applying this as well would print the note twice; past-ability could (podía, sabía) cannot go here either, since only era, estaba, tenía and había are in by u06.
quote: *No pude* is more than I couldn't: it means I tried and it didn't happen.
replacement: *No pude* is more than I couldn't: it means I tried and it didn't happen. A few verbs shift like this in this past. *No quise ir* is I refused to go, *conocí a Vale* is I met Vale, and *supe la verdad* is I found out the truth.

problem: Convertirse en, the normal verb for "turn into" with a noun, is in 0 of 916 scripts, though the bank has convertir from u12. "Become" is a named trouble spot and the list in both g:verbs-of-change and x:hacerse-llegar-a-ser leaves out the commonest noun case.
reason: Grep confirms convertirse is in 0 of 916 scripts, while u30-0557, u30-0566 and u30-0610 drill se convirtió en under this very node, so the count must rise with CX-036. Standard description of verbs of becoming; Butt and Benjamin ch. 27 cited from memory.
quote: Where English has one word, Spanish has four, and each says how the change happened:
replacement: Where English has one word, Spanish has five, and each says how the change happened:

problem: See the previous claim: add the fifth verb here.
reason: La casa se convirtió en un café is natural, echoes u12-0956, and the -ió stem change is met at u11. One knock-on: the smallPrint line "Each one takes a describing word or a noun straight after it" is no longer true of convertirse en and needs a small edit alongside this.
quote: *Hacerse* + a job or status: you worked for it. *Quiere hacerse famosa.*
replacement:
*Hacerse* + a job or status: you worked for it. *Quiere hacerse famosa.*
*Convertirse en* + a noun: it turned into something else. *La casa se convirtió en un café.*

problem: tengo calor is taught as "I'm hot", and the English transfer is estoy caliente, which means aroused in Colombia and everywhere else. No script warns of it, though p:bien-mal-vs-bueno-malo sets the precedent by warning about estoy bueno. The matcher only says "estoy" isn't the word here.
reason: No script warns of this, and the warning is safe in any variety: learner references report the sexual reading across most of the Spanish-speaking world, and tengo calor is the only way to say it, though I found no Colombia-specific source. The claim's insertion cut Think of it away from tener, so the warning moves to the end.
quote: So never *estoy hambre*. Think of it as carrying the feeling around for a while.
replacement: So never *estoy hambre*. Think of it as carrying the feeling around for a while. And never *estoy caliente* for I'm hot: that says you're aroused.

problem: The node title promises "por for time", but the rule gives only rate, means and swap. The commonest English use of "for", a stretch of time, is taught nowhere as a por or para question. Learners will write para dos horas. Spanish often needs no word at all.
reason: The title promises por for time and the bank uses it from u18 (u18-0466), yet no por-para script teaches it and p:durar-durante covers only durar and durante. Examples lower-cased to match the list; follow-up: the closing line and smallPrint should gain length of time.
quote: *a swap*: *lo cambié por otro*, trading one thing for another
replacement:
*a swap*: *lo cambié por otro*, trading one thing for another
*how long*, where English says for: *trabajé ahí por dos años*. Often Spanish needs no word at all: *estudié dos horas*. Not *para*.

problem: "Always" is false. After verbs of going and coming the goal is very often a: Fui al mercado a comprar fruta, Vine a hablar contigo, and the bank does this (u05-0843, u09-0364, u34-0161). The owner asked for this check by name. The false rule is enforced: 0 of 14 bank sentences with motion + para + infinitive accept a + infinitive, and the reverse also fails, so "Voy al parque para caminar un rato" gets "para" isn't the word here, check the meaning.
reason: Always is false (NGLE and Butt and Benjamin from memory, the web search budget was used up), but the claim's text only says a is often used, and this same lesson has Tomás vino al café para hablar, so the learner cannot tell whether para is now wrong; this text says both work and names the verbs. It must ship with yourTurn[4] accept gaining Tomás vino al café a hablar con Vale., which matchTranslation fails today, plus the two-way accept on the bank rows.
quote: English uses plain to for goals (to send, to live). In Spanish that to is always *para*.
replacement: English uses plain to for goals (to send, to live). In Spanish that to is usually *para*. After *ir* and *venir* you can use *para* or *a*, and *a* is the everyday choice: *Fui al mercado a comprar fruta.* *Vine a hablar contigo.*

problem: Treated as a transparent cognate and never carded, but "introduce someone" is presentar. Introducir a una persona is a classic English-speaker error.
reason: The false friend is real and unwarned: no script mentions introducir, and p:te-presento-a never says not to use it. But this note is not learner-facing and is read by code (tools/vocab/retime.ts and report.ts test startsWith('receptive')), so the swap teaches nothing and silently moves the word out of the refill pool; the fix is a card plus a pitfall in p:te-presento-a, and the gloss to introduce needs narrowing.
quote: receptive: met in reading from u35, not carded (cognate)
replacement: false friend: *introducir* is to put in or bring in; to introduce a person is *presentar*. Teach it, do not treat it as a cognate.

problem: Treated as a transparent cognate, but atender is to serve or look after; "attend a meeting" is asistir a. The matcher says only "atendí" isn't the word here.
reason: Real gap: p:asistir-faltar gives asistir a for attend and warns against assist, but nothing warns against atender, and no bank row targets l:atender. As with CX-040, the note is a machine-read build tag (startsWith('receptive')), so replacing it teaches nothing and changes tooling; the fix is a card plus a pitfall in p:asistir-faltar.
quote: receptive: met in reading from u33, not carded (cognate)
replacement: false friend: *atender* is to serve or deal with; to attend a meeting is *asistir a*. Teach it, do not treat it as a cognate.

problem: English "ran out into" is satellite-framed; Spanish puts the path in the verb and the manner in a gerund. Corrió a la calle is a word-for-word English frame and is the one calque of this kind found in 153 reviewed motion sentences; the rest of the bank gets it right (u31-0527, u40-0025, u46-0039).
reason: The Spanish is not a calque (corrió a + goal is ordinary, as in u12-0604 Corrí al banco), and the proposed salió corriendo breaks the sequence, since manner gerunds arrive with g:gerund-ways at u26. The real defect is the English, which adds out into, so that is what changes.
quote: The man ran out into the dark street.
replacement: The man ran to the dark street.

problem: One form has at least seven names: wish form (74 scripts), opposite vowel, other vowel, "opposite" ending, changed ending or changed verb, "maybe" form, and subjunctive (51 scripts in body text). They switch between neighbouring contrasts (x:creo-no-creo wish form; x:cuando-ind-subj other vowel; x:impresion-vs-no-estoy-seguro "maybe" form; x:decir-que-ind-subj "opposite" ending). "Wish form" is also false for its largest uses: me alegra que estés, no creo que venga, cuando llegues and aunque llueva are not wishes. The learner never gets one name and one model to reuse, and cannot search look-up for it.
reason: Confirmed by grep: wish form in 72 scripts, plus other or opposite vowel (6), changed ending or verb (14), "maybe" form (3) and "opposite" ending (3), switching between neighbouring contrasts such as x:creo-no-creo and x:cuando-ind-subj. Choosing one label is an owner decision that spans about 90 scripts, not a string; replacements in this batch keep wish form until then.
quote: wish form

problem: One hint serves four different contrasts. For El café es en La Candelaria and La fiesta está en mi casa it offers the wrong model: location and events are neither "what it is" nor "how it is right now". It also fires for Era lloviendo.
